bio_edx.4.0.summary: The World Health Organization defines health as **a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity**. Diseases are either **communicable** (caused by pathogens and able to spread between people or organisms) or **non-communicable** (not caused by pathogens and not passed on). Having one disease can make a person more likely to catch or develop others, because it can weaken the immune system or the body as a whole; the classic example is HIV making people far more likely to develop tuberculosis.

core.p: Health is much more than not being ill. The **World Health Organization (WHO)** definition is one you should learn word for word because mark schemes reward its exact wording.
bullets: Health = **complete physical, mental and social well-being**.
It is **not merely the absence of disease or infirmity**.
A person with no disease can still be unhealthy, for example if they are very stressed or isolated.
A person with a controlled disease, such as well-managed diabetes, may still have good overall well-being.

callouts.p: A state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.
Writing health is not having a disease will score zero. Include all three types of well-being.

core.p: Each part of health affects the others, so a problem in one area often causes problems in another.
bullets: **Physical well-being**: the body working properly, free of illness and injury, with good fitness and diet.
**Mental well-being**: feeling emotionally well, coping with stress, not suffering from conditions such as depression or anxiety.
**Social well-being**: having good relationships, support from friends and family, and being part of a community.
Factors affecting health include diet, exercise, stress, income, housing and access to healthcare.

core.p: A **disease** is a condition that harms the normal functioning of the body or mind. Diseases are sorted by whether or not they can be **passed from one individual to another**.
bullets: **Communicable diseases** can spread between people (or animals or plants).
**Non-communicable diseases** cannot spread from person to person.
The difference depends on the **cause**: pathogens cause communicable diseases.

core.p: A **communicable disease** is caused by a **pathogen** and can be **transmitted** from one organism to another, directly or indirectly.
bullets: **Pathogens** are microorganisms that cause disease: **bacteria, viruses, fungi and protists**.
They can spread through air (droplets), water, food, contact, body fluids or by **vectors** such as mosquitoes.
Examples: **tuberculosis** (bacterium), **cholera** (bacterium), **HIV** (virus), **malaria** (protist), **Chalara ash dieback** (fungus, in trees).
Communicable diseases can be reduced by hygiene, vaccination, treatment and controlling vectors.
They can cause **epidemics** when many people are infected quickly.

callouts.p: A disease caused by a pathogen that can be transmitted from one person or organism to another.
A microorganism that causes disease, such as a bacterium, virus, fungus or protist.

core.p: A **non-communicable disease** is **not caused by a pathogen** and **cannot be transmitted** between people. These diseases usually develop over a long time and have several **risk factors**.
bullets: Examples: **cardiovascular disease**, many **cancers**, **type 2 diabetes**, **liver disease** linked to alcohol, lung disease linked to smoking, **malnutrition**.
Causes and risk factors include **genetics**, **lifestyle** (diet, smoking, alcohol, exercise) and **environment** (pollution, radiation).
They are now the **leading cause of death** worldwide, particularly in higher-income countries.
You cannot catch them from someone else, though families may share genes and lifestyle.

callouts.p: A disease that is not caused by a pathogen and cannot be transmitted from one person to another.
If a non-communicable disease runs in a family, explain it by shared alleles or shared lifestyle, not by infection.

core.p: This comparison is a common 2 to 4 mark question. Always state both sides of each difference.
bullets: Cause: pathogen versus genes, lifestyle and environment.
Spread: transmitted versus not transmitted.
Onset: often quick versus usually slow and long lasting (chronic).
Prevention: hygiene and vaccination versus lifestyle changes and screening.

head: Feature
Communicable
Non-communicable
rows: Not a pathogen: genes, lifestyle, environment

core.h: One disease can increase susceptibility to others
core.p: Diseases rarely act alone. Having one disease can make a person **more susceptible** (more likely to get) other diseases, both communicable and non-communicable.
bullets: A disease that **damages the immune system** means pathogens are not destroyed, so other infections develop more easily.
A disease that weakens the body generally, such as **malnutrition**, reduces the ability to fight infection.
Some **viruses** can trigger changes in cells that lead to **cancer**, for example certain types of HPV and cervical cancer.
Long-term physical illness can lead to **mental illness** such as depression, and poor mental health can reduce physical health.
Immune reactions to the environment can trigger **allergies** and asthma.

callouts.p: How likely a person is to catch or develop a disease.
Weakened immune system, so pathogens are not destroyed, so other infections develop.

core.p: The example Edexcel expects you to know is **HIV increasing the risk of TB**. HIV is a communicable virus; TB is a communicable bacterial disease of the lungs.
bullets: HIV infects and destroys **white blood cells** (lymphocytes) that are part of the **immune system**.
Over time the immune system is weakened so much that the person develops **AIDS**.
With a weakened immune system, the body cannot destroy **Mycobacterium tuberculosis**, the bacterium that causes TB.
TB bacteria may already be present in a **latent (dormant)** form and become active.
So people with HIV are **far more likely to develop TB**, and TB is a leading cause of death in people with HIV.
People with HIV are also more likely to get other **opportunistic infections**.

callouts.p: HIV makes TB more likely by weakening the immune system. TB is still caused by a bacterium.

core.p: Grade 9 answers apply the idea of susceptibility to unfamiliar examples by explaining the **mechanism**.
bullets: **Malnutrition** (a non-communicable disease) lowers immunity, so infections such as measles are more severe.
**Type 2 diabetes** increases the risk of heart disease and of infections in wounds.
**Obesity** increases the risk of cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes.
Smoking-related lung damage makes respiratory infections more likely.
Being ill and unable to work may lead to poverty and isolation, affecting **social and mental** well-being.

callouts.p: If given a new disease, ask: does it weaken immunity, damage an organ, or affect mental or social well-being? Then explain the link.

core.h: Linking physical, mental and social health
core.p: Because health includes three types of well-being, a disease can affect a person in ways beyond the body.
bullets: A person with a long-term illness may become **depressed** or anxious.
Being unable to go out or work can cause **social isolation**.
Stress and poor mental health can lead to poor diet, smoking or drinking, increasing physical disease risk.
Good social support can improve recovery and mental well-being.

core.p: Questions often give graphs or tables of disease rates. Describe the pattern with numbers, then explain it.
bullets: Quote figures with units, for example deaths per 100 000 people.
Distinguish **correlation** from **causation**: a link between two factors does not prove one causes the other.
Compare communicable and non-communicable trends, for example communicable disease deaths falling as sanitation and vaccination improve.
Calculate percentage changes accurately: change divided by original, times 100.

callouts.p: Marks are often lost by describing a trend without quoting any numbers from the graph.

analogy.t: Health as a three-legged stool, the immune system as a castle wall
analogy.p: Health is like a stool with three legs: physical, mental and social well-being. If any one leg is short, the stool wobbles, even if the other two are perfect, which is why not having a disease is not enough to be healthy. For susceptibility, think of the immune system as a castle wall. HIV knocks down the guards and the wall, so other invaders such as TB bacteria get in easily. Where it breaks down: a castle wall stays down once breached, but the body can partly rebuild immunity with treatment (for example antiretroviral drugs for HIV), and non-communicable diseases are not invaders at all.

terms.d: A state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity (WHO).
The United Nations agency responsible for international public health.
A condition that harms the normal functioning of the body or mind.
A disease caused by a pathogen that can be transmitted between individuals.
A disease not caused by a pathogen that cannot be transmitted between individuals.
A disease-causing microorganism: a bacterium, virus, fungus or protist.
An organism that carries a pathogen from one host to another, such as a mosquito.
Something that increases the likelihood of developing a disease, such as smoking.
How likely an individual is to catch or develop a disease.
The body's defence system, including white blood cells, that destroys pathogens.
Human immunodeficiency virus, which destroys white blood cells and weakens the immune system.
Acquired immune deficiency syndrome: the late stage of HIV infection when the immune system is severely damaged.
A communicable lung disease caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
An infection that takes hold because the immune system is weakened.
A condition caused by a diet lacking the right balance of nutrients; a non-communicable disease.
A rapid spread of a communicable disease to many people in an area.

mistakes.w: Health means not having a disease.
mistakes.r: Health is complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.

mistakes.w: Communicable diseases are diseases you can communicate about.
mistakes.r: Communicable diseases are caused by pathogens and can be transmitted between individuals.

mistakes.w: Non-communicable diseases are caused by bacteria that cannot spread.
mistakes.r: Non-communicable diseases are not caused by pathogens; causes include genes, lifestyle and environment.

mistakes.w: HIV causes TB.
mistakes.r: HIV weakens the immune system by destroying white blood cells, so the body cannot fight the TB bacterium; TB is caused by a bacterium.

mistakes.w: Cancer is communicable because it runs in families.
mistakes.r: Families share alleles and lifestyles; cancer is not transmitted by a pathogen (though some viruses increase cancer risk).

mistakes.w: People with HIV get ill because the virus attacks all body cells.
mistakes.r: HIV specifically infects and destroys white blood cells (lymphocytes) of the immune system.

mistakes.w: Susceptible means already infected.
mistakes.r: Susceptible means more likely to catch or develop a disease.

mistakes.w: Mental and social health are not part of biology answers.
mistakes.r: The WHO definition includes mental and social well-being, so they must be included.

exam.q: Give the WHO definition of health.
model: (A state of complete) physical, mental and social well-being.
And not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.
exam.tip: Learn it word for word.

exam.q: What is meant by a communicable disease?
model: A disease caused by a pathogen that can be transmitted / passed from one person or organism to another.
exam.tip: Mention transmission.

exam.q: Which of these is a non-communicable disease? A cholera B tuberculosis C cardiovascular disease D malaria
model: C cardiovascular disease.
exam.tip: The other three are caused by pathogens.

exam.q: Describe two differences between communicable and non-communicable diseases.
model: Communicable are caused by pathogens whereas non-communicable are not.
Communicable can be transmitted between people whereas non-communicable cannot.
exam.tip: Give both sides of each difference.

exam.q: A person has no diseases but is very lonely and stressed. Explain whether this person is healthy using the WHO definition.
model: Not healthy.
Health includes mental and social well-being, not just absence of disease; their mental/social well-being is poor.
exam.tip: Apply the definition to the person described.

exam.q: Name the type of pathogen that causes tuberculosis.
model: Bacterium.
exam.tip: TB: Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

exam.q: Explain why a person infected with HIV is more likely to develop tuberculosis.
model: HIV destroys white blood cells / lymphocytes.
So the immune system is weakened.
So TB bacteria are not destroyed / the body cannot fight the TB infection.
exam.tip: Three linked steps: virus, immune system, TB bacteria.

exam.q: Suggest why people with malnutrition are more likely to suffer from communicable diseases.
model: Lack of nutrients weakens the immune system / fewer white blood cells or antibodies made.
So pathogens are less likely to be destroyed and infections develop.
exam.tip: Apply the same immune system reasoning.

exam.q: Give one example of how a physical disease can affect mental well-being.
model: Long-term illness may cause depression / anxiety / stress.
exam.tip: Link to the WHO definition.

exam.q: Explain how the presence of one disease can lead to a higher susceptibility to other diseases. Use examples in your answer.
model: Some diseases damage the immune system, so pathogens are not destroyed.
Example: HIV destroys white blood cells / lymphocytes.
So people with HIV are more likely to develop TB / other infections.
Malnutrition weakens the immune system so infections are more likely or severe.
Some viral infections can lead to cancer, for example HPV and cervical cancer.
Physical illness can lead to mental illness such as depression, affecting overall well-being.
Some diseases damage organs, for example lung damage making respiratory infections more likely.
exam.tip: Use at least two different examples with the mechanism explained for each.

worked.q: In a country, 2.0 million people have HIV. Of these, 180 000 also developed TB in one year. In the rest of the population of 48 million, 96 000 developed TB. Compare the percentage of each group that developed TB and explain the difference.
steps: 9.0 / 0.2 = 45, so TB is 45 times more common in people with HIV.
Explanation: HIV destroys white blood cells, weakening the immune system, so TB bacteria are not destroyed.
worked.ans: 9.0% compared with 0.2%, about 45 times higher in people with HIV because their immune system is weakened.

worked.q: Classify each disease as communicable or non-communicable and give a reason: cholera, type 2 diabetes, malaria, lung cancer.
steps: Cholera: communicable, caused by a bacterium spread in contaminated water.
Type 2 diabetes: non-communicable, linked to lifestyle and genes, not a pathogen.
Malaria: communicable, caused by a protist carried by mosquitoes (vector).
Lung cancer: non-communicable, linked to risk factors such as smoking; not transmitted.
worked.ans: Communicable: cholera, malaria. Non-communicable: type 2 diabetes, lung cancer.

worked.q: Model answer: A student says a top athlete with depression is healthy because they are physically fit. Evaluate this statement.
steps: The athlete has good physical well-being.
However, the WHO defines health as complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely absence of disease.
Depression means their mental well-being is poor.
Poor mental health may also affect social well-being and physical health, for example sleep and diet.
worked.ans: The statement is wrong: the athlete is not fully healthy because mental well-being is part of health.

bio_edx.4.1.summary: A **pathogen** is a microorganism that causes **communicable (infectious) disease**. Edexcel names four types: **bacteria**, **viruses**, **fungi** and **protists**, and you must link each named disease to its pathogen type, how it damages the host and the signs it causes. The named examples are **cholera** and **tuberculosis** (bacteria), **Chalara ash dieback** (fungus), **malaria** (protist), **HIV** and **Ebola** (viruses) and **stomach ulcers** caused by the bacterium **Helicobacter pylori**.

core.p: A pathogen is any microorganism that causes disease. Diseases caused by pathogens are **communicable**: they can be passed from one organism to another. Pathogens infect animals and plants, and they cause harm in two main ways: by **damaging or destroying host cells**, or by **releasing toxins** (poisons) that harm tissues.
bullets: The four types of pathogen on the spec are **bacteria, viruses, fungi and protists**.
Pathogens need a **host**: they get nutrients and a place to reproduce from the host organism.
Symptoms (signs) of disease are caused by cell damage, toxins, or the body's response to the pathogen.
Because they reproduce quickly, a small number of pathogens can become millions inside a host in hours or days.
Not all microorganisms are pathogens: many bacteria and fungi are harmless or useful (for example gut bacteria and yeast).

callouts.p: A microorganism that causes disease.
A disease caused by a pathogen that can be transmitted from one organism to another.

core.p: Bacteria are **prokaryotic** single-celled organisms: they have **no nucleus**, and their DNA is a loop of chromosomal DNA free in the cytoplasm, plus small rings called **plasmids**. They have a cell wall, cell membrane and cytoplasm, and some have a flagellum. Pathogenic bacteria reproduce rapidly by dividing in two inside the body and many **release toxins** that damage cells and tissues.
bullets: Size: roughly 1 to 5 micrometres, much smaller than human cells but much bigger than viruses.
Under ideal conditions some bacteria can divide every 20 minutes, so numbers grow exponentially.
Harm is caused mainly by **toxins** and by damaging tissue as the population grows.
Named bacterial diseases: **cholera**, **tuberculosis (TB)** and **stomach ulcers** (Helicobacter pylori). Chlamydia (5.8) is also bacterial.
Bacterial infections can be treated with **antibiotics** (see 5.16), unlike viral infections.

callouts.p: Bacteria have no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria.

core.p: Viruses are **not cells**. A virus is a small piece of **genetic material (DNA or RNA) inside a protein coat**. Viruses cannot reproduce on their own: they must **invade a host cell** and use the cell's machinery to make copies of themselves. The new viruses then burst out, **destroying the host cell**, and go on to infect more cells.
bullets: Viruses are far smaller than bacteria (around 20 to 300 nanometres).
Every type of organism, including bacteria and plants, can be infected by viruses.
Damage comes from host cells being **destroyed** as new viruses are released.
Named viral diseases: **HIV** and **Ebola** (also influenza, measles and many others outside the spec list).
**Antibiotics do not work on viruses**: viruses have no cell wall or bacterial ribosomes for an antibiotic to target, and they live inside our own cells.
Triple Biology (5.7B) covers how viruses replicate by the lytic and lysogenic pathways.

callouts.p: Never describe a virus as a cell or say it has a nucleus, cytoplasm or cell membrane.

core.p: Fungi are **eukaryotic** organisms. Some are single-celled (yeasts) but most pathogenic fungi grow as a network of thread-like **hyphae** that penetrate tissues. Fungi have cell walls made of **chitin** and reproduce by producing huge numbers of **spores**, which are spread by wind, water or contact.
bullets: Hyphae grow into host tissue and digest it, absorbing nutrients.
Spores are tiny and light, so they can travel long distances in the air.
Named fungal disease: **Chalara ash dieback** in ash trees.
Other examples outside the spec list include athlete's foot in humans and rusts in plants.

core.p: Protists are **single-celled eukaryotic** organisms (their cell has a nucleus). Some are pathogens and many are **parasites**, living in or on a host and harming it. Pathogenic protists are often transferred by a **vector**: an organism that carries the pathogen from one host to another without itself getting the disease.
bullets: The named protist disease is **malaria**, caused by **Plasmodium**.
The vector for malaria is the female **Anopheles mosquito**.
Protists are bigger and more complex than bacteria because they are eukaryotic.
Because protists are eukaryotic, like our own cells, they are harder to target with drugs that do not also harm human cells.

callouts.p: An organism that carries a pathogen from one host to another.

core.h: Comparing the four types of pathogen
core.p: Many exam questions ask you to compare pathogen types. Focus on whether they are cells, whether they have a nucleus, how they reproduce and how they cause harm.
bullets: Only viruses are **non-cellular**.
Only bacteria are **prokaryotic** among the cellular pathogens.
Fungi and protists are both **eukaryotic**.
Size order (smallest to largest): virus < bacterium < protist (fungal hyphae can be very long).

head: Feature
Bacteria
Viruses
Fungi
Protists
rows: Damage cells, e.g. red blood cells

core.p: Cholera is caused by the bacterium **Vibrio cholerae**. It is spread in **water contaminated with sewage** (faeces of infected people). The bacteria grow in the small intestine and release a **toxin** that makes the intestine lining secrete large amounts of water and salts into the gut.
bullets: Sign: severe **watery diarrhoea**.
This leads to rapid **dehydration** and loss of salts, which can kill within hours if untreated.
Most common where there is poor sanitation and no clean drinking water, for example after floods, wars or natural disasters.
Link to 5.6: prevented by clean water supplies and proper sewage treatment.

callouts.p: Bacterium, spread in contaminated water, toxin causes watery diarrhoea and dehydration.

core.p: Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by the bacterium **Mycobacterium tuberculosis**. It is spread through the air in **droplets** when infected people cough or sneeze. The bacteria infect the lungs and **damage lung tissue**.
bullets: Signs: **lung damage**, a persistent cough (sometimes coughing up blood), fever, weight loss and tiredness.
Spreads most easily in crowded conditions where people share air in close contact.
Can be treated with a long course of antibiotics, but antibiotic-resistant strains exist.
The BCG vaccine gives some protection.

core.p: Many stomach ulcers are caused by the bacterium **Helicobacter pylori**, which can survive in the acidic stomach. It damages the protective lining of the stomach, so acid and enzymes can attack the stomach wall, forming an open sore called an **ulcer**.
bullets: Sign: **stomach pain**; the ulcer can bleed, causing nausea and vomiting.
Spread by **oral transmission**: contaminated food or water, or contact with saliva, vomit or faeces of an infected person.
Treated with **antibiotics** (because it is a bacterium), often with drugs that reduce stomach acid.
This was a surprising discovery: ulcers used to be blamed only on stress and diet.

callouts.p: A stomach ulcer here is caused by a bacterium, so the answer is bacteria, not a virus.

core.p: Chalara ash dieback is a disease of **ash trees** caused by a **fungus** (Hymenoscyphus fraxineus, formerly called Chalara fraxinea). It is spread by **airborne spores** carried on the wind, and over long distances by moving infected young trees.
bullets: Signs: **leaf loss** and **bark lesions** (damaged patches of bark), with dieback of the crown of the tree.
The fungus blocks the water-transport tissue (xylem), so leaves wilt and die.
It can kill the tree, especially young trees.
It was brought into the UK on imported infected ash saplings; import of ash was then restricted.

core.p: Malaria is caused by the protist **Plasmodium**. It is spread by the **Anopheles mosquito**, which acts as a **vector**. When an infected mosquito bites someone, Plasmodium enters the blood and travels to the **liver**, where it multiplies, then invades **red blood cells** and reproduces inside them until they burst.
bullets: Signs: **damage to blood and liver**, causing repeated bouts of **fever** and shaking as red blood cells burst; it can be fatal.
When another mosquito bites an infected person, it takes in the protist and can pass it on.
Malaria is not spread directly from person to person.
Link to 5.6: controlled by stopping the vector, for example mosquito nets and insecticides, and draining standing water where mosquitoes breed.

callouts.p: The pathogen is Plasmodium (a protist). The mosquito is the vector, not the pathogen.

core.p: **HIV** (human immunodeficiency virus) infects and **destroys white blood cells** (lymphocytes) of the immune system. Over time this weakens the immune system so much that the person develops **AIDS**, and they then die from other infections or cancers that the body can no longer fight. **Ebola** is a virus that causes **haemorrhagic fever**: it damages blood vessels so the patient bleeds internally and externally, and it is often fatal.
bullets: HIV is spread by **body fluids**: unprotected sex, sharing needles, blood products, and from mother to baby (see 5.8).
HIV is controlled (not cured) by **antiretroviral drugs**, which stop the virus replicating.
Ebola is spread by **body fluids** (blood, vomit, faeces) of infected people, including from dead bodies.
Ebola sign: **haemorrhagic fever** (fever with internal bleeding).
Ebola outbreaks are controlled by isolating patients, protective clothing for health workers and safe burial.

callouts.p: HIV is the virus. AIDS is the condition that develops when HIV has destroyed enough white blood cells.

core.p: Learn this table: the exam often gives a disease and asks for the pathogen type, the way it spreads or its signs.
bullets: Remember the pattern: **cause, spread, sign**.
If the question asks how the pathogen causes the signs, explain the damage, for example a toxin causing water loss, or cells bursting.

head: Disease
Pathogen type
How it spreads
Signs / effects
rows: Damage to blood and liver, fever
Destroys white blood cells, leads to AIDS

analogy.t: Pathogens as different kinds of burglars
analogy.p: Think of the body as a house. **Bacteria** are burglars who move in, multiply and leave poison (toxins) around. **Viruses** are like hijackers who cannot do anything alone: they take over the house's own factory (a host cell) to build copies of themselves, then wreck the building on the way out. **Fungi** are like roots pushing through the walls (hyphae) and scattering seeds (spores) on the wind. **Protists** are burglars who need a getaway driver (a vector, such as a mosquito) to reach the next house. Where it breaks down: real pathogens are not trying to do anything, they have no intentions; and the house analogy hides that viruses are not living cells at all.

terms.d: A microorganism that causes disease.
A disease caused by a pathogen that can be passed from one organism to another.
The organism a pathogen lives in or on and gets its nutrients from.
A single-celled prokaryotic organism with no nucleus; some are pathogens that release toxins.
Describes a cell with no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles.
Describes a cell whose DNA is enclosed in a nucleus.
A non-cellular particle of genetic material inside a protein coat that can only reproduce inside a host cell.
A eukaryotic organism, often made of thread-like hyphae, that reproduces using spores.
Thread-like structures that make up the body of most fungi and grow into tissues.
A tiny reproductive cell of a fungus that can be spread by wind or water.
A single-celled eukaryotic organism; some are pathogens, such as Plasmodium.
An organism that carries a pathogen from one host to another, such as the mosquito for malaria.
A poisonous substance released by a pathogen that damages tissues.
The protist that causes malaria.
Acquired immune deficiency syndrome: the condition that develops when HIV has destroyed many white blood cells, so the body cannot fight other infections.
A fever with bleeding caused by damage to blood vessels; the sign of Ebola.

mistakes.w: Malaria is caused by a mosquito.
mistakes.r: Malaria is caused by a protist (Plasmodium); the mosquito is the vector that carries it.

mistakes.w: Viruses are very small cells.
mistakes.r: Viruses are not cells; they are genetic material in a protein coat and only reproduce inside host cells.

mistakes.w: Bacteria have a nucleus.
mistakes.r: Bacteria are prokaryotic; their DNA is a loop free in the cytoplasm plus plasmids.

mistakes.w: Antibiotics can cure HIV or Ebola.
mistakes.r: Antibiotics only work against bacteria; HIV and Ebola are viruses.

mistakes.w: HIV and AIDS are the same thing.
mistakes.r: HIV is the virus; AIDS develops later when the immune system has been badly damaged.

mistakes.w: Chalara ash dieback is caused by bacteria.
mistakes.r: It is caused by a fungus, spread by airborne spores.

mistakes.w: Cholera is spread through the air.
mistakes.r: Cholera is spread by water contaminated with sewage; TB is the one spread by airborne droplets.

mistakes.w: Stomach ulcers are caused by stress or a virus.
mistakes.r: Many are caused by the bacterium Helicobacter pylori.

mistakes.w: Viruses release toxins that kill cells.
mistakes.r: Viruses damage the body mainly by reproducing inside cells and bursting (destroying) them; releasing toxins is how bacteria harm.

exam.q: Name the type of pathogen that causes malaria.
model: Protist (Plasmodium).
exam.tip: Do not write mosquito: that is the vector.

exam.q: Name the type of pathogen that causes Chalara ash dieback.
model: Fungus.
exam.tip: Plant disease on this spec point is the fungal one.

exam.q: State two signs of Chalara ash dieback.
model: Leaf loss.
Bark lesions (or dieback of the crown).
exam.tip: Use the spec wording: leaf loss and bark lesions.

exam.q: Describe how cholera causes illness in humans.
model: Vibrio cholerae bacteria release a toxin in the intestine.
This causes watery diarrhoea, leading to dehydration (loss of water and salts).
exam.tip: Mention both the toxin and the watery diarrhoea.

exam.q: Give two differences between the structure of a bacterium and a virus.
model: A bacterium is a cell; a virus is not a cell.
A bacterium has cytoplasm / cell membrane / cell wall / ribosomes; a virus has only a protein coat around genetic material.
A bacterium is larger than a virus.
exam.tip: Each difference must compare both organisms.

exam.q: Explain why HIV infection eventually leads to the death of a patient if it is not treated.
model: HIV infects and destroys white blood cells / lymphocytes.
The immune system is weakened, leading to AIDS.
The body cannot fight other infections (or cancers), which cause death.
exam.tip: The chain is: destroys white blood cells, weak immune system, other infections.

exam.q: Tuberculosis is a communicable disease. State the type of pathogen that causes tuberculosis and describe the damage it causes.
model: Bacterium.
Damages the lungs (lung tissue), causing coughing.
exam.tip: Lung damage is the key phrase.

exam.q: Ebola is caused by a virus. State the main sign of Ebola and how it is spread.
model: Haemorrhagic fever (bleeding / fever).
Contact with body fluids of an infected person.
exam.tip: Learn the phrase haemorrhagic fever.

exam.q: Explain why a doctor would prescribe antibiotics to treat a stomach ulcer but not to treat Ebola.
model: Stomach ulcers are caused by a bacterium (Helicobacter pylori).
Antibiotics kill (or stop the growth of) bacteria.
Ebola is caused by a virus, and antibiotics do not affect viruses.
exam.tip: Name the pathogen type for both diseases.

exam.q: Describe the life cycle of the malaria pathogen, explaining how it causes the signs of the disease.
model: Plasmodium (protist) enters the blood when an infected mosquito bites.
It travels to the liver and multiplies.
It then infects red blood cells, reproduces and bursts them.
This causes damage to blood and liver / fever; a mosquito that bites the infected person picks up the protist and passes it on.
exam.tip: Name the vector, the liver and red blood cells.

exam.q: Compare the structure of bacteria, viruses, fungi and protists and the ways they cause disease.
model: Bacteria are prokaryotic cells with no nucleus, a cell wall and plasmids.
Bacteria cause disease by multiplying and releasing toxins, e.g. cholera toxin causes watery diarrhoea.
Viruses are not cells: genetic material in a protein coat.
Viruses reproduce inside host cells and burst them, e.g. HIV destroys white blood cells.
Fungi are eukaryotic, grow hyphae into tissue and spread by spores, e.g. Chalara ash dieback causes leaf loss and bark lesions.
Protists are single-celled eukaryotes, often spread by a vector, e.g. Plasmodium bursts red blood cells and damages the liver in malaria.
exam.tip: For 6 markers cover all four types with structure, effect and an example.

worked.q: A student says: 'Cholera and tuberculosis are both caused by bacteria, so they spread in the same way.' Evaluate this statement.
steps: Agree with the first part: both are bacterial diseases (Vibrio cholerae and Mycobacterium tuberculosis).
Cholera spreads in water contaminated with sewage.
TB spreads through the air in droplets from coughs and sneezes.
So pathogen type does not decide the route of spread: each pathogen has its own route.
worked.ans: The statement is wrong: although both are bacterial, cholera is waterborne while TB is airborne, so they need different prevention measures.

worked.q: A forest has ash trees with brown, dead leaves and dark patches on their bark. Scientists find thread-like structures in the bark. Identify the disease and pathogen type and explain how it could reach trees several kilometres away.
steps: Leaf loss and bark lesions are the signs of Chalara ash dieback.
Thread-like structures are hyphae, so the pathogen is a fungus.
Fungi produce spores, which are light and carried by the wind.
Spores landing on other ash trees can start new infections far away; moving infected saplings also spreads it.
worked.ans: Chalara ash dieback, caused by a fungus; it spreads long distances as airborne spores (and through moved infected trees).

worked.q: A patient with untreated HIV dies of pneumonia. Explain why the death is linked to HIV even though pneumonia was caused by a different pathogen.
steps: HIV is a virus that infects and destroys white blood cells (lymphocytes).
As white blood cell numbers fall, the immune system can no longer defend the body; the patient has AIDS.
The pneumonia pathogen is normally destroyed by the immune system, but now it is not.
So the pneumonia infection can grow unchecked and kill the patient.
worked.ans: HIV destroyed the white blood cells so the patient developed AIDS and could not fight the pneumonia infection, which then killed them.

bio_edx.4.10.summary: Immunisation (vaccination) gives a person **artificial active immunity** by making their immune system produce **memory lymphocytes** before they ever meet the real pathogen. Its big advantages are protecting the individual and, when enough people are vaccinated, **herd immunity**, which protects people who cannot be vaccinated and can stop epidemics or even **eradicate** a disease such as smallpox. Its disadvantages include **side effects** (usually mild, very rarely a serious allergic reaction), the fact that it does not work for everyone or for every pathogen, the need for **boosters**, and the cost and difficulty of vaccinating whole populations.

core.p: Immunisation means giving a person a vaccine containing an **inactive (dead or weakened) form of a pathogen**, or just its **antigens**. The body treats it like a real infection and makes a specific immune response, but the person does not become ill. This spec point (5.15B) is about weighing up whether this is a good thing, so you need the mechanism in your head first.
bullets: The vaccine contains **antigens** specific to one pathogen.
Specific **lymphocytes** with matching receptors recognise the antigen, divide (clone) and produce **antibodies**.
Some of the lymphocytes become **memory lymphocytes**, which stay in the blood for a long time.
If the real pathogen later enters the body, memory lymphocytes trigger a **secondary response**: faster, bigger and longer-lasting antibody production.
The pathogen is destroyed **before it can cause symptoms**, so the person is **immune**.
Every advantage and disadvantage in this topic comes back to this mechanism.

callouts.p: Giving a vaccine containing an inactive or weakened pathogen (or its antigens) so that the body produces memory lymphocytes, giving immunity to that pathogen.

fig.cap: Antibody levels after vaccination and after later infection. The vaccine causes a small, slow primary response. When the real pathogen arrives, memory lymphocytes give a much faster and larger secondary response that rises above the protective level before symptoms appear.

core.p: The most obvious advantage is that the vaccinated person is very unlikely to catch the disease, or will only get a mild form of it. This matters most for diseases that can kill or cause lifelong damage.
bullets: The person has **memory lymphocytes** ready, so the secondary response destroys the pathogen quickly.
They avoid **symptoms**, complications and possible **death**.
Examples: measles can cause brain damage (encephalitis) and death; polio can cause paralysis; rubella in pregnancy can harm the unborn baby.
Being protected also means less time off school or work.

callouts.p: For full marks do not just write 'they will not get ill'. Write 'memory lymphocytes produce antibodies more rapidly, so the pathogen is destroyed before it causes symptoms'.

core.p: **Herd immunity** is the protection given to unvaccinated people when a large proportion of the population is immune. If most people are immune, a pathogen cannot find enough susceptible people to pass between, so the chain of transmission breaks.
bullets: An infected person mostly meets people who are **immune**, so they pass the pathogen on to **few or no** others.
The pathogen **cannot spread** through the population, so cases die out.
Unvaccinated people are therefore **less likely to come into contact** with an infected person.
This protects people who **cannot** be vaccinated: very young babies, people with weakened immune systems (for example during chemotherapy or with HIV), and people allergic to vaccine ingredients.
It also protects the small number of people for whom the vaccine **did not work**.
The proportion that must be immune depends on how infectious the disease is; for a very infectious disease such as measles it is about **95%**.

callouts.p: When a large proportion of a population is immune to a disease, the spread of the pathogen is greatly reduced, so people who are not immune are also protected because they are unlikely to meet an infected person.

callouts.t: Herd immunity does not make unvaccinated people immune
callouts.p: Unvaccinated people still have no memory lymphocytes. They are protected only because they are unlikely to be exposed to the pathogen.

fig.cap: Herd immunity. Left: with few people vaccinated, an infected person easily passes the pathogen to unvaccinated people and it spreads. Right: when most people are vaccinated, the few unvaccinated people are surrounded by immune people, so the pathogen cannot reach them and the outbreak dies out.

core.p: Because vaccination reduces the number of people who can catch and pass on a disease, large outbreaks become much less likely.
bullets: An **epidemic** is a large outbreak in one area; a **pandemic** is one that spreads across many countries.
Fewer susceptible people means each case causes fewer new cases, so outbreaks stay **small and local**.
Mass vaccination campaigns are used to control outbreaks quickly.
This protects health services from being overwhelmed.

core.p: If vaccination keeps a disease from spreading for long enough worldwide, the pathogen can disappear completely. This is called **eradication**.
bullets: **Smallpox** was declared eradicated in **1980** after a worldwide vaccination programme.
**Polio** has been eliminated from most countries and is close to eradication.
Eradication is only possible for pathogens that infect **only humans** (no animal reservoir) and whose antigens **do not change** much.
Once a disease is eradicated, vaccination against it can **stop**, saving money and removing any side-effect risk.

callouts.p: The only human disease so far completely eradicated, thanks to vaccination.

core.p: Vaccination is usually far cheaper than treating the disease, so it benefits society as well as individuals.
bullets: Fewer people needing **hospital treatment**, saving health service (NHS) money.
Fewer days lost from **work and school**, so less harm to the economy.
Fewer people suffering **long-term disability** that needs care.
Fewer bacterial infections also means **less antibiotic use**, which helps slow antibiotic resistance.

core.p: Vaccines are very safe, but like any medicine they can cause side effects. Most are mild and short-lived because the body is making a real immune response.
bullets: Common: **soreness, redness or swelling** where the injection went in.
Common: a **mild fever**, headache or feeling tired for a day or two.
Rare: a **severe allergic reaction** (anaphylaxis) to the vaccine or an ingredient in it; this is why people are watched for a short time after vaccination.
With a **live (weakened)** vaccine there is a very small risk in people with weak immune systems, so they are not given live vaccines.

callouts.t: A vaccine cannot give you the disease
callouts.p: A vaccine contains an inactive or weakened pathogen, so it cannot cause the full disease in a healthy person. Mild symptoms are the immune response, not the infection.

core.p: A vaccine does not guarantee immunity for everyone or for ever.
bullets: Some people **do not produce enough memory lymphocytes** after vaccination, so they are not protected.
Memory lymphocytes and antibody levels can **fall over time**, so **booster** doses may be needed.
Some vaccines need **several doses**, and people may not complete the course.
Vaccines must be stored correctly (often **cold**); if not, they may stop working.

core.h: Disadvantage 3: pathogens that change or cannot be vaccinated against
core.p: Vaccines only work against the specific antigens they contain. Some pathogens change their antigens, and for some diseases there is no effective vaccine yet.
bullets: Memory lymphocytes are **specific** to one antigen shape.
Viruses such as **influenza** mutate, so their antigens change; old memory lymphocytes no longer recognise them, which is why a **new flu vaccine** is needed each year.
There is **no vaccine for HIV** yet, partly because the virus changes rapidly and attacks the immune system itself.
A vaccine for one strain may give **no protection** against a different strain.

callouts.p: If the antigen on the pathogen changes, the antibodies and memory lymphocytes made after vaccination no longer fit it, so the person is not protected.

core.h: Disadvantage 4: cost, practical and ethical issues
core.p: Vaccinating a whole population is expensive and hard to organise, and not everyone agrees to it.
bullets: Developing, testing, making, transporting and storing vaccines **costs money**; some countries cannot afford them.
Reaching remote areas and keeping vaccines cold (the **cold chain**) is difficult.
Some people refuse vaccines for **religious, ethical or personal** reasons, or because they are worried about side effects.
In the UK vaccination is **voluntary**, so uptake depends on public trust.

core.h: When uptake falls: losing herd immunity
core.p: Herd immunity only works while the proportion of immune people stays above the threshold. If uptake drops, the protection collapses and outbreaks return, which hits the most vulnerable first.
bullets: In **1998** a study (later shown to be wrong and withdrawn) wrongly linked the **MMR** vaccine to autism.
Many parents stopped vaccinating their children, so MMR uptake fell well **below the herd immunity threshold**.
This led to **more cases and outbreaks of measles** in the UK in the following years.
Lesson: the benefit of vaccination to the **population** depends on enough **individuals** choosing to be vaccinated.

callouts.p: In data questions, link a fall in % vaccinated to a rise in cases a few years later, and explain it using loss of herd immunity.

core.p: Exam questions often ask you to **evaluate** immunisation. You must give both sides and then a justified conclusion. For almost all vaccines the benefits far outweigh the risks, because the disease is much more dangerous than the vaccine.
bullets: Compare the **risk from the disease** (e.g. death, disability) with the **risk from the vaccine** (usually mild side effects, very rare serious reactions).
Consider the **individual** and the **population** (herd immunity).
Use any **data** given: percentages vaccinated, number of cases, number of side effects.
Finish with a **conclusion** that says which side is stronger and why.

analogy.p: Think of a population as a forest and an infectious disease as a fire. Each vaccinated person is like a tree that cannot burn. If most trees are fireproof, a spark cannot jump from tree to tree, so the fire dies out, and the few ordinary trees are safe because the flames never reach them. That is herd immunity. Each fireproof tree may get slightly scorched (mild side effects), but far less than burning down. Where it breaks down: trees do not choose to be fireproof, and a vaccinated person's protection can fade over time or fail against a new strain, whereas a fireproof tree stays fireproof. Also, an unprotected tree is never actually made fireproof by its neighbours; it is just never reached.

terms.d: Giving a vaccine so that a person becomes immune to a specific pathogen.
A preparation containing an inactive (dead or weakened) pathogen or its antigens, used to cause immunity.
A molecule (usually a protein) on the surface of a pathogen that is recognised by lymphocytes.
A protein made by lymphocytes that binds to a specific antigen.
A type of white blood cell that produces antibodies.
A lymphocyte that stays in the blood after an immune response and quickly produces antibodies if the same antigen is met again.
The slow, small immune response the first time an antigen is met.
The faster, larger and longer-lasting response when the same antigen is met again, due to memory lymphocytes.
Being able to destroy a pathogen before it causes symptoms.
Protection of non-immune people because a large proportion of the population is immune, so the pathogen cannot spread.
The proportion of a population that must be immune for the spread of a disease to stop (about 95% for measles).
An unwanted effect of a vaccine or medicine, such as soreness or mild fever.
A rare, severe and rapid allergic reaction.
An extra dose of vaccine given later to keep immunity high.
A large outbreak of a disease in one region.
An outbreak of a disease that spreads across many countries.
Complete removal of a disease worldwide, as happened with smallpox.

mistakes.w: The vaccine contains antibodies.
mistakes.r: The vaccine contains an inactive pathogen or its antigens; the person's own lymphocytes make the antibodies.

mistakes.w: Herd immunity means unvaccinated people become immune.
mistakes.r: Unvaccinated people are protected because they are unlikely to come into contact with an infected person; they have no memory lymphocytes.

mistakes.w: Vaccination kills the pathogen in the vaccine.
mistakes.r: The pathogen in the vaccine is already inactive or weakened; vaccination makes memory lymphocytes.

mistakes.w: Memory cells remember the disease.
mistakes.r: Memory lymphocytes recognise the specific antigen and produce antibodies rapidly in a secondary response.

mistakes.w: Herd immunity works if just over half of people are vaccinated.
mistakes.r: A large proportion must be immune; the exact threshold depends on the disease (about 95% for measles).

mistakes.w: The flu vaccine wears off because the virus becomes resistant.
mistakes.r: The flu virus mutates so its antigens change, so memory lymphocytes no longer recognise it; a new vaccine is needed each year.

mistakes.w: A disadvantage is that the vaccine gives you the disease.
mistakes.r: Vaccines can cause mild side effects such as a sore arm or mild fever, and rarely an allergic reaction, but not the full disease.

mistakes.w: Vaccines treat people who already have the disease.
mistakes.r: Vaccines prevent disease by giving immunity before infection; they are not a cure.

exam.q: State what is meant by herd immunity.
model: When a large proportion of the population is immune, so the pathogen cannot spread and non-immune people are protected.
exam.tip: Mention both 'large proportion immune' and 'protects others'.

exam.q: Give two advantages of immunisation.
model: Protects the individual from the disease.
Gives herd immunity / prevents epidemics / can eradicate a disease / reduces cost of treatment.
exam.tip: Two different ideas, not the same one reworded.

exam.q: Give two disadvantages of immunisation.
model: Side effects such as soreness or mild fever / rare allergic reaction.
Not always effective / boosters needed / pathogen may mutate / cost.
exam.tip: 'It hurts' alone is too vague; name a side effect.

exam.q: Explain why a baby too young to be vaccinated can be protected from measles if most people around them are vaccinated.
model: Most people are immune so the measles virus cannot spread / fewer people are infected.
So the baby is less likely to come into contact with an infected person.
exam.tip: This is herd immunity: explain it, the word alone may not score both marks.

exam.q: Explain why people need a new influenza vaccine each year.
model: The influenza virus mutates so its antigens change.
Memory lymphocytes / antibodies from the old vaccine are specific and no longer recognise the new antigens.
exam.tip: Use the word antigen and the idea of specificity.

exam.q: Explain why some people who have been vaccinated still catch the disease.
model: Their immune system did not produce enough memory lymphocytes / the vaccine did not work for them.
Or immunity faded over time / the pathogen was a different strain with different antigens.
exam.tip: Any two valid reasons, each explained.

exam.q: Explain why the vaccination of more than 95% of children against measles protects the whole population.
model: Vaccinated children have memory lymphocytes so are immune.
So few people can be infected and pass the virus on / chain of transmission is broken.
So unvaccinated people are unlikely to meet an infected person (herd immunity).
exam.tip: Build a chain: individual immunity, then reduced spread, then protection of others.

exam.q: In 1998 the number of children receiving the MMR vaccine in the UK fell. Over the next few years the number of measles cases rose. Explain this.
model: Fewer children were immune to measles.
Vaccination rate fell below the level needed for herd immunity.
So the virus could spread between unvaccinated children, causing more cases.
exam.tip: Link the data with the term herd immunity.

exam.q: A vaccine is given to a group of 2000 people. 6 have a severe allergic reaction. Calculate the percentage of people who had a severe reaction.
exam.tip: Show the working; this kind of figure helps you judge risk in an evaluation.

exam.q: Evaluate the use of immunisation to control the spread of disease.
model: Vaccine contains inactive pathogen / antigens, so memory lymphocytes are produced.
On infection, a faster, larger secondary response destroys the pathogen before symptoms.
If a large proportion is vaccinated, herd immunity protects those who cannot be vaccinated (babies, immunocompromised).
Prevents epidemics and can eradicate a disease, e.g. smallpox; reduces cost of treatment.
But side effects such as soreness, fever and rarely severe allergic reaction; not effective in everyone; boosters needed.
Pathogens such as flu mutate so new vaccines are needed; no vaccine for some diseases (HIV); cost and refusal reduce uptake.
Conclusion: benefits outweigh risks because the disease is far more dangerous than the vaccine, provided uptake is high.
exam.tip: An evaluation needs both sides AND a justified conclusion to reach the top level.

worked.q: A town has 24 000 children. 21 840 have had two doses of MMR vaccine. Measles needs about 95% of people to be immune for herd immunity. Has the town reached herd immunity? How many more children would need vaccinating?
steps: Percentage vaccinated = 21 840 / 24 000 x 100 = 91%.
91% is below the 95% threshold, so herd immunity has not been reached.
Children needed for 95% = 0.95 x 24 000 = 22 800.
Extra children needed = 22 800 - 21 840 = 960.
worked.ans: No: only 91% are vaccinated, so 960 more children need vaccinating to reach 95%.

worked.q: A parent says: 'My child does not need the vaccine because everyone else is vaccinated, so herd immunity will protect them.' Explain the problem with this argument.
steps: The child would have no memory lymphocytes, so would not be immune themselves.
Herd immunity only works if a large proportion is vaccinated.
If many parents think the same way, the proportion vaccinated falls below the threshold.
Then the pathogen can spread again and outbreaks return, as happened with measles after MMR uptake fell.
worked.ans: Herd immunity depends on most individuals being vaccinated; if many people opt out it disappears and unvaccinated children are at risk.

bio_edx.4.11.summary: Antibiotics are medicines that **kill bacteria or stop them growing** inside the body. They can do this without harming us because they **inhibit processes or structures found in bacterial cells but not in human (host) cells**, such as the **bacterial cell wall** and the **smaller bacterial ribosomes**. Because viruses have none of these structures and reproduce **inside our own cells**, antibiotics **only treat bacterial infections** and are useless against viral diseases such as colds, flu and HIV.

core.p: An **antibiotic** is a substance that kills bacteria (**bactericidal**) or stops them from growing and dividing (**bacteriostatic**). The first antibiotic, **penicillin**, was discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928 from the mould Penicillium. Antibiotics are used to treat **bacterial infections** such as tuberculosis, cholera, Chlamydia and infected wounds.
bullets: Antibiotics are taken as tablets, by injection or applied to the skin.
They work **inside the body**, unlike antiseptics, which are used on surfaces or skin.
Different antibiotics work in different ways and against different types of bacteria.
The key idea of this spec point: they must harm the **bacterium** but **not the host** (the person).

callouts.p: A substance that kills bacteria or inhibits their growth, by inhibiting cell processes in the bacterium but not in the host organism.

core.p: Antibiotics are **selective**. They target something that bacteria have and need, but that human cells either do not have or have in a different form. So the antibiotic damages bacterial cells while human cells carry on as normal. This is only possible because bacteria are **prokaryotic** cells and human cells are **eukaryotic**, so they are built differently.
bullets: Antibiotics **inhibit cell processes in the bacterium but not in the host organism**: this is the phrase mark schemes reward.
A good target is a structure **only bacteria have** (the cell wall).
Another good target is a structure that is **different in bacteria** (ribosomes, some enzymes).
If a drug hit something identical in both cells, it would harm the patient too.

callouts.p: Antibiotics inhibit cell processes in the bacterium but not the host organism.

core.h: Bacterial cells and human cells compared
core.p: To explain how an antibiotic is selective you must know how bacterial (prokaryotic) cells differ from human (eukaryotic) cells.
bullets: Bacteria have a **cell wall**; human cells have **no cell wall**.
Bacterial ribosomes are **smaller** and a **different shape** from human ribosomes.
Bacteria have **no nucleus**: their DNA is a loop in the cytoplasm, and many have **plasmids**.
Bacteria have no mitochondria; human cells do.
Some bacterial **enzymes** and metabolic pathways do not exist in human cells.

core.p: Many antibiotics, including **penicillin**, stop bacteria from **building their cell walls**. The wall normally stops the cell bursting when water enters by osmosis. Without a strong wall, a growing bacterium takes in water and **bursts**.
bullets: Penicillin **inhibits the enzymes** that make new cell wall.
As the bacterium grows and divides, its wall becomes **weak**.
Water moves into the bacterium by **osmosis** (its cytoplasm is more concentrated).
The weak wall cannot resist the pressure, so the cell **bursts (lyses)** and dies.
Human cells have **no cell wall**, so there is nothing for penicillin to act on: they are **not harmed**.

callouts.p: Antibiotic stops cell wall forming, water enters by osmosis, cell bursts; human cells have no cell wall so are unaffected.

core.h: Target 2: bacterial ribosomes and protein synthesis
core.p: All cells need **ribosomes** to make proteins, including enzymes. Bacterial ribosomes are **smaller and a different shape** from human ribosomes, so some antibiotics (for example **tetracycline** and **streptomycin**) can bind to bacterial ribosomes but not to ours.
bullets: The antibiotic **binds to the bacterial ribosome** because it fits its shape.
This **stops protein synthesis** in the bacterium.
Without new proteins and enzymes, the bacterium **cannot grow, divide or survive**.
Human ribosomes are a **different shape**, so the antibiotic does not bind and our cells keep making proteins.
This is why it is still selective even though both cell types have ribosomes.

callouts.p: Do not say 'human cells do not have ribosomes'. They do; they are just larger and a different shape, so the antibiotic does not affect them.

fig.cap: Some antibiotics bind only to the smaller bacterial ribosome and stop protein synthesis. Human ribosomes are larger and a different shape, so the antibiotic does not bind and the human cell is unharmed.

core.h: Other bacterial processes antibiotics can target
core.p: Some antibiotics block other **enzymes or metabolic pathways** that bacteria need but humans either do not have or have in a different form.
bullets: Blocking bacterial **enzymes** involved in copying bacterial DNA, so bacteria cannot divide.
Blocking a pathway that bacteria use to make a substance they need, which humans get from their diet instead.
The rule is always the same: the target must be **absent or different** in human cells.
At GCSE you only need the general idea and the cell wall or ribosome examples.

core.h: Why antibiotics cannot treat viral infections
core.p: Antibiotics **only work on bacteria**. Viruses are not cells: they have **no cell wall, no ribosomes and no metabolism of their own**. They reproduce **inside host cells**, using the host cell's ribosomes and enzymes to make new viruses.
bullets: There is **no bacterial structure** in a virus for the antibiotic to act on.
The virus uses the **host's own** processes, so anything that stopped the virus this way would also damage the **host cell**.
So antibiotics are **useless** against colds, flu, measles and HIV.
Viral infections are treated with **antiviral drugs** (which are hard to develop) or prevented with vaccines.
Antibiotics are also not effective against fungi or protists in general, because these are eukaryotic like us.

callouts.p: Antibiotics can only be used to treat bacterial infections because they inhibit cell processes in the bacterium but not the host organism. Viruses have no such processes of their own.

fig.cap: Viruses reproduce inside host cells using the host's ribosomes and enzymes. They have no cell wall or ribosomes of their own, so an antibiotic has nothing to target and cannot kill them without harming the host cell.

core.h: Why doctors do not prescribe antibiotics for colds and flu
core.p: Because colds and flu are caused by **viruses**, an antibiotic would do nothing to the infection. Prescribing it anyway is harmful in other ways.
bullets: It would **not cure** the illness.
It would kill some **harmless or useful bacteria** in the body, for example in the gut.
It exposes bacteria to the antibiotic unnecessarily, which increases the chance of **antibiotic resistance** developing.
It wastes money and medicine.

core.p: Not every antibiotic kills every bacterium. Different species have different cell walls and enzymes, so a doctor may need to choose a specific antibiotic.
bullets: **Broad-spectrum** antibiotics act on many types of bacteria.
**Narrow-spectrum** antibiotics act on only a few types.
Testing a sample can show which antibiotic works best on the bacteria causing an infection.
Using the right antibiotic reduces harm to useful bacteria.

core.p: Although antibiotics do not damage human cells directly, they can still cause side effects. Knowing this helps in evaluation questions.
bullets: Killing **useful gut bacteria** can cause diarrhoea or let other microorganisms (such as fungi) overgrow.
Some people have an **allergic reaction**, for example to penicillin.
These effects are not caused by the antibiotic attacking human cell processes, so the principle of selectivity still holds.

core.p: Because antibiotics kill bacteria selectively, they act as a **selection pressure**. A random **mutation** may make a bacterium resistant; it survives and reproduces, so resistant strains such as **MRSA** spread.
bullets: Resistance makes antibiotics stop working, so infections become harder to treat.
To slow it: only prescribe antibiotics for **bacterial** infections, and patients should **complete the course**.
Avoid overusing antibiotics in farming.
This is covered in more detail in evolution (Topic 4), but often appears alongside this point.

callouts.p: It is the bacteria that become resistant, not the person.

analogy.t: A key that only fits one lock
analogy.p: Think of an antibiotic as a key cut to fit a lock found only on bacterial 'houses'. The cell wall is like a door that only bacterial houses have, so penicillin can break that door and the house collapses, while human houses have no such door and are untouched. Ribosomes are like locks that both houses have, but the bacterial lock is a different shape, so the key only turns in the bacterial one. A virus is like a burglar hiding inside a human house and using its rooms: there is no separate bacterial lock to open, so the key is useless. Where it breaks down: a key does not destroy anything by itself, and real antibiotics can sometimes affect useful bacteria in our gut, which an analogy of only 'bad houses' does not show; also bacteria can change their locks through mutation and become resistant.

terms.d: A medicine that kills bacteria or stops their growth by inhibiting processes in the bacterium but not in the host.
Kills bacteria.
Stops bacteria growing and dividing, so the immune system can destroy them.
The organism (for example a human) in which a pathogen lives.
Harming the pathogen without harming the host's cells.
A cell with no nucleus, such as a bacterium; its DNA is free in the cytoplasm.
A cell with a nucleus, such as a human, plant or fungal cell.
A rigid outer layer of a bacterial cell that stops it bursting; human cells do not have one.
The organelle where proteins are made; bacterial ribosomes are smaller than human ones.
The making of proteins at ribosomes.
Net movement of water from a dilute solution to a more concentrated one across a partially permeable membrane.
Bursting of a cell.
The first antibiotic, discovered by Fleming; it stops bacteria building cell walls.
A non-living particle that can only reproduce inside a host cell, using the host's processes.
A drug that acts against viruses; much harder to develop than antibiotics.
When bacteria are no longer killed by an antibiotic, due to a mutation that is then selected for.

mistakes.w: Antibiotics kill viruses.
mistakes.r: Antibiotics only treat bacterial infections; viruses have no cell wall or ribosomes of their own and reproduce inside host cells.

mistakes.w: Antibiotics kill all cells but bacteria are weaker.
mistakes.r: Antibiotics inhibit processes or structures found in bacteria but not in host cells.

mistakes.w: Human cells do not have ribosomes.
mistakes.r: Human ribosomes are larger and a different shape, so the antibiotic does not bind to them.

mistakes.w: Penicillin breaks down the cell membrane.
mistakes.r: Penicillin stops the cell wall being made, so water enters by osmosis and the cell bursts.

mistakes.w: Antibiotics boost the immune system.
mistakes.r: Antibiotics act directly on bacteria; they are not part of the immune response.

mistakes.w: The person becomes resistant to the antibiotic.
mistakes.r: The bacteria become resistant, through mutation and natural selection.

mistakes.w: Antibiotics are used to clean wounds and surfaces.
mistakes.r: That is an antiseptic or disinfectant; antibiotics are medicines that work inside the body.

mistakes.w: Antibiotics kill the cells infected by viruses.
mistakes.r: Antibiotics do not target host cells at all; a virus inside a host cell is unaffected.

exam.q: State what is meant by an antibiotic.
model: A substance that kills bacteria / inhibits the growth of bacteria.
exam.tip: Name bacteria specifically, not 'germs' or 'pathogens'.

exam.q: Explain why antibiotics can be used to treat bacterial infections without harming the patient.
model: Antibiotics inhibit cell processes / structures in bacteria.
That are not present in (or are different in) human / host cells.
exam.tip: Two halves: what happens to bacteria, and why human cells are not affected.

exam.q: Explain why antibiotics cannot be used to treat influenza.
model: Influenza is caused by a virus.
Viruses do not have the cell processes / structures that antibiotics target / they reproduce inside host cells.
exam.tip: Say it is a virus AND why that matters.

exam.q: Penicillin prevents bacteria from making new cell walls. Explain how this kills the bacteria.
model: Cell wall becomes weak as the bacterium grows.
Water enters the bacterium by osmosis.
Cell bursts / lyses.
exam.tip: Use the word osmosis.

exam.q: Explain why penicillin does not damage human cells.
model: Human cells do not have a cell wall.
exam.tip: Short and precise.

exam.q: Tetracycline binds to bacterial ribosomes. Explain how this stops an infection and why human cells are not affected.
model: Stops protein synthesis in the bacteria.
So bacteria cannot make enzymes / grow / divide (and die).
Human ribosomes are a different size / shape.
So tetracycline does not bind to human ribosomes / human protein synthesis continues.
exam.tip: Two marks for the effect on bacteria, two for why humans are unaffected.

exam.q: Give one structure found in a bacterial cell but not in a human cell.
model: Cell wall / plasmid / (accept) loop of DNA free in cytoplasm.
exam.tip: Do not write 'ribosomes': humans have them too.

exam.q: A patient with a cold asks their doctor for antibiotics. Explain why the doctor refuses.
model: A cold is caused by a virus, so antibiotics will not work.
Antibiotics would kill useful bacteria in the body.
Unnecessary use increases the chance of antibiotic-resistant bacteria developing.
exam.tip: Include the resistance point for the third mark.

exam.q: Antibiotics are rarely effective against fungal infections. Suggest why.
model: Fungal cells are eukaryotic like human cells.
So a drug that damaged fungal cell processes would be likely to damage human cells too / few unique targets.
exam.tip: Apply the same principle: is the target present in human cells?

exam.q: Explain how antibiotics are able to treat bacterial infections but not viral infections. Refer to the structure of bacteria, viruses and human cells in your answer.
model: Antibiotics inhibit cell processes in the bacterium but not in the host.
Bacteria have a cell wall which human cells lack; e.g. penicillin stops cell wall formation.
Water enters by osmosis and the bacterium bursts, but human cells are unaffected.
Bacterial ribosomes are smaller / different shape; some antibiotics bind and stop protein synthesis in bacteria only.
Viruses are not cells: no cell wall, no ribosomes, no metabolism of their own.
Viruses reproduce inside host cells using host processes, so antibiotics have no target / cannot act without harming the host.
exam.tip: Cover bacteria, human cells AND viruses, with a reason for each, to reach the top level.

worked.q: A new drug X stops cells from making cell walls. Drug Y stops all ribosomes from making protein, in any cell. Which would be a suitable antibiotic? Explain.
steps: Drug X targets the cell wall.
Bacteria have cell walls; human cells do not.
So X harms bacteria but not human cells: it is selective.
Drug Y affects all ribosomes, including human ones.
So Y would stop protein synthesis in the patient's cells too, harming them.
worked.ans: Drug X is suitable because it acts on a structure only bacteria have; drug Y is not, because it would harm the host's cells as well.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain why a patient with HIV is not treated with penicillin to kill the virus, but might be given an antibiotic if they develop tuberculosis.
steps: HIV is a virus; it reproduces inside host cells (lymphocytes) using the host's processes.
HIV has no cell wall, so penicillin has nothing to act on.
Tuberculosis is caused by a bacterium.
Antibiotics inhibit processes in the TB bacterium (e.g. its cell wall or ribosomes) that human cells do not have, so the bacteria are killed without harming the patient.
worked.ans: Antibiotics only work against bacteria, so they can treat the bacterial TB infection but not the HIV virus itself.

bio_edx.4.12.summary: **Aseptic techniques** are the methods used to culture microorganisms safely and without contamination. They make sure that **only the microorganism you want** grows on the agar (so results are valid) and that **no harmful microorganisms** grow or escape (so it is safe). Key steps are **sterilising** equipment and agar, **flaming the inoculating loop**, working **near a Bunsen flame**, opening the lid **only slightly**, **taping the lid** without sealing it, storing plates **upside down**, and **incubating at no more than 25 C** in school labs.

core.h: What aseptic technique means and why it matters
core.p: Microorganisms such as bacteria and fungi are everywhere: on skin, benches, in the air and on equipment. **Aseptic** means free from contamination by unwanted microorganisms. When we grow (culture) microorganisms on agar we must stop other microbes getting in and stop the culture getting out.
bullets: **Reason 1, valid results**: contaminating microbes would compete with the one being studied and grow colonies that would be counted or measured by mistake.
**Reason 2, safety**: a contaminant could be a **pathogen**, and growing millions of them is dangerous.
**Reason 3, protecting the environment**: cultures must not escape from the lab.
Every step below can be explained by one of these reasons, and mark schemes usually want the step **and** the reason.

callouts.p: A set of methods used to prevent contamination of cultures by unwanted microorganisms and to prevent microorganisms escaping into the environment.

core.p: Bacteria are grown on **nutrient agar** in a **Petri dish**, or in a **nutrient broth** (liquid). Agar is a jelly that contains the nutrients microorganisms need: carbohydrates for energy, and amino acids, minerals and vitamins.
bullets: A single bacterium divides by **binary fission** to form a visible **colony**.
Agar is melted, cooled a little and **poured** into a Petri dish, then left to set.
Microorganisms are transferred to the agar using an **inoculating loop** (streaking) or spread with a sterile **spreader**.
The plate is then **incubated** so the microorganisms grow.

core.h: Step 1: sterilise the Petri dishes and agar before use
core.p: Everything that will touch the culture must be **sterile** (no living microorganisms) before you start.
bullets: Petri dishes and nutrient agar are sterilised in an **autoclave**, which uses steam at high pressure at about **121 C** to kill all microorganisms, including their spores.
Plastic Petri dishes are often bought **pre-sterilised** (sterilised by radiation) and kept sealed until use.
This **kills any microorganisms already present**, so the only microorganism that grows is the one you add.
Pour the agar soon after sterilising, keeping the lid of the dish on as much as possible.

callouts.p: Free from all living microorganisms.

core.h: Step 2: hygiene and a clean work area
core.p: Before starting, reduce the number of microorganisms around you.
bullets: **Wash your hands** before and after the practical.
**Disinfect the bench** before and after use to kill microorganisms on the surface.
Do not eat or drink, and keep your fingers away from your mouth.
Cover any cuts.

core.h: Step 3: sterilise the inoculating loop by flaming
core.p: The **inoculating loop** is a thin wire loop used to transfer microorganisms. It is sterilised by holding it in a **hot (blue) Bunsen flame until it glows red hot**.
bullets: Heating to red hot **kills any microorganisms** on the loop.
Let the loop **cool** for a few seconds before touching the culture, otherwise the heat would **kill the microorganisms** you want to transfer.
Do not put the cooled loop down on the bench; use it straight away.
**Flame the loop again** after use to kill the microorganisms left on it.
Single-use plastic sterile loops can be used instead of flaming.

callouts.p: 'Pass the loop through a Bunsen flame until red hot (1) to kill microorganisms on it (1). Allow it to cool (1) so it does not kill the bacteria being transferred (1).'

fig.cap: Sterilising an inoculating loop: the wire loop is held in the hottest part of a blue Bunsen flame until it glows red hot, killing any microorganisms on it. It is then allowed to cool before use.

core.h: Step 4: work near a Bunsen flame
core.p: Work close to (but not in) a lit Bunsen burner. The flame heats the air, which rises, creating an **upward current of air**.
bullets: The rising air **carries microorganisms away** from the open dish, so they do not fall into it.
Flame the **neck of culture bottles** briefly when they are opened and before they are closed, for the same reason.
Keep culture bottles open for as short a time as possible.

core.h: Step 5: inoculate with the lid lifted only slightly
core.p: When transferring microorganisms onto the agar, **lift the lid of the Petri dish only a little**, at an angle, and only for as short a time as possible.
bullets: This **reduces the chance of microorganisms from the air** landing on the agar.
Hold the lid **above** the dish like a shield; never place it face up on the bench.
Streak or spread the microorganisms gently on the surface without digging into the agar.
Replace the lid **immediately**.

fig.cap: Inoculating an agar plate. The lid is lifted only slightly to let the sterile loop in, while a nearby Bunsen flame creates an upward current of air that carries airborne microorganisms away from the agar.

core.h: Step 6: tape the lid, but do not seal it
core.p: After inoculation, secure the lid with **two (or four) short strips of tape**. Do **not** seal the dish all the way round.
bullets: The tape **stops the lid coming off**, so microorganisms cannot get in or out and no one can open it.
Not sealing it fully lets **oxygen** get in.
This **stops anaerobic bacteria growing**; many dangerous **pathogens are anaerobic**.
**Label the base** (not the lid) with your name, date and what was added, so labels cannot be mixed up if lids are swapped.

callouts.t: Do not seal all the way round
callouts.p: Sealing the dish completely would create anaerobic conditions that favour harmful anaerobic bacteria.

core.h: Step 7: store and incubate the plate correctly
core.p: Plates are incubated **upside down** (lid at the bottom) and, in school labs, at a **maximum of 25 C**.
bullets: Upside down stops **condensation** dripping from the lid onto the agar, which would spread the colonies and mix them up.
Incubating at **25 C or below** greatly **reduces the chance of growing human pathogens**, which grow best at body temperature (about **37 C**).
Industrial and hospital labs may use higher temperatures, because they have stricter safety controls.
Bacteria are grown for about **48 hours** in school to see colonies.

callouts.p: Because human pathogens grow best at around 37 C, keeping cultures at 25 C or below makes it much less likely that harmful bacteria grow.

fig.cap: The lid is held on with two strips of tape (not sealed all round, so oxygen can enter), the base is labelled, and the dish is stored upside down so condensation cannot drip onto the agar. It is incubated at no more than 25 C.

core.p: When the experiment is finished, all cultures and contaminated equipment must be made safe.
bullets: Do **not open** the dishes once the microorganisms have grown.
Cultures are **sterilised in an autoclave** before disposal, killing all the microorganisms.
Wash hands and disinfect the bench again.
Any spills are covered with **disinfectant** and reported.

core.p: Exam questions usually give one step and ask for the reason, or ask you to describe the method. Learn this table.
bullets: Each step has a **contamination** reason, a **safety** reason, or both.
When describing a method, put the steps in a **logical order**.
