analogy.t: Cooking for someone with a severe allergy
analogy.p: Imagine making a meal for someone with a serious nut allergy. You scrub the worktop and wash your hands (disinfect the bench), use pans straight from a very hot dishwasher (sterilised equipment), keep the lid on the pot except for quick stirs (lift the lid slightly), and cover the dish with a label before it goes in the fridge (taped and labelled plate). Every step stops something unwanted getting into the food, just as aseptic technique stops unwanted microbes getting onto the agar. Where it breaks down: in the kitchen you only worry about things getting in, but in the lab you also worry about the culture getting out and harming people; and nothing in cooking matches the reasons for incubating at 25 C or leaving gaps for oxygen.

terms.d: Methods that prevent contamination of a culture by unwanted microorganisms and stop microorganisms escaping.
The presence of unwanted microorganisms in a culture.
Free from all living microorganisms.
To kill all microorganisms on or in something.
A machine that sterilises using steam at high pressure, at about 121 C.
A population of microorganisms grown in a lab on agar or in broth.
A jelly containing nutrients on which microorganisms are grown.
A liquid containing nutrients for growing microorganisms.
A shallow, lidded dish used to hold agar.
A wire loop used to transfer microorganisms.
To add microorganisms to a growth medium.
A visible group of microorganisms grown from a single cell.
To keep a culture at a set temperature so it grows.
A microorganism that causes disease.
Bacteria that grow without oxygen; many are pathogens.
A chemical used to kill microorganisms on surfaces such as benches.

mistakes.w: Flame the loop to clean it.
mistakes.r: Heat the loop in a Bunsen flame until red hot to kill (sterilise) microorganisms on it.

mistakes.w: The lid is sealed all the way round so nothing gets in.
mistakes.r: Two strips of tape hold the lid on but let oxygen in, so anaerobic pathogens do not grow.

mistakes.w: Incubate at 37 C so bacteria grow fastest.
mistakes.r: In school, incubate at 25 C maximum to reduce the chance of growing human pathogens.

mistakes.w: Plates are kept upside down so the agar does not fall out.
mistakes.r: Upside down stops condensation dripping onto the agar.

mistakes.w: Use the loop straight from the flame.
mistakes.r: Let the loop cool first, otherwise it kills the microorganisms being transferred.

mistakes.w: Open the lid fully to spread the bacteria.
mistakes.r: Lift the lid only slightly to reduce contamination from airborne microorganisms.

mistakes.w: The Bunsen is there to kill bacteria in the air.
mistakes.r: The flame creates an upward air current that carries microorganisms away from the dish.

mistakes.w: Label the lid.
mistakes.r: Label the base, so the label stays with the culture if lids are swapped.

exam.q: State what is meant by aseptic technique.
model: Methods to prevent contamination of a culture by unwanted microorganisms.
exam.tip: Use the word contamination.

exam.q: Explain why an inoculating loop is passed through a Bunsen flame before use.
model: Heated until red hot / sterilised.
To kill microorganisms on the loop so they do not contaminate the culture.
exam.tip: Say 'kill microorganisms', not 'clean'.

exam.q: Explain why the loop is allowed to cool before it is used.
model: A hot loop would kill the microorganisms being transferred.
exam.tip: One clear reason.

exam.q: Give two reasons why the Petri dish lid is taped with only two strips of tape.
model: Tape stops the lid coming off / prevents contamination or escape.
Gaps allow oxygen in so anaerobic bacteria / pathogens do not grow.
exam.tip: One reason for using tape, one for not sealing fully.

exam.q: Explain why Petri dishes are stored upside down during incubation.
model: So condensation does not drip onto the agar / disturb colonies.
exam.tip: Key word: condensation.

exam.q: Explain why cultures in school labs are incubated at 25 C rather than 37 C.
model: Human pathogens grow best at body temperature / 37 C.
So at 25 C harmful bacteria are less likely to grow.
exam.tip: Link 37 C to body temperature and pathogens.

exam.q: Explain why Petri dishes and agar are sterilised before use.
model: To kill any microorganisms already present.
So only the chosen microorganism grows / results are valid.
exam.tip: Mention the effect on results.

exam.q: Explain why a student works near a lit Bunsen burner when inoculating an agar plate.
model: The flame causes an upward current of air.
Which carries microorganisms away / stops them landing on the agar.
exam.tip: The flame does not kill airborne microbes directly.

exam.q: Suggest why a culture should be sterilised in an autoclave before it is thrown away.
model: To kill all microorganisms so none (including possible pathogens) escape / infect people.
exam.tip: Safety reason.

exam.q: Describe how a student could use aseptic technique to prepare an agar plate of bacteria for an investigation.
model: Use sterile (autoclaved) Petri dishes and nutrient agar; disinfect bench and wash hands.
Sterilise inoculating loop in Bunsen flame until red hot, then allow to cool.
Work near Bunsen flame so upward air current carries microorganisms away; flame neck of culture bottle.
Lift lid of Petri dish only slightly and briefly; streak / spread bacteria onto agar; replace lid.
Secure lid with two strips of tape (not fully sealed) so oxygen enters and anaerobic pathogens do not grow; label base.
Store upside down so condensation does not drip; incubate at 25 C maximum to reduce growth of human pathogens.
exam.tip: Give steps in order AND a reason for each to reach the top level.

worked.q: A student's plate shows several different colours and shapes of colony, but they only added one type of bacterium. Suggest two mistakes they may have made and how to avoid them.
steps: Different colony types mean the plate was contaminated by other microorganisms.
Possible mistake 1: the lid was lifted too high or for too long, letting airborne microbes in. Fix: lift the lid slightly, briefly, near a Bunsen flame.
Possible mistake 2: the loop was not flamed until red hot, or was put down on the bench. Fix: flame until red hot, cool in the air, use immediately.
Other possible mistakes: unsterilised agar or dish, bench not disinfected.
worked.ans: The plate was contaminated; the student should sterilise the loop and equipment properly and minimise opening the lid, working near a Bunsen flame.

worked.q: Model answer: A student taped their Petri dish all the way round with tape and incubated it at 37 C. Explain why this is unsafe.
steps: Sealing all the way round stops oxygen getting into the dish.
This creates anaerobic conditions in which anaerobic bacteria, many of which are pathogens, can grow.
37 C is human body temperature, which is the optimum for many human pathogens.
So both choices increase the risk of growing large numbers of harmful bacteria.
worked.ans: Use two strips of tape only so oxygen can enter, and incubate at 25 C maximum to reduce the risk of growing human pathogens.

bio_edx.4.13.summary: In this triple-only core practical you test how well different **antiseptics, antibiotics or plant extracts** stop bacteria growing. Bacteria are spread evenly over a sterile **nutrient agar** plate, paper discs soaked in each substance are placed on top, and after incubation a **clear zone (zone of inhibition)** forms where the bacteria have been killed or prevented from growing. The **larger the area of the clear zone, the more effective** the substance, so you measure the diameter, calculate area using pi r squared, and use **aseptic technique** throughout so the results are valid and safe.

core.p: You are comparing how effective different substances are at killing bacteria or stopping their growth. The **independent variable** is the type (or concentration) of antiseptic, antibiotic or plant extract. The **dependent variable** is the size of the clear zone around each disc.
bullets: **Antiseptics** (e.g. TCP, mouthwash, hand gel, disinfectant diluted) kill microorganisms outside the body, on skin or surfaces
**Antibiotics** (e.g. penicillin, streptomycin) kill bacteria or stop them growing; they can be used inside the body
**Plant extracts** (e.g. garlic, mint, tea tree oil, ginger) may contain antimicrobial chemicals plants make as chemical defences
A **clear zone** shows where bacteria could not grow because the substance diffused out of the disc into the agar
Bigger clear zone = substance more effective (or more concentrated, or diffuses better through agar)

callouts.p: The clear area around a disc on an agar plate where bacteria have not grown because the substance has killed them or inhibited their growth.

fig.cap: An agar plate after incubation. Discs A, B and C were soaked in different antiseptics; W is the control disc soaked in sterile water, which has no clear zone. A is the most effective because its clear zone is largest.

core.p: You need equipment that is sterile and lets you grow a uniform layer of bacteria so that the only thing that differs between discs is the substance being tested.
bullets: Sterile **Petri dish** containing sterile **nutrient agar** (the agar provides nutrients and water for bacteria)
Broth culture of a safe bacterium, e.g. **Escherichia coli** (non-pathogenic lab strain) or Micrococcus luteus
**Inoculating loop** or sterile spreader, or sterile pipette to add culture
**Bunsen burner** (to sterilise loop and create upward air current)
Sterile **filter paper discs** of the same size (cut with a hole punch)
Sterile **forceps**
Solutions of antiseptics / antibiotics / plant extracts, plus **sterile distilled water** for the control
Adhesive tape, marker pen, **incubator** set at 25 C, ruler

core.p: Follow these steps in order; each one has a reason that examiners love to ask about.
bullets: Wash hands and **disinfect the bench** with disinfectant
**Sterilise the inoculating loop** by heating it in a Bunsen flame until it glows red hot, then let it cool (so it does not kill the bacteria you are transferring)
Briefly **flame the neck of the culture bottle** after removing the lid and before replacing it
Lift the Petri dish lid only slightly, at an angle, and **spread the bacteria evenly** over the whole agar surface to make a 'lawn'
Soak equal-sized paper discs in each test solution for the **same time**; soak one disc in **sterile water** as the control
Use **sterile forceps** to place discs on the agar, **evenly spaced** and not too close to the edge or each other
**Tape the lid** on with two or four short strips of tape, but **do not seal it all the way round**
Label the base of the dish, then **incubate upside down at 25 C** for about 48 hours
**Measure the diameter** of each clear zone, calculate radius and then **area = pi r squared**
Repeat for each substance and calculate a **mean**

callouts.p: In 'describe the method' questions, marks often come for the reason behind a step: e.g. 'tape lid so it cannot be opened accidentally but oxygen can still get in'.

core.h: Why each safety and aseptic step matters
core.p: Aseptic technique stops **contamination** of the culture by microorganisms from the air, skin or equipment, and stops the bacteria escaping. Contamination would add other microbes that respond differently to the antiseptics, making results invalid, and could include **pathogens**.
bullets: **Lid taped but not fully sealed**: oxygen can still enter, so **anaerobic bacteria** (many of which are dangerous pathogens) are not encouraged to grow
**Dish stored upside down**: condensation drips onto the lid, not onto the agar, so colonies are not spread or disturbed
**Incubate at 25 C (maximum) in school labs**: reduces the chance of growing **human pathogens**, which grow best near body temperature (37 C)
**Flaming the loop**: kills microorganisms on it
**Lid open as little as possible**: reduces microbes falling in from the air
**Bunsen nearby**: hot air rising carries airborne microbes away from the plate
**Disinfect bench and wash hands** before and after; dispose of plates by **autoclaving** (high temperature and pressure sterilising)

callouts.p: Never say 'incubate at 37 C because that is body temperature, so bacteria grow faster' for a school lab. The mark scheme wants 25 C to reduce the risk of growing pathogens.

core.p: A fair test changes only one thing. Everything else that could affect the size of the clear zone must be controlled.
bullets: **Independent variable**: type of antiseptic / antibiotic / plant extract (or its concentration)
**Dependent variable**: area (or diameter) of the clear zone

**Control variables**: same species of bacteria and same volume of culture; same type and depth of agar; same size of paper disc; same volume or soaking time of solution; same incubation temperature and time; same concentration (if comparing types)
**Control disc** soaked in sterile water: shows that any clear zone is caused by the substance, not by the paper disc or by handling

head: Variable
In this practical
How controlled / measured
rows: Measure diameter, area = pi r squared
Same species, same volume of broth

core.p: The control is a disc soaked in **sterile distilled water** (or the solvent used to make a plant extract, e.g. ethanol, if one was used).
bullets: If no clear zone forms around the water disc, the paper itself does not kill bacteria
If the plant extract was made in ethanol, the control should be ethanol alone, because ethanol is itself antiseptic
It lets you **compare** and show the effect is due to the antimicrobial substance
Without a control you cannot conclude that the substance caused the clear zone

callouts.p: To show that the result is due only to the independent variable (the substance), not to another factor.

core.p: You measure from the **underside of the dish** without opening it, using a ruler. Then convert diameter into area, because area reflects the full amount of agar where growth was inhibited.
bullets: Measure the **diameter** across the clear zone in mm (through the centre of the disc)
If the zone is not a perfect circle, measure two diameters at right angles and take the mean
**radius = diameter / 2**
**area = pi r squared** (pi = 3.14), units **mm2**
Some questions use **clear zone area minus disc area** to give only the area where bacteria were killed
Repeat with several plates and calculate a **mean** to improve reliability and identify anomalies

callouts.p: Give area in mm2 or cm2 and round sensibly (e.g. 3 significant figures). Forgetting to halve the diameter is the most common calculation error.

core.p: The substance that produces the **largest clear zone** is the most effective against that bacterium under those conditions.
bullets: A larger zone means the substance **killed more bacteria** or **diffused further** at a concentration high enough to inhibit growth
No clear zone means the substance had no effect on that bacterium (or bacteria are **resistant**)
An antibiotic that works on one species may not work on another, so results only apply to the bacterium tested
Clear zone size also depends on **how fast the substance diffuses** through agar, so it is not a perfect measure of effectiveness in the body
Effect of concentration: higher concentration usually gives larger zones

core.h: Antiseptics versus antibiotics versus plant extracts
core.p: These substances are all antimicrobial but are used in different ways, which links this practical to the rest of Topic 5.
bullets: Antibiotics only act on **bacteria**, not viruses, because they target bacterial structures (e.g. cell wall) or processes
Antiseptics are usually too harmful to use inside the body
Plant extracts are a source of new medicines, e.g. **aspirin** came from willow and **digitalis** from foxgloves

core.p: Even safe lab strains can mutate or become contaminated, so treat all cultures as potentially harmful.
bullets: **Hazard**: contamination with pathogens; **precaution**: aseptic technique, 25 C, do not open plates after incubation
**Hazard**: Bunsen burner and hot loop; **precaution**: tie hair back, let loop cool on a heatproof mat
**Hazard**: antiseptics may be irritants; **precaution**: wear eye protection, wash skin if splashed
**Do not open** incubated plates; view through the lid
Dispose of cultures by **autoclaving** or as instructed

core.p: Grade 9 answers evaluate the method and suggest specific improvements, not just 'repeat it'.
bullets: Uneven spreading of bacteria gives patchy lawns; improve by using a sterile spreader and fixed culture volume
Discs soaking up different volumes; improve by using a micropipette to add a fixed volume to each disc
Discs too close together so zones merge; place fewer discs, evenly spaced
Zones not perfectly circular; measure two diameters at right angles
Contaminant colonies (different colour/shape) indicate poor aseptic technique; discard that plate
Repeat at least three times and calculate a mean; ignore anomalies

core.p: Bacteria grow by **binary fission**, dividing roughly every 20 minutes in ideal conditions, so a lawn quickly covers the agar. Anywhere an antimicrobial substance has diffused at a high enough concentration, cells are killed or cannot divide, leaving clear agar.
bullets: The substance diffuses outward from the disc, so concentration is **highest near the disc** and falls further away
The edge of the clear zone is where the concentration becomes too low to stop growth
Nutrient agar supplies **carbohydrates, amino acids, minerals and water** needed for growth

callouts.p: Diffusion of the antimicrobial into the agar creates a concentration gradient; bacteria cannot grow where the concentration is high enough.

analogy.p: Imagine sowing grass seed evenly across a lawn, then putting a drop of different weedkillers at several spots. Where a strong weedkiller soaks into the soil, a bare circle appears; the stronger or better spreading the weedkiller, the bigger the bare patch. The grass is the bacterial lawn, the drops are the soaked discs and the bare patches are clear zones. A spot of plain water is the control. Where it breaks down: grass grows slowly from seeds, whereas bacteria reproduce by binary fission every 20 minutes, and the zone size also depends on how quickly the chemical diffuses through agar, not only on how deadly it is.

terms.d: A chemical that kills or inhibits microorganisms on living tissue such as skin.
A medicine that kills bacteria or stops them growing, without harming human cells.
A solution of chemicals taken from a plant, which may have antimicrobial properties.
A jelly containing nutrients on which microorganisms are grown.
An even layer of bacterial growth covering the whole surface of the agar.
The area around a disc where bacteria have not grown.
Methods used to prevent contamination of cultures by unwanted microorganisms and prevent their escape.
A wire loop used to transfer microorganisms; sterilised by heating red hot in a flame.
Unwanted microorganisms getting into a culture.
Keeping cultures at a controlled temperature so microorganisms can grow.
A microorganism that causes disease.
A disc soaked in sterile water to show the clear zone is caused by the substance tested.
Bacteria that grow without oxygen; many are pathogens, so lids are not fully sealed.
A machine that sterilises equipment using steam at high temperature and pressure.
The way bacteria reproduce, by one cell dividing into two.

mistakes.w: Incubate at 37 C so bacteria grow faster.
mistakes.r: Incubate at 25 C (maximum in schools) to reduce the risk of growing human pathogens.

mistakes.w: Seal the lid all the way round with tape to stop bacteria escaping.
mistakes.r: Tape the lid with a few strips but not all the way round, so oxygen can enter and anaerobic pathogens do not grow.

mistakes.w: The smallest clear zone is the most effective antiseptic.
mistakes.r: The largest clear zone shows the most effective substance.

mistakes.w: Area = pi x diameter squared.
mistakes.r: Area = pi r squared, where r = diameter / 2.

mistakes.w: The control is a plate with nothing on it.
mistakes.r: The control is a disc soaked in sterile water (or the solvent) on the same plate.

mistakes.w: Heat the loop then use it immediately.
mistakes.r: Heat the loop until red hot, then allow it to cool so it does not kill the bacteria being transferred.

mistakes.w: Open the plate to measure the clear zone.
mistakes.r: Measure through the base without opening the dish, to avoid contamination and exposure.

mistakes.w: Antibiotics kill viruses as well as bacteria.
mistakes.r: Antibiotics only work against bacteria.

mistakes.w: Store the plate the right way up.
mistakes.r: Store upside down so condensation does not drip onto the agar.

exam.q: State the dependent variable in an investigation into the effect of different antiseptics on bacterial growth.
model: Area (or diameter) of the clear zone around each disc
exam.tip: Name what you measure, not just 'bacterial growth'.

exam.q: Explain why the Petri dish lid is taped but not fully sealed.
model: Tape stops the lid being opened or contamination entering
Not fully sealed so oxygen can enter / prevents anaerobic conditions
Which would encourage growth of anaerobic (harmful) pathogens
exam.tip: Two separate reasons: why tape, and why not all the way round.

exam.q: Explain why the plate is incubated at 25 C in a school laboratory.
model: Human pathogens grow best at around 37 C (body temperature)
25 C reduces the risk of growing pathogens / harmful bacteria
exam.tip: Link to safety, not to speed of growth.

exam.q: Give the purpose of the disc soaked in sterile water.
model: It is a control to show the clear zone is due to the antiseptic, not the disc or handling
exam.tip: Use the word 'control'.

exam.q: Describe two aseptic techniques used when transferring bacteria onto agar.
model: Heat the inoculating loop in a Bunsen flame until red hot then cool
Flame the neck of the culture bottle
Lift the lid only slightly / at an angle
Disinfect the bench / work near a Bunsen flame
exam.tip: Any two; each must be a specific action.

exam.q: Explain why the plate is stored upside down during incubation.
model: Condensation forms on the lid
Stops water dripping onto the agar and disturbing / spreading colonies
exam.tip: Mention condensation.

exam.q: A clear zone has a diameter of 18 mm. Calculate its area. Use pi = 3.14.
model: r = 9 mm
exam.tip: Halve the diameter first; include units.

exam.q: Suggest why a large clear zone does not always mean the antibiotic would be the best treatment for an infection.
model: Zone size also depends on how fast the substance diffuses through agar
Substance may be toxic to human cells / effective concentration may not be reached in body
Only tested on one type of bacterium
exam.tip: Think about differences between agar and the human body.

exam.q: Describe a method to compare the effectiveness of three plant extracts on the growth of bacteria.
model: Sterilise equipment / use aseptic technique, e.g. flame loop
Spread bacteria evenly over sterile nutrient agar
Soak equal-sized paper discs in each extract for the same time
Include a control disc soaked in sterile water / solvent
Place discs evenly spaced on agar using sterile forceps
Tape lid (not fully sealed) and incubate upside down at 25 C for 48 hours
Measure diameter of clear zones and calculate area using pi r squared
Repeat and calculate means; largest area = most effective extract
exam.tip: Six-mark method: give a logical sequence with controls, measurement and how you reach a conclusion.

exam.q: A student finds small coloured colonies inside a clear zone. Suggest an explanation.
model: Contamination by a different microorganism (poor aseptic technique)
Or some bacteria are resistant to the substance (mutation)
exam.tip: Either explanation, with a reason.

exam.q: Explain why the discs must be the same size.
model: Larger disc holds more solution / more substance diffuses out
Would give a larger clear zone so the test would not be fair / valid
exam.tip: Link the control variable to its effect on the dependent variable.

worked.q: Antiseptic X gave clear zone diameters of 14 mm, 16 mm and 15 mm. Calculate the mean area of the clear zone. Use pi = 3.14.
steps: Mean diameter = (14 + 16 + 15) / 3 = 15 mm
Radius = 15 / 2 = 7.5 mm
worked.ans: Mean clear zone area = 177 mm2 (3 s.f.)

worked.q: The clear zone around a 6 mm diameter disc is 20 mm in diameter. Calculate the area where bacteria were killed, not counting the disc.
steps: Zone radius = 10 mm, area = 3.14 x 10 x 10 = 314 mm2
Disc radius = 3 mm, area = 3.14 x 3 x 3 = 28.26 mm2
Inhibited area = 314 - 28.26 = 285.74 mm2
worked.ans: About 286 mm2

worked.q: Results: garlic 154 mm2, mint 50 mm2, water 0 mm2. Write a conclusion.
steps: Identify largest zone: garlic
Compare with control: water shows no zone, so effect is due to extracts
Limit conclusion to this bacterium and these conditions
worked.ans: Garlic extract was the most effective at inhibiting growth of this bacterium because it produced the largest clear zone (154 mm2, about three times that of mint); the water control showed no zone, so the effect was caused by the extracts.

bio_edx.4.14.summary: In the triple-only part of Topic 5 you must calculate the **cross-sectional area** of bacterial colonies and of the **clear zones (zones of inhibition)** produced by antiseptics, antibiotics or plant extracts. Because colonies and clear zones are roughly circular, you use **area = pi r squared**, remembering that the **radius is half the diameter** you measure. Area is a better measure than diameter because it reflects the whole region where bacteria grew or were killed, and doubling the diameter quadruples the area. You also need to convert between **mm2 and cm2**, calculate means, percentage changes and round to sensible significant figures.

core.p: When you grow bacteria on agar or test an antiseptic, the result is a roughly circular patch. Its **area** tells you how much the colony has grown, or how large the region is where the substance stopped bacteria growing. Comparing areas lets you compare growth rates or the effectiveness of different substances.
bullets: A **colony** is a visible group of millions of bacteria that grew by binary fission from one original cell
A **clear zone** is where bacteria have been killed or inhibited
Larger clear zone area = more effective antimicrobial substance (in that test)
Area is used rather than diameter because it scales with the **square** of the radius, so it shows the true size of the effect

callouts.p: Area of a circle = pi r squared, where r is the radius and pi = 3.14 (or use the pi button).

fig.cap: A clear zone around a paper disc. You measure the diameter with a ruler; the radius is half the diameter; then use area = pi r squared.

core.p: In practicals you nearly always measure the **diameter**, the full distance across the circle through its centre, because the centre is hard to locate exactly. The equation needs the **radius**.
bullets: Always halve the diameter **before** squaring
If a question gives the radius directly, do not halve it again
Read the question carefully: 'diameter of 12 mm' means r = 6 mm

callouts.p: Putting the diameter straight into pi r squared gives an answer four times too large and loses the marks.

core.p: Use the same routine every time so you never skip a step.
bullets: 1. Write down the diameter and units
2. Halve it to get radius
3. Square the radius (r x r)
4. Multiply by pi (3.14)
5. Give the units squared (mm2 or cm2)
6. Round to a sensible number of **significant figures**, usually the same as the data (often 2 or 3)

core.p: Accurate area depends on an accurate diameter. Measure from the **underside of the closed Petri dish** with a ruler marked in mm.
bullets: Measure through the **centre** of the disc or colony
If the zone is not circular, measure **two diameters at right angles** and use the mean
Repeat with several plates and calculate a **mean diameter** (or mean area)
Do not open the dish to measure; this risks contamination and exposure
Resolution of a mm ruler is 1 mm, so small zones have a large percentage uncertainty

callouts.p: Either is accepted if done consistently, but the mark scheme usually follows the question: if asked for 'mean area', calculating each area then averaging is safest.

core.h: Area of the clear zone not including the disc
core.p: Some questions ask for the area where bacteria were actually inhibited. The paper disc sits in the middle of the clear zone, so subtract its area.
bullets: **Inhibited area = pi R squared minus pi r squared**, where R = clear zone radius and r = disc radius
Calculate both areas separately, then subtract
Discs are usually 5 or 6 mm in diameter (from a hole punch)
Only do this if the question asks; otherwise give the whole clear zone area

fig.cap: The inhibited area is the ring between the edge of the clear zone (radius R) and the edge of the paper disc (radius r). Subtract the disc area from the whole zone area.

core.p: Areas are in **square units**, so the conversion factor is squared too. There are 10 mm in 1 cm, so there are **10 x 10 = 100 mm2 in 1 cm2**.
bullets: mm2 to cm2: **divide by 100**
cm2 to mm2: **multiply by 100**
Or convert the diameter to cm first, then calculate: 20 mm = 2 cm, r = 1 cm, area = 3.14 cm2
Do not divide by 10 when converting areas

callouts.p: 314 mm2 is 3.14 cm2, not 31.4 cm2.

fig.cap: A 1 cm by 1 cm square contains 10 rows of 10 small 1 mm squares, so 1 cm2 = 100 mm2.

core.p: Because area depends on **r squared**, small changes in diameter make big changes in area. This is why comparing areas exaggerates differences that diameters hide.
bullets: Double the diameter = **four times** the area
Triple the diameter = **nine times** the area
So a clear zone of 20 mm diameter is four times the area of one of 10 mm, not twice

fig.cap: Doubling the diameter from 10 mm to 20 mm increases the area from 78.5 mm2 to 314 mm2, which is four times larger.

core.p: Repeat readings reduce the effect of random error. Exclude any **anomalous** result that clearly does not fit, then calculate a mean.
bullets: Mean = sum of values / number of values
Give the mean to the same number of decimal places or significant figures as the data (or one more)
State which value you excluded and why if it is anomalous
Range of the repeats shows how spread out (how repeatable) the results are

core.p: You may be asked how much bigger one area is than another, or the percentage increase in colony area over time.
bullets: **Percentage change = (new - original) / original x 100**
Ratio comparison: 'Zone A is 314 / 78.5 = 4 times larger than zone B'
Rate of growth of a colony = change in area / time, units mm2 per hour
A negative percentage change means a decrease

callouts.p: Calculation questions usually give one mark for correct working even if the final answer is wrong, so always write each step.

core.p: Give the answer to a sensible precision. Raw measurements to the nearest mm justify two or three significant figures, not six decimal places from the calculator.
bullets: Do not round in the middle of the calculation; round only at the end
If the question says 'give your answer to 2 decimal places', follow it exactly

core.p: Calculated areas turn observations into data you can compare, plot and evaluate.
bullets: The substance with the **largest mean clear zone area** is the most effective against that bacterium
Plot a **bar chart** for different substances (categoric) or a **line graph** for concentration (continuous)
Compare with the **control** (sterile water disc) which should have zero clear zone area
Overlapping ranges between substances mean the difference may not be significant
Clear zone area also depends on how far the substance **diffuses** through agar, so it is not a perfect measure

core.p: You can also track a growing colony by measuring its diameter at intervals. The area shows how growth speeds up as the number of cells increases by binary fission.
bullets: Measure diameter at fixed times, calculate area for each
Plot area against time; the gradient is the rate of growth
Growth slows when nutrients run out or waste builds up

analogy.p: A 12 inch pizza sounds only a bit bigger than a 6 inch pizza, but you get four times as much pizza, because the area depends on the radius squared. Clear zones work the same way: a zone that looks only twice as wide covers four times the area of agar where bacteria were stopped. And just as the pizza size quoted is the diameter, the size you measure on a plate is the diameter, so you must halve it first. Where it breaks down: pizzas are perfect circles cut to size, whereas clear zones are often slightly irregular and have fuzzy edges, so real measurements carry uncertainty.

terms.d: The area of a flat slice or surface, here the area of agar covered by a colony or clear zone.
The distance across a circle passing through its centre.
The distance from the centre of a circle to its edge; half the diameter.
A constant, about 3.14, linking a circle's radius to its area and circumference.
pi r squared.
Area around an antimicrobial disc where bacteria have not grown.
A visible cluster of bacteria grown from a single cell by binary fission.
An even layer of bacteria covering the agar surface.
Square millimetre; 100 mm2 = 1 cm2.
Sum of repeat values divided by the number of values.
A result that does not fit the pattern of the others.
The digits in a number that carry meaning about its precision.
(new value - original value) / original value x 100.
The smallest change a measuring instrument can detect, 1 mm for a ruler.

mistakes.r: r = 9 mm, so area = pi x 9 x 9 = 254 mm2.

mistakes.w: Area = 2 x pi x r.
mistakes.r: That is circumference; area = pi r squared.
Divide by 100: 314 mm2 = 3.14 cm2.

mistakes.w: Doubling the diameter doubles the area.
mistakes.r: Doubling the diameter quadruples the area.

mistakes.w: Answer given as 254.469004941 mm2.
mistakes.r: Round sensibly, e.g. 254 mm2 (3 s.f.).

mistakes.w: Units given as mm.
mistakes.r: Area units are squared: mm2 or cm2.

mistakes.w: pi x r squared calculated as (pi x r) squared.
mistakes.r: Square the radius first, then multiply by pi.

mistakes.w: Smallest clear zone area shows best antiseptic.
mistakes.r: Largest clear zone area shows most effective substance.

exam.q: State the equation used to calculate the area of a circular clear zone.
model: Area = pi r squared
exam.tip: Define r as radius if asked.

exam.q: A clear zone has a diameter of 14 mm. Calculate its area. Use pi = 3.14.
model: r = 7 mm
exam.tip: One mark for halving, one for the answer with units.

exam.q: A colony has a radius of 3 mm. Calculate its cross-sectional area in mm2.
exam.tip: Radius given, so do not halve.

exam.q: Convert 452 mm2 into cm2.
exam.tip: Divide by 100 for area.

exam.q: Explain why area is a better measure of the effectiveness of an antiseptic than diameter.
model: Area shows the total region of agar where bacteria were inhibited
Area increases with the square of the radius so differences between substances are shown more clearly / diameter underestimates difference
exam.tip: Mention r squared.

exam.q: Clear zone diameters for antibiotic Y were 12 mm, 13 mm and 11 mm. Calculate the mean area. Use pi = 3.14.
model: Mean diameter = 12 mm
r = 6 mm
exam.tip: Mean, halve, square, multiply.

exam.q: The clear zone around a 6 mm disc has a diameter of 24 mm. Calculate the area in which bacteria were inhibited, excluding the disc. Use pi = 3.14.
model: Zone area = 3.14 x 12 x 12 = 452.16 mm2
Disc area = 3.14 x 3 x 3 = 28.26 mm2
Difference = 423.9 = 424 mm2
exam.tip: Two areas, then subtract.

exam.q: Zone A has area 314 mm2 and zone B has area 78.5 mm2. Calculate how many times larger zone A is.
exam.tip: Divide the larger by the smaller.

exam.q: A colony grew from a diameter of 4 mm to 8 mm in 10 hours. Calculate the percentage increase in area.
model: Initial area = 3.14 x 2 x 2 = 12.56 mm2
Final area = 3.14 x 4 x 4 = 50.24 mm2
Percentage increase = (50.24 - 12.56) / 12.56 x 100 = 300%
exam.tip: Doubling diameter gives 4 times area, which is a 300% increase, not 400%.

exam.q: A student tested four plant extracts and measured clear zone diameters. Describe how they should process and present their results to decide which extract is most effective.
model: Measure diameter of each zone in mm through centre / two diameters at right angles
Repeat for several plates and identify anomalies
Calculate radius as diameter / 2
Calculate area using pi r squared for each, in mm2
Calculate a mean area for each extract
Compare with the control disc of sterile water (zero area)
Plot a bar chart of mean area for each extract
Largest mean area = most effective; consider overlap of ranges
exam.tip: Cover measurement, calculation, presentation and conclusion.

worked.q: Antiseptic P gives a clear zone of diameter 2.6 cm. Calculate the area in mm2. Use pi = 3.14.
steps: Convert: 2.6 cm = 26 mm
r squared = 169
worked.ans: 531 mm2 (3 s.f.), which is 5.31 cm2

worked.q: Three discs of garlic extract gave diameters 15 mm, 17 mm and 30 mm. The 30 mm value is anomalous. Calculate the mean area of the valid zones. Use pi = 3.14.
steps: Exclude anomaly 30 mm
worked.ans: Mean area = 202 mm2

worked.q: Two colonies: X has diameter 6 mm, Y has diameter 18 mm. How many times larger is the area of Y?
steps: Check: diameter tripled, so area x 3 squared = 9
worked.ans: Y is 9 times larger in area

bio_edx.4.15.summary: New medicines go through a long series of stages: **discovery**, **development**, **preclinical testing** and **clinical testing**, before they can be licensed and prescribed. Preclinical testing uses **cells, tissues and live animals** to check the drug is not toxic and that it works; clinical testing uses **healthy volunteers** and then **patients**, starting at very low doses, to check **safety (side effects)**, **efficacy (does it work)** and the **optimum dose**. Most candidate drugs fail along the way, so the process can take over 10 years and cost huge amounts, but each stage is needed to protect people from harmful or useless medicines.

core.p: Edexcel expects you to describe the process in order: discovery, development, preclinical testing (on cells and tissues, then on animals), clinical testing (on healthy volunteers, then on patients), and finally licensing. A drug only moves on if it passes the previous stage.
bullets: **Discovery**: find a chemical that might treat a disease
**Development**: make and modify the chemical, work out how to produce it and deliver it
**Preclinical testing**: test on **cultured cells and tissues**, then on **live animals**
**Clinical testing**: test on **healthy volunteers**, then on **patients** with the disease
**Licensing**: a regulatory body (in the UK the **MHRA**) approves it if it is safe and effective
**Monitoring** continues after release to find rare side effects

callouts.p: Every new medicine is tested for toxicity / safety, efficacy (how well it works) and dosage (the best dose to use).

fig.cap: The stages of developing a new medicine in order. Many candidate drugs are rejected at each stage, so only a few are ever licensed.

core.p: Scientists search for chemicals that could affect a disease, often by targeting a specific molecule such as a receptor or enzyme involved in the illness.
bullets: Many medicines come from **plants**: e.g. **aspirin** from willow bark, **digitalis** from foxgloves (heart conditions)
Some come from **microorganisms**: e.g. **penicillin** from the Penicillium mould, discovered by Alexander Fleming
Many are now made by **chemists** or designed by **computer modelling** to fit a target molecule
Large libraries of chemicals are **screened** to find ones with an effect

core.p: Once a promising chemical is found, it is improved and made in a form that can be given to people.
bullets: Chemists alter the structure to make it more effective or reduce side effects
Work out how to **manufacture** it in large amounts and keep it **stable**
Decide how it will be taken, e.g. tablet, injection, inhaler
Check it can be **absorbed** and reach the right part of the body

core.h: Preclinical testing on cells and tissues
core.p: The first tests are carried out in the laboratory on **cultured human cells and tissues**. This is cheap, quick and avoids harming people or animals.
bullets: Checks whether the drug is **toxic** to cells (kills or damages them)
Checks whether it has the **desired effect** on target cells (efficacy)
Many drugs fail here
Limitation: cells and tissues cannot show how the drug affects a **whole organism** with many interacting organs

core.p: Drugs that pass cell tests are given to **live animals**, usually mammals such as mice or rats, because their body systems work in a similar way to ours.
bullets: Tests effect on a **whole body**, including on organs such as liver and kidneys
Checks **toxicity** and **side effects** at different doses
Checks the drug is **absorbed**, reaches the target and is removed from the body
Law requires testing on at least **two different mammal species** (one non-rodent) before human trials
Limitation: animals are not identical to humans, so a drug safe in animals may still be harmful to people
**Ethical issue**: some people object to causing animals suffering

callouts.p: Cells and tissues come before animals, and animals come before humans. Students often reverse these.

core.p: The first human tests use a small number of **healthy volunteers** and **very low doses**. The main aim is **safety**, not whether it cures the disease.
bullets: Checks for **side effects** and that the drug is **not toxic** in humans
Doses are started very low and **gradually increased**
Healthy people are used so any effects can be linked to the drug rather than the illness, and to avoid risking ill patients who may be more vulnerable
Studies how the drug is absorbed and removed in humans

core.p: If the drug is safe, it is tested on **patients who have the disease**, first in small groups and then large groups of hundreds or thousands.
bullets: Checks **efficacy**: does it treat the disease?
Finds the **optimum dose**: the dose that works best with fewest side effects
Large numbers are needed so results are **reliable** and rare side effects are found
Patients are compared with a **control group**
Results are **peer reviewed** and published so other scientists can check them

head: Stage
Who / what
Main purpose
rows: Toxicity and effect in whole body
Optimum dose, compare with existing treatment

fig.cap: Doses rise through the clinical trial: very low doses in healthy volunteers to test safety, then higher doses in patients to test efficacy and find the optimum dose.

core.p: To show a drug really works, patients taking it must be compared with a group that does not get it.
bullets: A **placebo** is a substance that looks like the drug but has **no active ingredient** (e.g. a sugar pill)
Control group gets the placebo (or the **current best treatment**)
Comparison removes the **placebo effect**, where patients feel better simply because they believe they are being treated
Patients are allocated to groups **randomly** to avoid bias
**Ethical issue**: giving a placebo to a seriously ill patient denies them treatment, so the existing drug is often used instead

callouts.p: A substance that looks like the drug being tested but does not contain the drug, given to a control group.

core.p: Knowing who has the real drug could affect how patients report symptoms or how doctors assess them, so trials are **blinded**.
bullets: **Blind trial**: patients do not know whether they have the drug or placebo
**Double-blind trial**: **neither the patients nor the doctors** know who has the drug or placebo until the end
Double-blind removes **bias** from both patients and doctors
Results are only revealed after data are collected

callouts.p: A trial in which neither the patients nor the doctors know who is receiving the drug and who is receiving the placebo.

fig.cap: A double-blind trial. Patients are randomly split into a group given the new drug and a control group given a placebo or existing drug; neither patients nor doctors know who is in which group.

core.p: If clinical trials show the drug is safe and effective, the company applies for a licence. Doctors can then prescribe it.
bullets: Regulators review all data before approval
**Post-licensing monitoring** continues because very rare side effects may only appear when millions of people use it
A drug can be withdrawn if serious problems appear

core.h: Why it takes so long and costs so much
core.p: Only a tiny fraction of discovered chemicals become medicines. Each stage is designed to catch problems before more people are exposed.
bullets: Process often takes **10 to 15 years**
Can cost **over a billion pounds** per successful drug
Most candidates fail due to toxicity, side effects or not working
Large trials are needed to get **valid, reliable** results
Trade-off: thorough testing protects patients but delays access to new treatments

fig.cap: Thousands of chemicals are discovered, but only a handful pass preclinical testing and clinical trials, and perhaps one becomes a licensed medicine.

core.p: 6 mark questions often ask you to evaluate or discuss the process. Give points on both sides.
bullets: **Animal testing**: necessary to see whole-body effects but causes suffering; animals may not respond like humans
**Placebos**: give fair comparison but may deny ill patients treatment
**Healthy volunteers**: take a risk for no medical benefit to themselves (e.g. the 2006 TGN1412 trial caused severe reactions)
**Informed consent**: volunteers and patients must be told the risks and agree
Balance between speed (e.g. urgent vaccines) and safety

callouts.p: For 'evaluate' questions, give advantages and disadvantages, then finish with a justified conclusion.

analogy.p: A new car design is first tested as individual parts in the factory (cells and tissues), then the whole car is crash-tested with dummies (animal testing). Next, trained test drivers drive it slowly on a closed track (healthy volunteers at low doses), and finally ordinary drivers use it on real roads, compared with an existing model (patients, with a control group). Even after sale, owners report faults and cars can be recalled (post-licensing monitoring). Where it breaks down: crash-test dummies are designed to mimic humans precisely, whereas animals differ from humans biologically, and in a drug trial people are placed in groups without knowing which 'car' they have.

terms.d: Finding a chemical that may be useful as a medicine, e.g. from plants, microorganisms or chemical libraries.
Modifying and producing a potential drug in a form that can be tested and given to people.
Testing a drug in the laboratory on cells, tissues and live animals before it is tested on humans.
Testing a drug on humans: first healthy volunteers, then patients.
How harmful a substance is to cells or the body.
How well a drug works in producing the desired effect.
An unwanted effect of a medicine.
The amount of drug given; the optimum dose is the one that works best with the fewest side effects.
A person without the disease who agrees to take part in early clinical trials to test safety.
A substance that looks like the drug but contains no active ingredient.
An improvement in symptoms because the patient believes they are being treated.
Group given a placebo or existing treatment for comparison.
A trial where patients do not know whether they receive the drug or placebo.
A trial where neither patients nor doctors know who receives the drug or placebo.
Checking of scientific results by other independent scientists before publication.
Official approval that allows a medicine to be sold and prescribed.

mistakes.w: Drugs are tested on humans first, then animals.
mistakes.r: Preclinical testing on cells, tissues and animals comes before any human testing.

mistakes.w: Healthy volunteers are given the drug to see if it cures the disease.
mistakes.r: Healthy volunteers test safety and side effects at low doses; efficacy is tested on patients.

mistakes.w: A double-blind trial is where patients don't know if they get the drug.
mistakes.r: That is single blind; in double blind neither patients nor doctors know.

mistakes.w: A placebo is a weaker version of the drug.
mistakes.r: A placebo contains no active drug.

mistakes.w: Animals are tested to see if the drug works on animals.
mistakes.r: Animals are used to test toxicity and effects in a whole living body before humans.

mistakes.w: Start with a high dose to see if it works.
mistakes.r: Start with a very low dose and increase gradually to check safety.

mistakes.w: Testing on cells shows how the drug will affect the whole body.
mistakes.r: Cells cannot show effects on whole organisms, so animal tests follow.

mistakes.w: Once licensed, testing stops.
mistakes.r: The drug is monitored after licensing for rare side effects.

mistakes.w: The placebo effect means the placebo cures the illness.
mistakes.r: The placebo effect is a perceived improvement due to belief in treatment.

exam.q: State what is meant by a placebo.
model: A substance that looks like the drug but contains no active ingredient / no drug
exam.tip: Include 'no active ingredient'.

exam.q: Give two things that are tested in preclinical testing.
model: Toxicity / safety
Efficacy / whether it works
Dosage
exam.tip: Any two.

exam.q: Name two types of model used in preclinical testing.
model: Cells / tissues (cultured)
Live animals
exam.tip: Cells and tissues come first.

exam.q: Explain why new drugs are first tested on healthy volunteers at low doses.
model: To check the drug is safe / find side effects / check it is not toxic
Low dose reduces risk of harm
Healthy people so effects are due to the drug not the disease
exam.tip: Two linked points.

exam.q: Explain why a double-blind trial is used.
model: Neither patients nor doctors know who has the drug or placebo
Removes bias / doctors cannot influence results or interpret them differently
exam.tip: Define, then give the reason.

exam.q: Explain why a control group given a placebo is used in a clinical trial.
model: To compare with the group given the drug
To account for the placebo effect / show improvement is due to the drug
exam.tip: Mention comparison.

exam.q: Suggest one reason why a drug that passed animal tests may fail in clinical trials.
model: Animals are physiologically different from humans so the drug may be toxic / ineffective in humans
exam.tip: Be specific: different metabolism or biology.

exam.q: Explain why large numbers of patients are used in the later stages of clinical trials.
model: Results are more reliable / repeatable / reduce effect of individual variation
More likely to detect rare side effects
exam.tip: Two different reasons.

exam.q: Suggest why it may be unethical to give a placebo to patients with a serious disease.
model: Patients in control group receive no treatment
Their condition could worsen / they may die; use the existing treatment instead
exam.tip: Give the alternative too.

exam.q: Describe the stages in the development of a new medicine, from discovery to licensing.
model: Discovery of a potential drug, e.g. from plants, microorganisms or computer modelling
Development: chemical modified and produced in a usable form
Preclinical testing on cells and tissues for toxicity and efficacy
Preclinical testing on live animals to test effects on whole body
Clinical testing on healthy volunteers at low doses for safety / side effects
Clinical testing on patients to test efficacy and find optimum dose
Use of placebo / control group and double-blind trial
Results peer reviewed; drug licensed and monitored
exam.tip: Six-mark answers need the correct sequence and the purpose of each stage.

exam.q: Evaluate the use of animals in drug testing.
model: For: shows effect on a whole living organism with interacting organs
For: protects humans from toxic drugs / required by law
Against: animals may suffer / ethical objections
Against: animals differ from humans so results may not apply
Conclusion with justification
exam.tip: Balance both sides and conclude.

worked.q: A trial tested a new painkiller on 2000 patients. 1000 received the drug and 1000 a placebo. 620 in the drug group and 410 in the placebo group reported less pain. Calculate the percentage in each group and comment.
steps: Placebo group: 410 / 1000 x 100 = 41%
Difference = 21 percentage points
The 41% improvement in the placebo group shows the placebo effect
worked.ans: 62% vs 41%; the drug is more effective than placebo, and the control shows that part of the improvement in the drug group is due to the placebo effect.

worked.q: A company has discovered a chemical in a plant that kills cancer cells in culture. Describe the next steps before it can be prescribed.
steps: Develop: purify and modify the chemical, make it in a stable form
Further preclinical testing on tissues, then on live animals for toxicity and whole-body effects
Clinical trial on healthy volunteers at very low, increasing doses to check side effects
Trial on small then large groups of patients to test efficacy and find optimum dose, double blind with control group
Peer review, licensing and ongoing monitoring
worked.ans: Development, animal testing, healthy volunteer trials, patient trials (double blind, controlled), then licensing and monitoring.

worked.q: Patient group results for three doses: 10 mg reduced symptoms in 30% with 2% side effects; 20 mg in 65% with 5% side effects; 40 mg in 68% with 25% side effects. Which is the optimum dose?
steps: Compare efficacy: 20 mg and 40 mg are similar (65% vs 68%)
Compare side effects: 40 mg has five times more side effects than 20 mg
Optimum dose = most effective with fewest side effects
worked.ans: 20 mg is the optimum dose: nearly as effective as 40 mg but with far fewer side effects.

bio_edx.4.2.summary: Pathogens pass from one host to another by a small number of routes: **water**, **air**, **direct contact**, **animal vectors**, **body fluids** and **oral transmission** (food, drink or saliva). For each named disease you must state how it spreads and suggest **how spread can be reduced or prevented**, always explaining which link in the chain of transmission the measure breaks. The named examples are **cholera** (water), **tuberculosis** and **Chalara ash dieback** (airborne), **malaria** (animal vector), and, in the Biology course, **Helicobacter pylori** (oral transmission) and **Ebola** (body fluids).

core.p: For a communicable disease to spread, the pathogen must **leave an infected host**, **travel** to a new host, and **enter** that host. Every way of preventing spread works by breaking one of these links. This is the reasoning that earns marks: say **what the measure does** and **why that stops the pathogen reaching a new host**.
bullets: Leaving: coughs, sneezes, faeces, blood, spores released from a plant.
Travelling: through water, air, food, on hands or surfaces, inside a vector.
Entering: breathed in, swallowed, through cuts, through mucous membranes, by a bite.
Reducing contact between infected and healthy hosts (isolation, quarantine) stops all routes at once.
Treating infected hosts (e.g. antibiotics, antimalarials) reduces the number of pathogens available to spread.
Vaccination (5.14) makes new hosts immune so the pathogen cannot establish itself.

callouts.p: For 'explain how this reduces spread' always add the effect: e.g. 'mosquito nets stop mosquitoes biting, so Plasmodium is not transferred into the blood'.

core.p: The route depends on where the pathogen lives in the host and how it can survive outside it.
bullets: **Water**: drinking or washing in water contaminated with sewage (cholera).
**Airborne**: droplets from coughs and sneezes (TB, flu), or fungal spores carried on wind (Chalara ash dieback).
**Animal vectors**: an animal carries the pathogen between hosts without having the disease, e.g. mosquitoes (malaria). Insects can also carry plant pathogens.
**Oral transmission**: eating or drinking contaminated food or water, or contact with saliva or vomit (Helicobacter pylori).
**Body fluids**: blood, semen, vomit, faeces, breast milk (Ebola, HIV).
**Direct contact**: touching an infected person or contaminated surface (in plants, contact between infected and healthy plants or contaminated soil).

callouts.p: An organism that carries a pathogen from one host to another.

core.p: The **Vibrio cholerae** bacterium is released in huge numbers in the watery diarrhoea of infected people. Where sewage is not treated it gets into rivers, wells and drinking water. Anyone who drinks the water, or eats food washed in it, swallows the bacteria.
bullets: Outbreaks are most common where there is **poor sanitation**: refugee camps, after floods, earthquakes or wars, and in poorer areas without clean water.
**Reduce or prevent**: treat sewage properly and keep it separate from drinking water.
Provide **clean, treated drinking water** (e.g. chlorination), or **boil** water before drinking, which kills the bacteria.
Good hygiene: washing hands with soap after using the toilet and before handling food.
Avoid eating raw food washed in contaminated water.

callouts.p: Clean water and sewage treatment break the route from the faeces of an infected person to the mouth of a healthy person.

core.p: **Mycobacterium tuberculosis** infects the lungs. When an infected person **coughs or sneezes**, tiny droplets containing the bacteria are released and can be breathed in by others nearby. TB spreads most in **crowded, poorly ventilated** living conditions.
bullets: **Reduce or prevent**: cover the mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing, and dispose of tissues safely.
**Isolate** infected people (especially those with active lung TB) so others do not breathe in the droplets.
Improve **ventilation** and reduce overcrowding in homes, prisons and hospitals.
**Treat** infected people with a full course of antibiotics, so they stop being infectious.
Vaccinate with the **BCG vaccine**, particularly children in high-risk areas.
Finding and testing contacts of a patient (contact tracing) catches cases early.

core.p: The fungus that causes ash dieback produces **spores** on fallen leaves. These spores are carried by the **wind**, so the disease spreads naturally between nearby ash trees. It can also be carried over long distances, including between countries, on **infected young trees (saplings)** that are moved or imported.
bullets: **Reduce or prevent**: **remove and destroy (burn)** infected trees and fallen leaves, removing the source of spores.
**Ban or restrict imports** of ash trees from infected areas, and restrict movement of ash within the country.
Replant areas with different tree species, or with ash varieties that show **resistance** to the fungus.
Clean boots, tools and vehicles leaving infected woodland so spores and leaf fragments are not carried away.
Monitor woodlands to detect new outbreaks early.

callouts.p: Ash dieback is not spread by vectors or water in the spec: the answer is airborne spores (and movement of infected trees).

core.p: Malaria is caused by the protist **Plasmodium**, carried by the female **Anopheles mosquito**. When a mosquito bites an infected person it takes in the protist with the blood; when it bites someone else it injects the protist. Malaria cannot be passed directly between people, so **controlling the mosquito vector** is the most important way to stop it.
bullets: **Mosquito nets** over beds (often treated with insecticide) stop mosquitoes biting at night.
**Insecticides** sprayed in homes kill adult mosquitoes.
**Drain or cover stagnant (still) water** where mosquitoes lay eggs and larvae develop, or add oil or fish that eat larvae.
Insect **repellent** and long clothing reduce bites.
**Antimalarial drugs** treat infected people and can be taken by travellers to prevent infection, so fewer people carry Plasmodium for mosquitoes to pick up.

callouts.p: Malaria control targets either the vector (nets, insecticides, draining water) or the pathogen in people (antimalarial drugs).

fig.cap: The malaria transmission cycle, with control measures (red) that break it: nets and repellent stop bites, antimalarials kill Plasmodium in people, insecticide and draining still water reduce mosquito numbers.

core.p: **Helicobacter pylori**, which causes many stomach ulcers, is passed on by **oral transmission**: it enters the mouth in contaminated food or water, or from the saliva, vomit or faeces of an infected person. It is most common where there is poor sanitation and crowded living conditions.
bullets: **Reduce or prevent**: good hygiene, especially **hand washing** after using the toilet and before preparing food.
Drink **clean (treated) water**.
Prepare food hygienically and cook it properly.
Avoid sharing cutlery or cups with infected people.
Treating infected people with **antibiotics** removes the bacteria so they cannot pass it on.

core.p: The **Ebola virus** is spread by direct contact with the **body fluids** of an infected person, such as blood, vomit, faeces, saliva and semen, or with objects contaminated by them. Bodies of people who have died of Ebola remain highly infectious. Health workers and family carers are at highest risk.
bullets: **Isolate** infected patients and **quarantine** people who have had contact with them.
Health workers wear **protective clothing** (gloves, gown, mask, goggles) to stop body fluids reaching their skin, eyes and mouth.
**Sterilise or safely dispose of** contaminated equipment, bedding and clothing.
**Safe burial**: avoid touching bodies at funerals; trained teams handle burials.
**Contact tracing** to find and monitor anyone who may be infected.
Avoid contact with infected wild animals (bushmeat), the original source of outbreaks.
Restricting travel from outbreak areas and screening at borders slows spread between countries.

core.p: HIV is also spread by body fluids (5.8 covers it in detail). It is worth linking because the same principle applies: stop fluids passing between people.
bullets: Use **condoms** during sex.
Do not share needles; use sterile needles (needle exchange schemes).
Screen donated blood.
Antiretroviral drugs reduce the amount of virus, making transmission less likely, including from mother to baby.

core.h: General hygiene and public health measures
core.p: Many measures work against several diseases because they break more than one route at once.
bullets: **Hand washing** with soap removes pathogens picked up from surfaces, food and faeces.
**Disinfecting** surfaces kills pathogens, reducing contact spread.
**Isolating** infected individuals reduces contact with healthy hosts.
**Vaccination** reduces the number of people who can be infected and pass the pathogen on (see 5.14).
Good **food hygiene**: storing food cold, cooking thoroughly, preventing cross-contamination.
In plants: **crop rotation**, removing infected plants and controlling insect vectors with pesticides.

callouts.t: Match the measure to the route
callouts.p: A mosquito net will not stop cholera; boiling water will not stop TB. Marks come from choosing a measure that blocks the route used by that pathogen.

core.h: Summary: spread and control of the named diseases
core.p: Learn this table so you can give a correct route and two suitable control measures for any named disease.
bullets: Two different measures are usually needed for 2 marks.
Measures must be realistic for the situation in the question (for example, boiling water in a refugee camp).

head: Disease (pathogen)
Route of spread

rows: Treat sewage; clean or boiled water; hand washing
Cover coughs; isolate patients; ventilation; antibiotics; BCG vaccine

core.p: Higher-level questions may ask you to evaluate a measure. Consider how well it breaks the chain, its **cost**, how **practical** it is, and any **side effects**.
bullets: Draining water and insecticides reduce mosquitoes for everyone, but insecticides can harm other insects and mosquitoes can become **resistant**.
Mosquito nets are cheap and effective at night, but need to be used every night and kept in good repair.
Destroying ash trees removes spores but loses healthy trees too and changes woodland habitats.
Import bans protect a country but can be too late if the pathogen has already arrived.
Isolation is effective but requires facilities and staff; in poorer areas this may not be possible.
Clean water and sewage systems are very effective long-term but are expensive to build.

analogy.t: Pathogens as parcels in a delivery network
analogy.p: Think of a pathogen as a parcel that must be posted from an infected host to a new one. Each disease uses a particular delivery service: cholera goes by **water pipe**, TB by **air mail**, malaria by **courier** (the mosquito), Ebola by **hand delivery** (body fluids). To stop deliveries you close that particular service: treat the water pipes, cover the post box (mouth) when coughing, ban the courier (kill mosquitoes), or wear gloves. Shutting down the wrong service does nothing. Where it breaks down: parcels do not multiply on the way, but many pathogens grow in number in water, food or the vector, and the receiving host can sometimes 'refuse delivery' through immunity.

terms.d: A disease caused by a pathogen that can be passed from one organism to another.
The passing of a pathogen from an infected host to a new host.
An organism that carries a pathogen from one host to another, such as a mosquito.
Spread of pathogens through the air in droplets or as spores.
Spread of pathogens in water, usually contaminated with sewage.
Spread of pathogens by entering the mouth in contaminated food, water or saliva.
Fluids such as blood, semen, saliva, vomit and faeces that can carry pathogens.
Safe disposal and treatment of sewage and provision of clean water.
Keeping an infected individual separate from others to stop them spreading the pathogen.
Keeping people who may have been exposed separate until it is known they are not infected.
Finding and monitoring people who have been in contact with an infected person.
A chemical that kills insects, used to control vectors such as mosquitoes.
A tiny reproductive cell released by fungi that can be carried by wind.
The protist that causes malaria, carried by Anopheles mosquitoes.
A drug that kills Plasmodium, used to treat or prevent malaria.

mistakes.w: Malaria is spread by mosquitoes, so people should drink clean water.
mistakes.r: Clean water does not stop a vector: use nets, insecticide, draining still water or antimalarial drugs.

mistakes.w: Cholera is spread through the air by coughing.
mistakes.r: Cholera is spread by water contaminated with sewage (faeces).

mistakes.w: Ash dieback is spread by insects.
mistakes.r: Ash dieback is spread by airborne fungal spores and by moving infected trees.

mistakes.w: Use antibiotics to stop the spread of Ebola.
mistakes.r: Ebola is a virus so antibiotics have no effect; use isolation, protective clothing and safe burial.

mistakes.w: Isolate the mosquito to stop malaria.
mistakes.r: Kill or avoid the vector (insecticide, nets, drain breeding sites); people with malaria can be treated with antimalarials.

mistakes.w: Washing hands stops TB.
mistakes.r: TB is mainly airborne; cover coughs, isolate patients, improve ventilation, vaccinate and treat with antibiotics.

mistakes.w: Mosquito nets kill the malaria pathogen.
mistakes.r: Nets stop mosquitoes biting, so Plasmodium is not transferred into the blood.

mistakes.w: Clean water is used to stop cholera (no explanation).
mistakes.r: Explain: clean or boiled water contains no cholera bacteria, so people do not swallow the pathogen.

exam.q: State how cholera is spread.
model: In water contaminated with sewage (faeces).
exam.tip: Say contaminated water, not just water.

exam.q: Name the vector that spreads malaria.
model: (Female Anopheles) mosquito.
exam.tip: The vector, not the pathogen.

exam.q: Give two ways the spread of tuberculosis can be reduced.
model: Cover mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing / isolate infected people / improve ventilation.
Treat with antibiotics / BCG vaccination.
exam.tip: Two different measures for two marks.

exam.q: Explain how using mosquito nets reduces the spread of malaria.
model: Nets stop mosquitoes biting people (at night).
So Plasmodium / the protist is not transferred into (or out of) the blood.
exam.tip: Link the measure to the pathogen.

exam.q: Explain why draining areas of still water reduces the number of cases of malaria.
model: Mosquitoes lay eggs / larvae develop in still water.
Fewer mosquitoes (vectors) so fewer people are bitten and infected.
exam.tip: Mention breeding.

exam.q: Chalara ash dieback has spread across the UK. Suggest two ways to reduce its spread and explain each.
model: Remove and burn infected trees / leaves.
This removes the source of spores.
Ban imports / movement of ash saplings.
So infected trees cannot carry the fungus to new areas.
exam.tip: One mark for each measure, one for each explanation.

exam.q: After a flood, many people in a town develop cholera. Explain why the flood increased the number of cases.
model: Sewage mixes with / contaminates drinking water.
People drink water containing cholera bacteria.
Treatment works / clean water supply damaged, so bacteria are not removed.
exam.tip: Link the event to contaminated water.

exam.q: Explain how the spread of Helicobacter pylori between people can be reduced.
model: Hand washing / good food hygiene / clean drinking water.
Prevents bacteria entering the mouth (oral transmission).
exam.tip: Name the route: oral.

exam.q: Explain why health workers treating Ebola patients wear protective clothing.
model: Ebola is spread by contact with body fluids.
Clothing (gloves, masks, goggles) stops body fluids touching skin, eyes or mouth, so the virus cannot enter.
exam.tip: Mention body fluids.

exam.q: A country wants to reduce malaria. Some people suggest spraying insecticide; others suggest giving out mosquito nets. Evaluate the two methods.
model: Insecticide kills mosquitoes (vector), so fewer are available to carry Plasmodium.
It covers a whole area and protects everyone, day and night.
But insecticide can harm other organisms / food chains, and mosquitoes can become resistant; it must be repeated and is costly.
Nets stop mosquitoes biting while people sleep, so Plasmodium is not transmitted.
Nets are cheap and do not harm other species, but only protect at night and must be used and maintained correctly.
Conclusion: using both together (plus draining water / antimalarials) is most effective.
exam.tip: Give advantages and disadvantages of each and a justified conclusion.

exam.q: Describe how the Ebola virus is spread and explain three ways its spread can be controlled during an outbreak.
model: Spread by contact with body fluids (blood, vomit, faeces) of infected people or bodies.
Isolate patients, so healthy people do not contact their body fluids.
Health workers wear protective clothing, so fluids cannot reach their skin, mouth or eyes.
Safe burial of bodies, because bodies remain infectious.
Sterilise / destroy contaminated equipment and bedding.
Contact tracing and quarantine so people who might be infected are found before they spread it.
exam.tip: Each measure needs a reason linked to body fluids.

worked.q: A refugee camp has an outbreak of cholera. Suggest and explain two practical actions an aid organisation could take straight away.
steps: Identify the route: cholera bacteria pass from faeces to drinking water.
Action 1: supply clean bottled water or chlorine tablets, or tell people to boil water. This kills or avoids the bacteria, so they are not swallowed.
Action 2: build separate latrines away from water sources. This stops faeces (containing bacteria) contaminating the water.
Extra: provide soap for hand washing to stop transfer from hands to food.
worked.ans: Provide clean or boiled water and safe toilets away from water sources; both break the faeces-to-water-to-mouth route of the cholera bacterium.

worked.q: Data show TB cases fell sharply in a city after new housing replaced crowded, poorly ventilated flats. Explain the link.
steps: TB is spread by airborne droplets from coughs and sneezes.
In crowded flats people are close together and share the same air, so they breathe in droplets from infected people.
Poor ventilation means droplets stay in the air longer.
New housing with more space and ventilation lowers the concentration of bacteria in the air, so fewer people are infected.
worked.ans: Less crowding and better ventilation reduce contact with airborne droplets carrying Mycobacterium tuberculosis, so transmission fell.

worked.q: Explain why a ban on importing ash saplings helped slow Chalara ash dieback in the UK, but did not stop it completely.
steps: The fungus was brought in on infected saplings, so a ban stops new infected trees arriving.
But the fungus was already in the UK by the time the ban was introduced.
Its spores are carried by wind, so it continues to spread naturally between trees.
Spores can also blow across the sea from mainland Europe.
worked.ans: The ban removed one long-distance route (infected saplings), but airborne spores from trees already infected kept spreading the disease.

bio_edx.4.3.summary: Viruses can only reproduce inside a host cell. In the **lytic pathway** the virus attaches, injects its genetic material, uses the cell to **replicate viral components**, **assembles** new viruses and then **bursts (lyses)** the cell to release them. In the **lysogenic pathway** the viral genetic material is **inserted into the host's DNA** and copied every time the cell divides, staying **dormant** until a trigger switches it into the lytic pathway. This is triple Biology content (5.7B) and is usually described using a **bacteriophage** infecting a bacterium.

core.h: Why viruses need a host cell
core.p: A virus is **not a cell**: it is genetic material (DNA or RNA) inside a **protein coat**. It has no ribosomes, no enzymes for respiration and no cytoplasm, so it **cannot make proteins or copy itself on its own**. Instead it hijacks a host cell, using the host's **ribosomes, enzymes, nucleotides, amino acids and ATP** to build new viruses.
bullets: Viruses infect every kind of organism: animals, plants and even bacteria.
Viruses that infect bacteria are called **bacteriophages** (phages).
Each virus infects only certain cell types: its proteins must fit **receptor** molecules on the host cell surface.
There are two pathways after infection: **lytic** (immediate reproduction and cell death) and **lysogenic** (hidden, dormant stage first).
The lysogenic pathway always ends with the lytic pathway when the virus becomes active.

callouts.p: Viral proteins are made by the host cell's ribosomes, and viral genetic material is copied using the host's enzymes and nucleotides.

fig.cap: A bacteriophage. The protein coat (capsid) protects the genetic material; the tail fibres attach to receptors on the bacterial cell surface and the tail injects the DNA.

core.p: The lytic pathway is the 'fast' route: the virus reproduces straight away and the host cell is destroyed. Edexcel names five stages, which you should learn in order using the spec words.
bullets: 1. **Attachment** of the virus to the host cell.
2. **Injection** of viral genetic material into the cell.
3. **Replication of viral components** (genetic material and proteins) using the host cell.
4. **Assembly** of new viruses.
5. **Lysis** of the host cell, releasing the new viruses.
The released viruses infect neighbouring cells and the cycle repeats, so numbers rise very quickly.

callouts.p: A I R A L: Attach, Inject, Replicate, Assemble, Lyse.

core.p: The virus collides with a host cell and **proteins on the virus bind to specific receptor molecules** on the cell surface membrane (or bacterial cell wall). The fit is specific, which is why a particular virus only infects certain species or tissues.
bullets: In a bacteriophage, the **tail fibres** attach to the bacterial cell wall.
No receptor match means no attachment, so no infection.
This specificity explains, for example, why HIV infects certain white blood cells.

core.p: The virus **injects its genetic material (DNA or RNA) into the host cell**. In a bacteriophage the tail contracts and acts like a syringe, pushing the DNA through the cell wall and membrane. The empty protein coat stays outside the cell.
bullets: Only the genetic material needs to enter: it carries the instructions for making new viruses.
Some animal viruses instead enter whole and release their genetic material inside the cell.
After injection the virus follows either the lytic or the lysogenic pathway.

core.p: The viral genetic material takes over the cell. The host cell's **enzymes copy the viral genetic material** many times, and the host's **ribosomes make viral proteins** (for new protein coats and tails), following the viral genes. The cell stops doing its normal jobs.
bullets: The cell's raw materials (nucleotides and amino acids) and energy (ATP from respiration) are used up making virus parts.
Many copies of the viral DNA and many protein coat subunits build up inside the cell.
The host cell's own DNA may be broken down by viral enzymes.

callouts.p: Viruses do not reproduce by dividing like bacteria. Their parts are made separately inside the cell and then assembled.

core.p: The newly made viral components are **put together (assembled) into complete new virus particles**: copies of genetic material are packed into new protein coats, and tails and fibres are added.
bullets: Hundreds of new viruses can be assembled inside one cell.
Each new virus is identical to the original (unless a mutation occurred during copying).

core.h: Stage 5: lysis of the host cell
core.p: Viral enzymes break down the host cell (in bacteria, the cell wall), so the cell **bursts open (lyses)** and **dies**, releasing all the new viruses. Each one can attach to and infect another host cell.
bullets: 'Lytic' comes from **lysis**, meaning splitting or bursting of a cell.
Destruction of host cells is what causes the symptoms of many viral diseases.
Because every lysis releases many viruses, infection spreads rapidly through a tissue or a bacterial culture.
In a lawn of bacteria on agar, clear patches (plaques) show where phages have lysed the cells.

core.p: In the lysogenic pathway, after attachment and injection, the viral genetic material is **incorporated (inserted) into the host cell's DNA**. The virus does **not** make new viruses straight away, and the host cell is not harmed at first. This dormant stage is often called a **latent** stage.
bullets: **Incorporation**: the viral DNA becomes part of the host's chromosome.
Each time the host cell divides, the viral DNA is **copied along with the host DNA**, so every daughter cell also contains the viral genes.
The number of infected cells rises without any symptoms.
The viral genes are **inactive (dormant)**: no viral proteins or new viruses are made.
A **trigger**, such as stress, damage to the cell, UV light or certain chemicals, causes the viral DNA to leave the host DNA and enter the **lytic pathway**.

callouts.p: The viral genetic material is inserted into the host DNA and replicated with it when the cell divides, remaining dormant until it becomes active and enters the lytic pathway.
