core.p: When the dormant viral genes are activated, the viral genetic material is cut out of the host DNA and the virus carries on with **replication, assembly and lysis**. Because the viral DNA has been copied into many cells during the dormant stage, many cells can become active at once.
bullets: This explains why some viral infections appear to go away and then come back.
A population of bacteria carrying dormant phage DNA can suddenly lyse when exposed to a trigger such as UV light.
HIV inserts its genetic material into the DNA of white blood cells, which is why it cannot easily be cleared from the body.

core.h: Comparing the lytic and lysogenic pathways
core.p: Questions often ask for similarities and differences. Both start with attachment and injection; the key difference is what happens to the viral genetic material straight after injection.
bullets: Similarity: both need a host cell and begin with **attachment** and **injection** of genetic material.
Similarity: both eventually produce new viruses (the lysogenic pathway does so when it switches to lytic).
Difference: lytic destroys the host cell quickly; lysogenic keeps it alive for a long time.

core.h: Why the pathways matter for disease and treatment
core.p: Understanding the pathways helps explain how viral diseases behave and why they are hard to treat.
bullets: Lysis of many cells causes **tissue damage** and symptoms.
During the lysogenic stage the virus is hidden in host DNA, so the **immune system cannot detect it** and drugs that target active viruses do not remove it.
Antibiotics do not work on viruses at any stage, because viruses use host cell machinery rather than bacterial structures.
Antiviral drugs must stop a viral stage (for example replication) without harming host cells, which is difficult because the virus uses the host's own machinery.
Bacteriophages that follow the lytic pathway are being studied as **phage therapy** to kill antibiotic-resistant bacteria.

callouts.p: Describe the stages in the correct order with the spec words, then compare: what happens to the viral DNA, when new viruses form and what happens to the host cell.

analogy.t: A virus as a computer virus or a hijacked factory
analogy.p: A host cell is like a factory with machines (ribosomes and enzymes) that follow instruction manuals (DNA). In the **lytic pathway** a saboteur sneaks in a new manual: the machines stop making normal products and build copies of the saboteur instead, until the factory is so full it bursts and the copies spill out to invade other factories. In the **lysogenic pathway** the saboteur glues its pages into the factory's own manual. Whenever the factory builds a new branch (cell division), the manual is photocopied, saboteur pages included, but nothing happens until an alarm (a trigger) switches those pages on. Where it breaks down: a real factory chooses what to build, but a cell has no choice or awareness, and a virus has no intentions; it is simply chemicals whose structure fits the cell's machinery.

terms.d: A non-cellular particle of genetic material in a protein coat that can only reproduce inside a host cell.
A virus that infects bacteria.
The cell a virus infects and uses to make new viruses.
The outer protein shell of a virus that surrounds and protects its genetic material.
A molecule on the host cell surface that a virus binds to during attachment.
The first stage of infection, when the virus binds to the surface of the host cell.
The stage in which the virus inserts its genetic material into the host cell.
The host cell copies viral genetic material and makes viral proteins, following viral genes.
Putting the new viral genetic material and proteins together to make complete new viruses.
The bursting of the host cell, which releases new viruses and kills the cell.
A virus life cycle in which the virus replicates immediately and the host cell bursts to release new viruses.
A virus life cycle in which viral genetic material is inserted into the host DNA and copied when the cell divides, staying dormant until it enters the lytic pathway.
Insertion of the viral genetic material into the host cell's DNA.
Inactive: viral genes are present but not being used to make new viruses.
A factor, such as stress or UV light, that causes dormant viral genes to become active and enter the lytic pathway.

mistakes.w: The virus divides inside the host cell.
mistakes.r: Viral components are replicated by the host cell and then assembled into new viruses; viruses do not divide.

mistakes.w: In the lysogenic pathway the host cell bursts straight away.
mistakes.r: In the lysogenic pathway viral DNA is inserted into host DNA and stays dormant; lysis only happens after it enters the lytic pathway.

mistakes.w: The whole virus enters the bacterium.
mistakes.r: A bacteriophage injects only its genetic material; the protein coat stays outside.

mistakes.w: The virus makes its own proteins.
mistakes.r: The host cell's ribosomes make viral proteins using the viral genes.

mistakes.w: Lysogenic means the virus is killed or destroyed.
mistakes.r: In the lysogenic pathway the virus is hidden and copied with the host DNA; it is not destroyed.

mistakes.w: In the lysogenic pathway the viral DNA is copied by the virus.
mistakes.r: It is copied along with the host's DNA each time the host cell divides.

mistakes.w: Stages written out of order, e.g. assembly before replication.
mistakes.r: Attachment, injection, replication of viral components, assembly, lysis.

mistakes.w: Lysis means the virus attaches to the cell.
mistakes.r: Lysis is the bursting of the host cell to release new viruses.

exam.q: State what is meant by lysis.
model: Bursting (splitting open) of the host cell, releasing new viruses.
exam.tip: Mention the host cell bursting.

exam.q: Name the first stage of both the lytic and lysogenic pathways.
model: Attachment (of the virus to the host cell).
exam.tip: Use the spec word.

exam.q: Explain why a virus cannot reproduce outside a host cell.
model: A virus has no ribosomes / enzymes / cytoplasm (it is not a cell).
So it needs the host cell's machinery to make viral proteins and copy its genetic material.
exam.tip: Say what the virus lacks and what it uses.

exam.q: Describe what happens to the viral genetic material in the lysogenic pathway.
model: It is inserted (incorporated) into the host cell's DNA.
It is copied every time the host cell divides (and stays dormant).
exam.tip: Two ideas: inserted, copied with host DNA.

exam.q: Give two differences between the lytic and lysogenic pathways.
model: Lytic: viral genetic material is not inserted into host DNA; lysogenic: it is inserted.
Lytic: new viruses made immediately and cell bursts; lysogenic: dormant, host cell survives and divides.
exam.tip: State both sides of each difference.

exam.q: A bacteriophage infects a bacterium and follows the lytic pathway. Describe the stages that lead to new phages being released.
model: Phage attaches to the bacterial cell (tail fibres bind to receptors).
Injects its DNA into the bacterium.
Bacterium's enzymes and ribosomes replicate viral DNA and make viral proteins (replication of viral components).
New phages are assembled and the cell bursts (lysis), releasing them.
exam.tip: Five spec stages in order.

exam.q: Suggest why a person infected with a virus that follows the lysogenic pathway may have no symptoms for many years.
model: Viral DNA is inserted into host DNA and is dormant / inactive.
No new viruses are made and host cells are not destroyed, so no tissue damage.
exam.tip: Link dormancy to no cell damage.

exam.q: Explain why the number of viruses in an infection can increase very rapidly in the lytic pathway.
model: Many new viruses (e.g. 100+) are assembled in each host cell.
Each released virus infects another cell, so numbers multiply each cycle.
exam.tip: Mention many viruses per cell and repeated cycles.

exam.q: Explain how the lysogenic pathway can lead to many cells in a tissue becoming infected even before the virus becomes active.
model: Viral DNA is inserted into host cell DNA.
When the host cell divides, the DNA (including viral DNA) is copied.
All daughter cells contain the viral DNA, so the number of infected cells increases with each division.
exam.tip: Link to mitosis copying the DNA.

exam.q: Describe and compare the lytic and lysogenic pathways of a virus life cycle.
model: Both start with attachment of the virus to the host cell and injection of genetic material.
Lytic: viral genetic material is copied and viral proteins made using the host's enzymes and ribosomes.
Lytic: new viruses are assembled and the cell lyses (bursts), releasing them to infect other cells.
Lysogenic: viral genetic material is incorporated into host DNA.
Lysogenic: it is copied every time the host cell divides and stays dormant; the host cell is not harmed.
Lysogenic: a trigger (e.g. stress / UV) makes the viral DNA enter the lytic pathway, ending in lysis.
exam.tip: Cover all stages of both, then a clear comparison.

worked.q: A scientist adds bacteriophages to a culture of bacteria. After 30 minutes there are no new phages; after 60 minutes the number of free phages has increased greatly and the culture becomes clear. Explain these results using the lytic pathway.
steps: 0 to 30 minutes: phages attach and inject DNA. Inside the cells, viral components are being replicated, but nothing has been released yet.
30 to 60 minutes: viruses are assembled inside each bacterium.
Then lysis bursts the bacterial cells, releasing many new phages, so the number of free phages rises sharply.
Bacteria are killed by lysis, so the cloudy culture becomes clear.
worked.ans: The delay is time for replication and assembly inside the cells; lysis then releases many phages at once and kills the bacteria, clearing the culture.

worked.q: A bacterium infected by a phage via the lysogenic pathway divides 5 times. How many cells contain the viral DNA? Explain.
steps: Viral DNA is inserted into the bacterial DNA, so it is copied every time the cell divides.
Each division doubles the number of cells: 1 becomes 2, 4, 8, 16, 32.
Number of cells = 2 to the power 5 = 32.
All 32 cells contain the viral DNA, but none has burst because the viral genes are dormant.
worked.ans: 32 cells, all carrying dormant viral DNA, because it is copied with the host DNA at every division.

worked.q: A culture of bacteria has been growing normally for many generations, although it was infected with a phage long ago. After the culture is exposed to UV light, most of the bacteria burst and the culture fills with phages. Explain these observations.
steps: The phage followed the lysogenic pathway: its DNA was inserted into the bacterial DNA.
Each time the bacteria divided, the viral DNA was copied too, so almost every cell carried it, but it was dormant, so the bacteria grew normally.
UV light acted as a trigger, activating the viral genes in many cells at once.
The virus entered the lytic pathway: viral components were replicated, new phages assembled, and the cells lysed, releasing phages.
worked.ans: The dormant (lysogenic) viral DNA had spread to nearly every cell by cell division; UV light triggered the lytic pathway in all of them, so they burst together.

bio_edx.4.4.summary: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are **communicable diseases** passed from person to person in body fluids during sexual contact. Edexcel names two: **Chlamydia**, caused by a **bacterium** (a non-viral STI that is often symptomless but can cause infertility and is cured with antibiotics), and **HIV**, a **virus** that destroys **lymphocytes** (white blood cells) and leads to **AIDS**. You must explain how each is spread (unprotected sex; for HIV also shared needles, infected blood and mother to baby) and how spread is reduced, linking each method to the route it blocks.

core.p: An STI is a **communicable** (infectious) disease caused by a **pathogen** that passes between people mainly through **sexual contact**, in body fluids such as semen, vaginal fluid and blood. Because the pathogen needs close contact with these fluids, the ways of stopping it all aim to stop fluids passing from one person to another.
bullets: **Communicable** = can be passed from one person to another, because it is caused by a pathogen.
Edexcel names two STIs: **Chlamydia** (bacterium) and **HIV** (virus).
STI pathogens do not survive long outside the body, so they are not spread by air, food or touching surfaces.
Spread depends on **behaviour**: unprotected sex, number of partners, sharing needles.
Many infected people show **no symptoms**, so they spread the infection without knowing.

callouts.p: An infection caused by a pathogen that is transmitted through sexual activity, in body fluids.

core.p: Chlamydia is caused by the **bacterium** Chlamydia trachomatis. Because the pathogen is a bacterium, Chlamydia is described in the spec as a **non-viral STI**. Bacteria are living cells, so they can be killed by **antibiotics**.
bullets: Pathogen type: **bacterium** (prokaryotic cell with cell wall, no nucleus).
The bacteria live and reproduce **inside cells** of the reproductive system (cervix, urethra).
Spread by **unprotected sexual contact** (vaginal, anal or oral sex) with an infected person.
Can also pass from a mother to her baby during **birth**, causing eye infections in the newborn.
Many people, especially women, have **no symptoms**, so it spreads easily.

callouts.p: Chlamydia is caused by a bacterium, not a virus, so it can be cured with antibiotics.

core.p: When symptoms happen they are usually mild, such as pain when urinating or unusual discharge. The serious problem is long-term damage: untreated infection can spread and cause **pelvic inflammatory disease** in women and damage the **oviducts** (fallopian tubes), which can lead to **infertility**.
bullets: Possible symptoms: pain when urinating, unusual discharge, pain in the lower abdomen.
Often **symptomless**, so infected people do not seek treatment.
Untreated: scarring of the oviducts can block them, so eggs cannot travel to the uterus, causing **infertility** or ectopic pregnancy.
In men it can cause inflammation of the testes.
Because it is symptomless but damaging, **screening** of sexually active young people is important.

callouts.p: Lack of symptoms is exactly why Chlamydia spreads widely and causes infertility without people knowing.

core.h: Chlamydia: treatment and why antibiotics work
core.p: Chlamydia is treated with **antibiotics**. Antibiotics work against bacteria because they target structures or processes found in bacterial cells but not in human cells, such as the bacterial cell wall or bacterial ribosomes. So the bacteria are killed or stopped from growing without harming the patient's cells.
bullets: Diagnosed by a simple **urine test** or **swab**, then treated with a short course of antibiotics.
The **whole course** must be taken to kill all the bacteria and reduce the risk of resistance.
Sexual partners should also be **tested and treated**, otherwise the infection passes back and forth.
Avoid sex until treatment is finished.
Being cured does not give lasting immunity: you can be **reinfected**.

callouts.p: If asked why Chlamydia can be cured but HIV cannot, say Chlamydia is a bacterium so antibiotics kill it; HIV is a virus and antibiotics do not affect viruses.

core.p: HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) is a **virus**. It is not a cell: it is genetic material (RNA) inside a protein coat. It can only reproduce inside host cells. HIV infects and destroys **lymphocytes**, a type of white blood cell that is part of the immune system.
bullets: Pathogen type: **virus**.
It enters **lymphocytes** (white blood cells) and uses them to make new viruses.
New viruses are released, **destroying** the lymphocyte and infecting more lymphocytes.
Over years, the number of lymphocytes falls and the immune system becomes weaker.
Early infection may cause mild flu-like symptoms, then often **no symptoms** for years.

callouts.p: A virus that infects and destroys white blood cells (lymphocytes), weakening the immune system and leading to AIDS.

fig.cap: Chlamydia is caused by a bacterium, a living cell, so antibiotics can kill it. HIV is a virus, a protein coat around genetic material, which is not a cell, so antibiotics have no effect on it.

core.p: **AIDS** (acquired immune deficiency syndrome) is the late stage of HIV infection. It develops when so many lymphocytes have been destroyed that the immune system can no longer fight off other pathogens. People with AIDS do not usually die of HIV itself but of **opportunistic infections** and some cancers that a healthy immune system would control.
bullets: HIV destroys lymphocytes, so fewer **antibodies** are made and fewer pathogens are destroyed.
The body becomes **more susceptible** to other infections, such as tuberculosis (TB) and pneumonia.
This is an example of **one disease increasing the risk of another** (links to spec 5.3).
Without treatment, AIDS usually develops several years (often around 10) after infection.
There is **no cure** and **no vaccine** for HIV.

callouts.t: HIV is not the same as AIDS
callouts.p: HIV is the virus; AIDS is the condition that develops when HIV has badly damaged the immune system.

fig.cap: Without treatment, lymphocyte numbers fall over several years as HIV destroys them. When they drop very low the immune system fails and AIDS begins, so other infections take hold.

core.p: HIV cannot be cured, but it can be controlled with **antiretroviral drugs**. These stop the virus reproducing inside lymphocytes, so the amount of virus in the blood (the viral load) falls and lymphocyte numbers stay higher. This delays or prevents AIDS and lets people live a near-normal lifespan.
bullets: Antiretrovirals must be taken **for life**; they control the virus but do not remove it.
Lower viral load means a person is **much less likely to pass HIV on**.
Treatment of a pregnant mother greatly reduces the chance of passing HIV to her baby.
Antibiotics **do not** treat HIV, though they may be used for the bacterial infections that people with AIDS catch.
Early **testing** matters: the sooner treatment starts, the less damage to the immune system.

callouts.p: Never say HIV is treated with antibiotics. It is treated with antiretroviral drugs.

core.h: How the two STIs are spread
core.p: Both Chlamydia and HIV pass in **body fluids**. The routes differ slightly: Chlamydia is spread almost entirely by sexual contact, while HIV is in the **blood** as well, so any route that mixes blood also spreads HIV.
bullets: **Unprotected sexual intercourse** with an infected person spreads both.
HIV: **sharing needles** (for example by intravenous drug users) transfers infected blood.
HIV: **mother to baby** across the placenta, during birth or in **breast milk**.
HIV: transfusion of **infected blood** (rare in the UK because donated blood is screened).
Neither is spread by kissing, sharing cups, toilet seats or insect bites.

core.p: Exam questions often ask you to compare the two STIs. Build every comparison on the pathogen type, because that explains the treatment and the outcome.
bullets: Both are **communicable** and spread through body fluids.
Both can be **symptomless** for a long time, which helps them spread.
Both are reduced by **condoms** and by **testing and treatment**.

head: Feature
Chlamydia
HIV
rows: Infection of reproductive system; can cause infertility
Unprotected sex; mother to baby at birth
Unprotected sex, shared needles, infected blood, mother to baby
Flu-like at first, then often none for years

core.p: Each prevention method works by **blocking a route** of transmission or by **reducing the number of infected people** who can pass the pathogen on. In an answer, always say which route the method blocks and why.
bullets: **Condoms** (male or female): a physical **barrier** so body fluids are not exchanged during sex. Protects against both STIs.
**Screening and testing**: people who are infected but symptomless are found and treated (Chlamydia cured; HIV controlled), so they stop spreading it. Includes contact tracing of partners.
**Fewer sexual partners**: fewer contacts means less chance of meeting an infected person.
**Needle exchange schemes** / not sharing needles: drug users get sterile needles, so blood is not passed on (HIV).
**Screening donated blood**: infected blood is not used in transfusions (HIV).
**Antiretroviral drugs**: lower viral load so HIV is less likely to be passed on; given in pregnancy to protect the baby.
**Avoiding breastfeeding** by HIV-positive mothers where safe alternatives exist (HIV).
**PrEP**: HIV-negative people at high risk can take antiretroviral drugs to prevent infection.

callouts.p: A mark scheme gives one mark for the method and one for how it works, e.g. 'use condoms (1) which act as a barrier so body fluids are not exchanged (1)'.

core.h: Why there is no vaccine or cure for HIV
core.p: Vaccines work by giving the immune system an inactive pathogen so memory lymphocytes are made. HIV is very hard to vaccinate against because it **mutates rapidly**, changing its surface antigens, and because it attacks the very **lymphocytes** that a vaccine relies on. It also hides inside host cells, so drugs cannot remove all of it.
bullets: Antigens change, so antibodies made against one form may not fit the next.
The virus lives **inside host cells**, so killing it would damage the cells.
This is why **prevention** (condoms, testing, needle exchange) is so important for HIV.

core.h: Applying the ideas to data and scenarios
core.p: Edexcel likes to give data, such as numbers of new Chlamydia diagnoses by age group, or HIV cases in different countries, and ask you to explain patterns or suggest how to reduce spread.
bullets: Higher rates in **young adults** (15 to 24) link to more partners and less condom use; more testing also finds more cases.
A rise in diagnoses may mean **more screening**, not only more infection: say this when evaluating data.
Higher HIV rates where there is less access to testing, condoms and antiretrovirals.
In a 6 mark answer, link each named route to a matching prevention method.
Use the words **pathogen, bacterium, virus, body fluids, barrier, lymphocytes** precisely.

callouts.p: When asked whether data prove more people have Chlamydia, mention that more testing would also increase the number of cases found.

analogy.t: STIs as uninvited guests using secret doors
analogy.p: Think of the body as a house. STIs can only get in through a few secret doors: sexual contact, shared needles, blood and mother to baby. Condoms, needle exchange and blood screening are locks on those doors. Chlamydia is a burglar (a living bacterium) the security guards can catch with the right tool (antibiotics). HIV is a saboteur that attacks the security guards themselves (lymphocytes), so eventually anyone can walk in (AIDS). Where it breaks down: a house can be secured once and stay safe, but people can be infected again and again, and there is no 'catch' for HIV, only drugs that slow the saboteur down.

terms.d: An infection caused by a pathogen that passes between people through sexual contact, in body fluids.
A disease caused by a pathogen that can be passed from one person to another.
A microorganism that causes disease, such as a bacterium, virus, fungus or protist.
A non-viral STI caused by a bacterium; often symptomless and can cause infertility; treated with antibiotics.
A single-celled prokaryotic organism with a cell wall and no nucleus; some are pathogens.
A non-living particle of genetic material in a protein coat that can only reproduce inside host cells.
Human immunodeficiency virus: a virus that destroys lymphocytes and leads to AIDS.
Acquired immune deficiency syndrome: the late stage of HIV infection, when the immune system is too weak to fight other infections.
A type of white blood cell that makes antibodies; the cell HIV infects and destroys.
An infection that a healthy immune system would control but which causes disease when the immune system is weakened, e.g. TB in AIDS.
A drug that kills bacteria or stops them growing without harming human cells; has no effect on viruses.
A drug that stops HIV reproducing, lowering viral load and delaying AIDS; does not cure HIV.
A barrier method of contraception that stops body fluids being exchanged during sex, reducing STI spread.
Testing people who may have no symptoms so infections are found and treated early.
A scheme giving drug users sterile needles so infected blood is not passed on.
Being unable to conceive; a possible result of untreated Chlamydia scarring the oviducts.

mistakes.w: Chlamydia is caused by a virus.
mistakes.r: Chlamydia is caused by a bacterium (a non-viral STI).

mistakes.w: HIV is treated with antibiotics.
mistakes.r: Antibiotics do not affect viruses; HIV is controlled with antiretroviral drugs.

mistakes.w: HIV and AIDS are the same thing.
mistakes.r: HIV is the virus; AIDS is the syndrome that develops when HIV has destroyed many lymphocytes.

mistakes.w: HIV kills you directly.
mistakes.r: HIV weakens the immune system so people die from other (opportunistic) infections or cancers.

mistakes.w: HIV attacks red blood cells.
mistakes.r: HIV attacks white blood cells, specifically lymphocytes.

mistakes.w: The contraceptive pill protects against STIs.
mistakes.r: Only barrier methods such as condoms stop exchange of body fluids; the pill does not.

mistakes.w: Condoms kill the pathogen.
mistakes.r: Condoms are a physical barrier that stops body fluids being exchanged.

mistakes.w: There is a vaccine for HIV.
mistakes.r: There is no vaccine and no cure for HIV.

mistakes.w: You can catch HIV from kissing or sharing cups.
mistakes.r: HIV is spread only in body fluids such as semen, vaginal fluid, blood and breast milk.

exam.q: Name the type of pathogen that causes Chlamydia.
model: Bacterium.
exam.tip: Spec calls Chlamydia a non-viral STI.

exam.q: State the type of cell that HIV infects and destroys.
model: Lymphocytes / white blood cells.
exam.tip: Red blood cells gets no mark.

exam.q: Give two ways HIV can be passed from one person to another other than by sexual contact.
model: Sharing needles (e.g. drug users).
Mother to baby (placenta, birth or breast milk) / transfusion of infected blood.
exam.tip: Be specific: 'blood' alone is too vague; say how the blood is transferred.

exam.q: Explain how using condoms reduces the spread of Chlamydia.
model: Condom acts as a (physical) barrier.
So body fluids / bacteria are not passed between partners.
exam.tip: Two marks need the method of action and what it stops.

exam.q: Explain why Chlamydia can be treated with antibiotics but HIV cannot.
model: Chlamydia is caused by a bacterium, which antibiotics kill.
HIV is a virus; antibiotics do not affect viruses (viruses live inside cells).
exam.tip: Name both pathogen types.

exam.q: Many people infected with Chlamydia have no symptoms. Explain why this makes screening important.
model: Infected people do not know they have it so would not seek treatment and may infect others.
Screening finds the infection so it can be treated with antibiotics before it causes infertility / spreads.
exam.tip: Link symptomless to both spread and long-term damage.

exam.q: Explain how HIV infection leads to AIDS.
model: HIV infects lymphocytes / white blood cells.
The virus reproduces inside them and destroys them, so lymphocyte numbers fall.
Immune system becomes too weak to fight other infections (AIDS), so opportunistic infections develop.
exam.tip: Show a chain of cause and effect.

exam.q: Explain why people with AIDS are more likely to develop tuberculosis.
model: Fewer lymphocytes so fewer antibodies made.
Body cannot destroy the TB bacteria, so the person is more susceptible.
exam.tip: Example of one disease increasing susceptibility to another.

exam.q: A government wants to reduce the number of new HIV infections among people who inject drugs. Suggest and explain two measures.
model: Needle exchange / provide sterile needles.
So infected blood is not passed on in shared needles.
Free HIV testing and antiretroviral treatment.
Lower viral load so less likely to pass HIV on (also education / condoms as a barrier).
exam.tip: Pair each measure with how it works.

exam.q: Compare Chlamydia and HIV in terms of the pathogen, how they are spread and how they can be treated or controlled.
model: Chlamydia is caused by a bacterium; HIV is caused by a virus.
Both spread by unprotected sex / body fluids.
HIV also spread by sharing needles, infected blood transfusion, and mother to baby (placenta, birth, breast milk).
Chlamydia can be cured with antibiotics; HIV cannot be cured, antibiotics do not work on viruses.
HIV controlled with antiretroviral drugs that lower viral load and delay AIDS.
Both reduced by condoms, screening and treatment, fewer partners; HIV also by needle exchange and blood screening.
exam.tip: Use 'both' and 'whereas' to make genuine comparisons, not two separate lists.

worked.q: Data: new Chlamydia diagnoses in a region rose from 12 000 to 15 000 in one year after free postal testing kits were introduced. Calculate the percentage increase and evaluate whether this shows Chlamydia is spreading faster.
steps: Percentage increase = 3 000 / 12 000 x 100 = 25%.
Free testing means more symptomless people were tested, so more existing cases were found.
So the rise may be due to more testing rather than more infection; we would need the percentage of tests that were positive to decide.
worked.ans: 25% increase; this does not prove faster spread because more testing finds more of the cases that were already there.

worked.q: A pregnant woman is found to be HIV positive. Explain how the risk of her baby becoming infected can be reduced.
steps: HIV can cross from mother to baby across the placenta, during birth and in breast milk.
Give the mother antiretroviral drugs during pregnancy: these lower her viral load so less virus reaches the baby.
The baby can be given antiretrovirals after birth.
Avoid breastfeeding (use formula) so HIV in breast milk is not passed on.
worked.ans: Antiretroviral treatment for mother (and baby) to lower viral load, and avoiding breastfeeding, block the main routes of mother-to-baby transmission.

worked.q: Model answer: explain two ways the spread of Chlamydia can be reduced (4 marks).
steps: Method 1: use condoms during sex.
Reason 1: the condom is a physical barrier so body fluids containing the bacteria are not exchanged.
Method 2: screening (testing) sexually active people and treating with antibiotics, including partners.
Reason 2: symptomless carriers are found and cured, so they can no longer pass the bacteria on.
worked.ans: Condoms (barrier stops fluid exchange) and screening plus antibiotic treatment (removes infected carriers).

bio_edx.4.5.summary: Plants cannot run away or make antibodies, so they rely on **physical barriers** (such as the **waxy leaf cuticle** and the **cellulose cell wall**) that stop pests and pathogens getting in, and **chemical defences** (such as **antimicrobial / antiseptic** substances and poisons) that kill or deter them. Many of these defence chemicals are useful to humans as **medicines**: for example **aspirin** from willow, **digitalis** from foxglove, **quinine** from cinchona and **taxol** from the yew tree. This is triple-only (B) content for Paper 1.

core.p: Plants are attacked by **pathogens** (viruses, bacteria, fungi, protists) and by **pests** such as insects that eat them. Plants cannot move away and have no white blood cells or antibodies, so they depend on **barriers** to keep attackers out and **chemicals** to kill or repel attackers that get in.
bullets: Pathogens of plants include tobacco mosaic virus (virus), ash dieback (fungus) and potato blight (protist-like).
Pests such as aphids and caterpillars damage leaves and can carry pathogens into the plant.
Damage reduces photosynthesis, so growth and crop yield fall.
Defences are grouped into **physical** and **chemical**.
These are triple biology (B) spec points 5.9B and 5.10B.

callouts.p: Physical defences stop entry; chemical defences kill or deter pests and pathogens.

core.h: Physical defence 1: the waxy leaf cuticle
core.p: The upper surface of a leaf is covered by a **waxy cuticle**, made by the epidermis cells. It is a continuous, waterproof layer that pathogens find hard to get through, so they cannot reach the living cells beneath.
bullets: Acts as a **physical barrier** to pathogen entry.
**Waterproof**: water runs off, so spores and bacteria are less likely to settle and germinate in a film of water.
Also reduces water loss by evaporation.
Pathogens often enter instead through **stomata** or **wounds**, where there is no cuticle.
Thicker cuticles give better protection.

callouts.p: A waxy, waterproof layer covering the leaf surface that acts as a barrier to pathogens.

core.h: Physical defence 2: the cellulose cell wall
core.p: Every plant cell is surrounded by a **cell wall** made of **cellulose**. Cellulose is strong and hard to break down, so the wall is a second barrier: even if a pathogen gets past the cuticle, it must break through the cell wall to get into a cell.
bullets: Cellulose fibres make the wall **tough**, so it is hard for pathogens to penetrate.
Many pathogens must make enzymes to digest cellulose before they can enter cells.
When attacked, cells can **thicken their walls** at the site to slow the pathogen.
Animal cells have no cell wall, which is why this defence is unique to plants (and some other organisms).

callouts.p: The defence named in the spec is the cellulose cell wall. The membrane controls what enters but is not the tough barrier.

core.p: Plants also have structural features that protect them, especially from animals. These are not all named in the spec but are commonly accepted in mark schemes as physical defences.
bullets: **Bark** on trees: a thick layer of dead cells that pathogens cannot easily get through.
**Thorns and spines** (e.g. roses, cacti) put off grazing animals.
**Hairs** on leaves and stems make it hard for insects to land, move or feed.
Leaves that **droop or curl** when touched (e.g. Mimosa) knock insects off and deter animals.
**Dead cells shed** from bark or leaves remove pathogens attached to them.
**Mimicry**: some plants look like they have insect eggs on them, so insects lay eggs elsewhere.

core.p: Plants make **antimicrobial** (antiseptic) chemicals that **kill microorganisms** or stop them growing. Some are always present in tissues; others are made in larger amounts when the plant is attacked.
bullets: **Antiseptics / antimicrobials** kill bacteria and fungi on the surface or in tissues.
Example: **pine trees** produce resin containing antimicrobial chemicals that seal wounds.
Example: **mint** and **witch hazel** contain antibacterial substances.
They work by damaging pathogen cells, so the infection cannot spread through the plant.
Making these chemicals uses energy and resources, so it is often switched on only when needed.

callouts.p: A chemical that kills microorganisms or stops them growing.

fig.cap: Plant tissue releases defence chemicals: antimicrobial substances kill or slow the growth of pathogens such as bacteria, while poisons and bitter tastes deter insects and other animals from feeding.

core.p: Many plants make **poisons** (toxins) or bad-tasting chemicals so animals avoid eating them. Insect pests that eat the plant may be harmed or killed.
bullets: **Toxins** in leaves (e.g. foxglove, deadly nightshade) make the plant poisonous to herbivores.
**Bitter or unpleasant taste** (e.g. caffeine, nicotine) deters insects.
**Insect-repelling chemicals**, e.g. pyrethrins from chrysanthemums, are used in insecticides.
Some plants release chemicals that **attract predators** of the pests attacking them.
Animals learn to avoid the plant, so less damage is done.

core.p: In an exam, sort defences into physical or chemical and say **how** each one protects the plant.
bullets: Physical = a structure that **stops entry** or makes feeding hard.
Chemical = a substance that **kills** pathogens or **deters** pests.

head: Defence
Type
How it protects
rows: Barrier to entry; waterproof so microbes do not settle
Tough barrier that pathogens must break through
Thick dead layer that blocks entry
Deter animals and insects from feeding
Harm or deter herbivores and insects

core.p: Because plants make so many chemicals to kill microbes and deter animals, many of them have powerful effects on the human body. Scientists have extracted these chemicals and used them as **medicines** to treat diseases or relieve symptoms. Many are now **made synthetically** in the lab, based on the plant chemical.
bullets: **Aspirin**: developed from a chemical (salicylic acid) in **willow** bark; relieves pain and fever and reduces blood clotting.
**Digitalis / digoxin**: from **foxglove**; strengthens the heartbeat, used for heart failure.
**Quinine**: from **cinchona** tree bark; treats **malaria**.
**Taxol** (paclitaxel): from the **Pacific yew** tree; used to treat some cancers (e.g. breast, ovarian).
**Morphine**: from the **opium poppy**; a strong painkiller.
Traditional medicine often gives clues about which plants contain useful chemicals.

callouts.p: Learn at least two plant-to-medicine examples, e.g. aspirin from willow and digitalis from foxglove.

core.p: A plant chemical is not used straight away. It must pass through the same stages as any new medicine (spec 5.20): discovery, preclinical testing and clinical trials.
bullets: **Discovery**: screening plant extracts, often guided by traditional medicine.
**Extraction and identification** of the active chemical.
**Preclinical testing** on cells, tissues and animals for toxicity and efficacy.
**Clinical trials** on healthy volunteers then patients to find the safe, effective dose.
Chemists often make the drug **synthetically** or modify it to reduce side effects (e.g. aspirin is gentler on the stomach than salicylic acid).

callouts.p: If asked why plant medicines must be tested, say plant chemicals can be toxic: digitalis is poisonous in large doses.

core.p: Only a small fraction of plant species have been tested for useful chemicals. If species become extinct, for example through deforestation, possible new medicines are lost before they are discovered.
bullets: Rainforests contain huge plant biodiversity and many untested chemicals.
Over-harvesting can endanger the source plant (e.g. the slow-growing Pacific yew for taxol).
Synthesising the chemical in a lab or growing plant cells in culture reduces pressure on wild plants.
Protecting biodiversity keeps future medicine options open.

core.p: Plants and humans both have barriers and chemicals, but only animals have a **specific immune response** with antibodies and memory cells.
bullets: Cuticle and cell wall in plants vs skin in humans: both physical barriers.
Antimicrobial chemicals in plants vs lysozyme in tears and stomach acid in humans: both chemical barriers.
Plants have **no antibodies** and **no lymphocytes**, so cannot be immunised.
This is why preventing plant disease relies on barriers, chemicals and good farming practice.

callouts.p: Never say plants make antibodies or white blood cells.

analogy.t: A plant as a medieval castle
analogy.p: The waxy cuticle is the smooth outer wall that attackers slide off; the cellulose cell wall around each cell is the strong inner wall of every room. Thorns and hairs are spikes along the walls. Chemical defences are boiling oil poured on anyone trying to climb in (antimicrobials) and poisoned food left out for raiders (toxins). People later discovered that some of that 'boiling oil' could be bottled and used as medicine. Where it breaks down: a castle has soldiers who learn to recognise enemies, but plants have no immune cells that remember a pathogen, and the cuticle has gaps (stomata) that a castle would never leave open.

terms.d: A microorganism that causes disease, such as a virus, bacterium, fungus or protist.
An animal, often an insect, that damages plants by feeding on them and may spread pathogens.
A structure that stops pests and pathogens entering or feeding, e.g. cuticle, cell wall, thorns.
A substance made by the plant that kills pathogens or deters pests, e.g. antimicrobials and toxins.
A waterproof layer of wax on the leaf surface that acts as a barrier to pathogens.
The tough wall around every plant cell, made of cellulose, which pathogens must break through to enter.
A strong polymer of glucose that forms plant cell walls.
A thick protective outer layer of dead cells on woody stems.
A chemical that kills microorganisms or stops them growing.
A substance that kills or slows the growth of microorganisms on surfaces; plants make natural ones.
A poisonous chemical; plants make toxins to deter herbivores and insects.
A painkiller and fever reducer developed from salicylic acid found in willow bark.
A drug from the foxglove plant that strengthens the heartbeat, used to treat heart failure.
A drug from cinchona tree bark used to treat malaria.
A cancer drug first extracted from the bark of the Pacific yew tree.

mistakes.w: Plants make antibodies to fight pathogens.
mistakes.r: Plants have no immune system with antibodies; they use physical and chemical defences.

mistakes.w: The cell membrane is a physical defence against pathogens.
mistakes.r: The cellulose cell wall is the physical barrier named by the spec.

mistakes.w: The cuticle stops pathogens because it is made of cellulose.
mistakes.r: The cuticle is made of wax; it is waterproof and forms a barrier. Cellulose is in the cell wall.

mistakes.w: Thorns are a chemical defence.
mistakes.r: Thorns are a physical defence; chemical defences are substances such as antimicrobials or toxins.

mistakes.w: Aspirin comes from foxglove.
mistakes.r: Aspirin is from willow; digitalis is from foxglove.

mistakes.w: Plant chemicals are natural, so they are safe and need no testing.
mistakes.r: Plant chemicals can be toxic and must go through preclinical and clinical testing.

mistakes.w: Antimicrobial chemicals protect the plant from insects.
mistakes.r: Antimicrobials act on microorganisms; poisons and bitter tastes deter insects.

mistakes.w: The cuticle covers the whole leaf so pathogens can never get in.
mistakes.r: Pathogens can still enter through stomata and wounds, where there is no cuticle.

exam.q: Name one physical defence that plants use against pathogens.
model: Waxy cuticle / cellulose cell wall / bark (any one).
exam.tip: Cuticle and cell wall are the two named in the spec.

exam.q: Explain how the waxy cuticle helps protect a leaf from infection.
model: Forms a (physical) barrier so pathogens cannot enter the leaf cells.
Waterproof so water (containing microbes) does not collect / spores cannot germinate on the surface.
exam.tip: Barrier plus why being waxy helps.

exam.q: Explain how the plant cell wall helps defend the plant against pathogens.
model: Made of cellulose, which is tough / hard to break down.
So pathogens cannot easily enter the cell.
exam.tip: Name cellulose for full marks.

exam.q: Describe one way plants use chemicals to defend themselves.
model: Produce antimicrobial / antiseptic chemicals that kill pathogens (or poisons).
Which stop infection spreading / deter animals and insects from eating them.
exam.tip: Say what the chemical does.

exam.q: Give the name of a medicine that comes from a plant and the plant it comes from.
model: Aspirin from willow / digitalis from foxglove / quinine from cinchona / taxol from yew.
Correct plant matched to medicine.
exam.tip: Mark for medicine and mark for its correct source.

exam.q: State what aspirin is used to treat.
model: Pain / fever / to reduce risk of blood clots.
exam.tip: Any one correct use.

exam.q: Suggest why many medicines come from plants.
model: Plants produce chemicals to defend against pathogens / pests.
These chemicals can also kill microorganisms or affect the human body, so can treat disease.
exam.tip: Link defence chemicals to medical effects.

exam.q: Explain why it is important to conserve plant species such as those in rainforests.
model: Many plants have not been tested yet and may contain chemicals useful as medicines.
If they become extinct these potential medicines are lost.
exam.tip: Mention undiscovered medicines.

exam.q: A scientist extracts a chemical from a plant leaf that may treat a bacterial infection. Describe how this chemical would be developed into a medicine.
model: Test extract on bacteria cultured on agar to see whether it kills them.
Preclinical testing on cells / tissues and animals for toxicity.
Clinical trials on healthy volunteers at low dose to check safety.
Then trials on patients (double blind with placebo) to find optimum dose and efficacy.
exam.tip: Links 5.10B to 5.18B and 5.20.

exam.q: Describe and explain the physical and chemical defences plants use against pests and pathogens, and explain how humans have benefited from plant chemical defences.
model: Waxy cuticle on leaves is a barrier and waterproof so microbes cannot enter / settle.
Cellulose cell walls are tough barriers that pathogens must break through.
Other physical features such as bark, thorns or hairs deter pests.
Antimicrobial chemicals kill pathogens; toxins / bitter chemicals deter herbivores and insects.
Humans extract these chemicals to use as medicines.
Examples: aspirin from willow for pain; digitalis from foxglove for heart; quinine for malaria; taxol for cancer.
exam.tip: Cover physical, chemical and medicines evenly with named examples.

worked.q: A student tests mint extract on a bacterial lawn. The clear zone has a diameter of 14 mm. Calculate the area of the clear zone (use pi = 3.14) and explain what it shows about mint's defences.
steps: Radius = diameter / 2 = 14 / 2 = 7 mm.
Area = pi x r squared = 3.14 x 7 x 7.
Area = 3.14 x 49 = 153.86 mm squared, about 154 mm squared.
A clear zone means bacteria were killed or could not grow near the extract, so mint contains an antimicrobial chemical (a chemical defence).
worked.ans: About 154 mm squared; mint contains antimicrobial chemicals that kill bacteria.

worked.q: Model answer: explain why a fungus might fail to infect a healthy leaf but succeed on a leaf damaged by insects.
steps: A healthy leaf has an unbroken waxy cuticle, which is a physical barrier to fungal spores.
The cuticle is waterproof, so spores are less likely to sit in water and germinate.
Insect bites break the cuticle and cell walls, making an open wound.
Spores can enter through the wound and reach the living cells, so infection happens.
worked.ans: Damage removes the physical barriers (cuticle and cell wall) so the fungus can get in.

worked.q: Applied example: classify each defence as physical or chemical: rose thorns, pine resin with antimicrobials, waxy cuticle, nicotine in tobacco leaves, cellulose cell wall.
steps: Rose thorns: a structure that deters animals, so physical.
Pine resin with antimicrobials: a substance that kills microbes, so chemical.
Waxy cuticle: a barrier, so physical.
Nicotine: a toxic chemical that deters insects, so chemical.
Cellulose cell wall: a barrier, so physical.
worked.ans: Physical: thorns, cuticle, cell wall. Chemical: antimicrobial resin, nicotine.

bio_edx.4.6.summary: Plant diseases are **detected** by spotting signs that a plant is unhealthy, and **identified** by finding out exactly which pathogen (or other cause) is responsible. **In the field**, growers look for **visible symptoms** (stunted growth, spots, decay, discolouration, abnormal growths, pests) and at the **pattern of distribution** of affected plants, and may use identification guides or **diagnostic test kits** that use **monoclonal antibodies**. **In the laboratory**, scientists confirm the pathogen by **microscopy**, **culturing** microorganisms, **antigen tests** and **DNA analysis**, so that the right control method can be chosen. This is triple-only (B) content.

core.p: **Detection** means noticing that a plant is diseased. **Identification** means working out the exact cause, such as which pathogen species. Both matter: detection tells you there is a problem; identification tells you the right treatment and whether the disease will spread.
bullets: Early detection stops a disease spreading through a crop and reduces **loss of yield**.
Identification is needed because different pathogens need different treatments (e.g. fungicide for a fungus, removal of infected plants for a virus).
Some symptoms look alike but have different causes, e.g. yellow leaves could be a virus, a fungus or a **mineral deficiency**.
Methods are grouped into **field** (on the farm) and **laboratory** methods.

callouts.p: Correct identification means the correct control method is used, saving money and crops.

core.p: The simplest method is to look carefully at the plants. Pathogens damage plant tissues in ways that can be seen with the naked eye or a hand lens.
bullets: **Stunted growth** (plant smaller than healthy neighbours).
**Spots** on leaves (e.g. black spot on roses, a fungus).
Areas of **decay** or rotting (e.g. potato blight).
**Discolouration**: yellowing or mosaic patterns (e.g. tobacco mosaic virus).
**Abnormal growths** such as galls or tumours (e.g. crown gall caused by bacteria).
**Malformed** stems or leaves, wilting.
**Presence of pests** (e.g. aphids) which may carry pathogens.

callouts.p: Mark schemes reward named symptoms: stunted growth, spots, decay, growths, discolouration, malformed leaves, pests.

core.p: Looking at **where** the diseased plants are in a field gives clues about the cause. A pathogen spreads from plant to plant, so infected plants are often **scattered** or spreading outwards from a point. A problem caused by the environment usually affects plants in **one area** where conditions are different.
bullets: **Scattered** or spreading pattern suggests a **pathogen** carried by wind, water or insects.
Affected plants all in **one area** (e.g. a low, wet corner) suggests **waterlogging**, poor soil or a **mineral deficiency**.
Affected plants only of **one species** among mixed plants suggests a pathogen specific to that species.
All plants affected in one go suggests an environmental cause such as frost or herbicide drift.
Recording the pattern over time shows whether the problem is **spreading**.

callouts.t: Not every sick plant has a pathogen
callouts.p: Symptoms can also be caused by lack of minerals, waterlogging or pests. Distribution helps tell these apart.

core.p: Once symptoms are noted, growers compare them with **gardening manuals**, **websites** or **identification keys** that describe and show photos of common diseases.
bullets: Compare symptoms with pictures and descriptions.
Quick and cheap but **not always reliable**, because different diseases can cause similar symptoms.
Gives a **likely** diagnosis that may need confirming in a lab.
Agricultural advisers and plant clinics can also help.

core.p: Rapid **diagnostic kits** can be used on the farm. They contain **monoclonal antibodies** that bind only to **antigens** on one specific pathogen. If the pathogen is in the plant sap, a coloured line appears on the strip, similar to a pregnancy test.
bullets: A sample of crushed leaf or sap is added to the kit.
Monoclonal antibodies on the strip are **specific**: they bind only to the antigen of one pathogen.
A **coloured line** shows the pathogen is present; a **control line** shows the test has worked.
Gives a result in minutes, without a lab.
Links to spec 5.21B-5.22B (uses of monoclonal antibodies).

callouts.p: A molecule (often a protein) on the surface of a pathogen that antibodies can bind to.

core.p: Samples of diseased tissue are examined under a **light microscope** (or electron microscope for viruses). Fungi and some bacteria can be recognised by the shape of their cells, hyphae or spores.
bullets: Fungal **hyphae** and **spores** have characteristic shapes.
Bacteria can be seen and their shape described (rods, spheres).
**Viruses** are too small for a light microscope and need an **electron microscope** or other tests.
Pests and their eggs can also be identified with a hand lens or microscope.

core.p: Using **aseptic technique**, a small piece of diseased tissue is placed on sterile **nutrient agar** and incubated. Bacteria and fungi grow into colonies, which can be identified by their appearance or tested further.
bullets: Aseptic technique (sterile equipment, flame the loop, lid on the plate) prevents contamination by other microbes.
Colony colour, shape and texture help identify the organism.
Pure cultures can be tested with antibiotics or fungicides to find which treatment works.
Viruses cannot be grown on agar because they need living host cells.

callouts.p: You cannot culture a virus on agar: it only reproduces inside living cells.

core.h: Laboratory method 3: antigen detection with antibodies
core.p: In the lab, **monoclonal antibodies** can be used to test for specific **antigens** of a pathogen. Because each monoclonal antibody binds only to one antigen, a positive result identifies the pathogen precisely.
bullets: Antibodies are often attached to a **coloured or fluorescent marker**, so binding can be seen.
Very **specific**: distinguishes between pathogens that cause similar symptoms.
Can detect pathogens **before symptoms appear**.
Can test many samples quickly.

callouts.p: Monoclonal antibodies bind to only one type of antigen, so they identify one particular pathogen.

core.p: Every pathogen species has its own **DNA** (or RNA) base sequence. Scientists extract genetic material from the diseased plant and test for sequences that belong to a known pathogen. A match identifies the pathogen.
bullets: DNA from the sample is compared with DNA of known pathogens.
Methods can make many copies of tiny amounts of pathogen DNA, so very small infections are found.
Works for **viruses, bacteria and fungi**, including those that cannot be cultured.
Very **accurate** but needs specialist equipment, so it is more expensive and slower than a field kit.

core.p: Field methods are fast and cheap but less certain; lab methods are slower and more costly but give a definite identification.
bullets: Use field observation first, then confirm in the lab if needed.
A combination of methods gives the most reliable diagnosis.

Where
Advantage
Disadvantage

Only tests for one pathogen per kit
Viruses too small for light microscope
Most accurate; finds any pathogen type

core.h: Ruling out other causes: mineral deficiencies
core.p: Not every unhealthy plant has a pathogen. Lack of minerals causes symptoms that can be confused with disease, so they must be ruled out, for example by soil testing.
bullets: Lack of **nitrate** ions: **stunted growth**, because nitrate is needed to make proteins.
Lack of **magnesium** ions: **yellow leaves** (chlorosis), because magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll.
Soil testing or adding fertiliser to a test patch shows whether a deficiency is the cause.
Deficiencies usually follow the **soil**, not spread from plant to plant.

core.p: Once the cause is known, the grower can act quickly and correctly.
bullets: Fungus: apply a suitable **fungicide**; remove infected leaves.
Virus: **remove and destroy** infected plants; control insect vectors such as aphids.
Bacteria: remove infected plants, avoid spreading on tools, use resistant varieties.
Mineral deficiency: add the correct **fertiliser**.
Report notifiable diseases (e.g. ash dieback) so spread between regions can be controlled.

callouts.p: Structure as: field methods (symptoms, distribution, guides, kits), then lab methods (microscope, culture, antigen tests, DNA), then why identification matters.

analogy.p: Diagnosing a crop is like a doctor seeing a patient. First the doctor looks at the symptoms (field observation) and asks where and when it started (distribution pattern), then checks a medical reference (identification guide). A quick rapid test in the surgery is like the antibody test kit. If unsure, samples go to the hospital lab for microscopy, culture and DNA tests. Where it breaks down: a plant cannot describe its symptoms, and a farmer has thousands of 'patients' at once, so the pattern across the whole field matters far more than for a single human patient.

terms.d: Noticing that a plant is diseased, usually from symptoms.
Finding the exact cause of a disease, e.g. which pathogen species.
A visible sign of disease, such as spots, decay or stunted growth.
A plant growing smaller than normal; a symptom of disease or nitrate deficiency.
A change in leaf colour, such as yellowing or a mosaic pattern.
An abnormal growth on a plant, caused by some bacteria, fungi or insects.
Where the affected plants are in a field, which gives clues to the cause of the disease.
On the farm or garden where the plants grow, as opposed to a laboratory.
A rapid test, often using monoclonal antibodies, that shows whether a specific pathogen is present.
Identical antibodies made from one clone of cells, which bind only to one specific antigen.
A molecule on the surface of a pathogen that a specific antibody binds to.
Growing microorganisms on a nutrient medium such as agar so they can be identified.
Methods that prevent contamination of a culture by unwanted microorganisms.
Testing genetic material from a sample to see if it matches the DNA of a known pathogen.
Lack of a mineral ion (e.g. nitrate, magnesium) that causes symptoms similar to disease.

mistakes.w: You can identify a plant virus by growing it on agar.
mistakes.r: Viruses only reproduce inside living cells, so they cannot be cultured on agar; use antigen or DNA tests.

mistakes.w: Yellow leaves always mean the plant has a pathogen.
mistakes.r: Yellow leaves could also be a mineral (magnesium) deficiency; further tests are needed.

mistakes.w: Look at the plant to see if it is ill.
mistakes.r: Name specific symptoms: stunted growth, spots, decay, discolouration, abnormal growths, pests.

mistakes.w: Antibodies in the kit kill the pathogen.
mistakes.r: In a test kit, monoclonal antibodies bind to the pathogen's antigen to show it is present.

mistakes.w: A light microscope can be used to see a virus.
mistakes.r: Viruses are too small; an electron microscope is needed.

mistakes.w: Diseased plants in one corner of the field show the pathogen is spreading.
mistakes.r: One area only suggests an environmental cause such as waterlogging or poor soil; a scattered or spreading pattern suggests a pathogen.

mistakes.w: Field tests are as accurate as lab tests.
mistakes.r: Field methods are quicker and cheaper but less reliable; lab tests such as DNA analysis confirm the identity.

exam.q: Give two visible symptoms that suggest a plant has a disease.
model: Stunted growth / spots on leaves / areas of decay.
Discolouration / abnormal growths / malformed leaves / presence of pests (any two).
exam.tip: Name specific symptoms.

exam.q: State one laboratory method that could be used to identify the pathogen causing a plant disease.
model: DNA analysis / antigen test with monoclonal antibodies / culturing / microscopy (any one).
exam.tip: Any named lab method.

exam.q: Explain why monoclonal antibodies can be used to identify a specific plant pathogen.
model: Monoclonal antibodies are specific / bind to only one antigen.
The antigen is found only on that pathogen, so binding shows that pathogen is present.
exam.tip: Key word: specific.

exam.q: A farmer notices that diseased plants are all in one low-lying, wet corner of a field. Suggest what this tells the farmer about the cause.
model: The cause may be environmental, e.g. waterlogging / poor soil / mineral deficiency.
Because a pathogen would usually spread to plants in other areas / be scattered.
exam.tip: Contrast with the pattern a pathogen gives.

exam.q: Explain why it is important to identify the cause of a plant disease correctly.
model: So the correct treatment / control method can be used (e.g. fungicide only works on fungi).
Stops spread / reduces loss of crop yield / saves money.
exam.tip: Link identification to treatment.

exam.q: Suggest why a scientist cannot identify a plant virus by growing it on nutrient agar.
model: Viruses can only reproduce inside living (host) cells.
exam.tip: Applies to all viruses.

exam.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using a diagnostic test kit in the field compared with DNA analysis in a lab.
model: Advantage: quick result on site / cheaper / no specialist equipment.
Disadvantage: only tests for one pathogen / less accurate or sensitive than DNA analysis.
exam.tip: Make it a comparison.

exam.q: Describe how a scientist could culture a pathogen from a diseased leaf to help identify it.
model: Use aseptic technique, e.g. sterilise equipment / work near a flame.
Place a small piece of diseased tissue on sterile nutrient agar and incubate.
Identify the colonies that grow by their appearance / under a microscope.
exam.tip: Link to aseptic technique (5.17B).

exam.q: Some leaves on a crop are yellow. Describe how the farmer could find out whether this is caused by a pathogen or by a lack of magnesium.
model: Look at the distribution: scattered/spreading suggests a pathogen; one area suggests soil problem.
Test the soil for magnesium / add magnesium fertiliser to some plants and see if they recover.
Test leaf samples with a diagnostic kit (monoclonal antibodies) for a pathogen.
Send samples to a lab for DNA analysis / culture / microscopy.
exam.tip: Plan both possibilities.

exam.q: Describe the methods used to detect and identify plant diseases in the field and in the laboratory.
model: Field: observe symptoms such as stunted growth, spots, decay, discolouration, abnormal growths.
Field: note presence of pests.
Field: look at the distribution pattern to separate pathogens from environmental causes.
Field: compare with gardening manuals / websites, or use diagnostic kits with monoclonal antibodies.
Lab: microscopy and culturing on agar using aseptic technique.
Lab: antigen tests with monoclonal antibodies and DNA analysis to identify the specific pathogen.
exam.tip: Split your answer into field and lab with at least three points each.

worked.q: A farmer counts diseased plants in a field of 1 200 plants. In week 1, 60 are diseased; in week 3, 210 are diseased. Calculate the percentage of plants diseased each week and say what this suggests.
steps: The percentage has risen more than three times in two weeks.
A rapid increase suggests a pathogen spreading from plant to plant, not a fixed soil problem.
worked.ans: 5% then 17.5%; the fast spread suggests an infectious pathogen, which should be identified in the lab.

worked.q: Model answer: a grower sees mosaic-patterned yellow leaves on tomato plants. Explain how the cause could be identified with certainty.
steps: The mosaic pattern suggests tobacco mosaic virus, but similar discolouration can have other causes.
Use a diagnostic kit containing monoclonal antibodies against the virus antigen; a coloured line shows it is present.
Confirm in the lab by DNA (genetic material) analysis, matching the sequence to the known virus.
Culturing on agar would not work because a virus needs living cells.
worked.ans: Use an antibody-based test kit, then confirm with DNA analysis; do not try to culture a virus.

worked.q: Applied example: decide whether each observation points to a pathogen or an environmental cause: (a) diseased plants scattered across the field and increasing each week; (b) all plants along a ditch are yellow; (c) only the oak trees in a mixed wood have spots.
steps: (a) Scattered and spreading over time: pathogen.
(b) Restricted to one wet area: environmental, such as waterlogging.
(c) Only one species affected among many: pathogen specific to that species.
worked.ans: (a) pathogen, (b) environmental, (c) pathogen.

bio_edx.4.7.summary: The human body has **non-specific** first-line defences that stop pathogens getting in or kill them before they can cause infection. **Physical barriers** (skin, mucus, cilia, and scabs over cuts) block or remove pathogens, while **chemical defences** (lysozymes in tears and hydrochloric acid in the stomach) destroy them. These defences work against all pathogens in the same way, so they act straight away, unlike the specific immune response, which takes days.

core.p: Edexcel 1BI0 point 5.12 asks you to **describe how the physical barriers and chemical defences of the human body provide protection from pathogens**, including physical barriers (mucus, cilia and skin) and chemical defences (lysozymes and hydrochloric acid). Exam questions usually ask you to name a barrier AND explain how it stops infection.
bullets: Physical barriers named: **skin**, **mucus**, **cilia**.
Chemical defences named: **lysozymes** (in tears) and **hydrochloric acid** (in the stomach).
You must link each defence to **how** it prevents pathogens entering or kills them.
These are the body's **first line of defence**; the immune system (white blood cells, antibodies) is the next line if pathogens get through.
Scabs and blood clotting over cuts are often accepted as a physical barrier and are worth knowing as the skin's back-up.

callouts.p: A microorganism that causes disease, such as a bacterium, virus, fungus or protist.
Physical barriers stop pathogens getting into the body; chemical defences kill or destroy pathogens.

core.p: Pathogens are everywhere: in the air, on surfaces, in food and water. To cause disease they must get **inside the body** and reproduce. The main entry routes are through the skin (cuts), the airways (breathing in), the digestive system (eating and drinking), the eyes and the reproductive organs. Each entry route has its own barrier.
bullets: Airborne pathogens (e.g. influenza virus, TB bacteria) enter through the **nose and airways** - defended by mucus and cilia.
Pathogens in food and water (e.g. cholera bacteria) enter through the **mouth** - defended by stomach acid.
Pathogens on surfaces enter through **cuts in the skin** - defended by intact skin and scabs.
The **eyes** are moist and exposed - defended by lysozymes in tears.
Stopping pathogens at entry is better than fighting them later, because the infection never starts.

core.p: Barriers are **non-specific**: they act in the same way against every type of pathogen and do not need to recognise it first. The specific immune response (spec point 5.13) uses lymphocytes that make antibodies for one particular antigen, which takes time.
bullets: Non-specific defences act **immediately** and against **all** pathogens.
They do not produce **memory** - they are no stronger the second time.
The specific response targets **one antigen** and produces memory lymphocytes.
If barriers are damaged (burns, smoking), more pathogens get through, so the immune system has more work to do.

callouts.p: Skin and mucus are not part of the specific immune response. Do not write that skin 'makes antibodies'.

core.p: The skin covers the whole outside of the body. Its outer layer is made of **tough, dead cells** that are tightly packed, so pathogens **cannot pass through** unbroken skin. It is the largest barrier and stops most pathogens on contact.
bullets: Acts as a **physical barrier** that prevents pathogens entering the tissues and blood.
The outer layer is **dead, dry and continually shed**, so microorganisms on it are lost with the flakes.
Skin is **waterproof**, so pathogens in water cannot soak in.
Pathogens get in mainly when skin is **broken** - cuts, grazes, burns, bites or needle injuries.
That is why wounds should be cleaned and covered, and why burns patients are at high risk of infection.

callouts.p: Write 'skin acts as a physical barrier which prevents pathogens from entering the body'. The word 'barrier' plus 'prevents entry' scores the mark.

fig.cap: Left: intact skin. The tough outer layer of dead cells is a physical barrier that pathogens cannot pass through. Right: when the skin is cut, platelets and a mesh of fibrin form a blood clot, which dries into a scab that seals the wound and stops pathogens entering while new skin grows underneath.

core.h: Scabs: sealing breaks in the skin
core.p: When the skin is cut, blood **clots** quickly. **Platelets** and a protein mesh (**fibrin**) trap red blood cells to form a clot, which dries and hardens into a **scab**. The scab seals the gap, so pathogens cannot enter while new skin grows underneath.
bullets: Clotting also **stops blood loss**.
The scab is a **temporary physical barrier** until the skin is repaired.
Picking a scab re-opens the wound and lets pathogens in.
This is the skin's back-up barrier - mention it when a question asks what happens if the skin is cut.

core.p: The airways (nose, trachea and bronchi) are lined with cells that make **mucus**. Mucus is a **sticky** liquid that **traps pathogens** and dust particles in the air we breathe in, so they cannot reach the lungs' delicate gas exchange surface (the alveoli).
bullets: Made by **goblet cells** in the lining of the airways.
Also found in the nose, where **nasal hairs** help trap larger particles.
Mucus lines other entry points too, such as the digestive and reproductive tracts.
Mucus contains some **lysozyme**, so it can also kill some bacteria it traps.
Trapping alone does not remove the pathogen - that is the job of the cilia.

callouts.p: The mark scheme word for mucus is 'traps' (pathogens / microorganisms / dust).

core.p: Many cells lining the trachea and bronchi have **cilia**: tiny hair-like projections on their surface. The cilia **beat (waft) in a wave**, moving the mucus and the trapped pathogens **up and away from the lungs** towards the throat. There the mucus is **swallowed** (or coughed out).
bullets: The cells with cilia are called **ciliated epithelial cells**.
Cilia sweep mucus **upwards, towards the throat** - not down into the lungs.
Swallowed mucus goes to the stomach, where **hydrochloric acid** kills the pathogens.
Mucus and cilia work **together**: mucus traps, cilia remove.
Smoking damages and paralyses cilia, so mucus builds up in the airways, causing a 'smoker's cough' and more chest infections.

callouts.p: Cilia are structures on the surface of ciliated cells. Do not call them 'hairs that trap pathogens' - mucus traps, cilia move it.

fig.cap: The trachea and bronchi are lined with ciliated epithelium. Goblet cells secrete sticky mucus that traps pathogens and dust; the cilia beat in a coordinated wave, sweeping the mucus up towards the throat, where it is swallowed so stomach acid can kill the trapped pathogens.

core.p: **Lysozymes** are **enzymes** found in **tears** (and also in saliva and mucus). They **break down (digest) the cell walls of bacteria**. Without its wall, water enters the bacterium by osmosis, so it swells and **bursts**, which kills it. This protects the eyes, which are moist, warm and exposed to the air.
bullets: A **chemical defence**, not a physical barrier.
Works on **bacteria** because bacteria have cell walls; it does not act on viruses in the same way.
Tears also **wash** particles and microbes off the surface of the eye.
As an enzyme, lysozyme is a **protein** and can be denatured by high temperature or extreme pH.
The word lysozyme comes from 'lysis', meaning bursting or splitting of a cell.

callouts.p: An enzyme in tears that destroys bacteria by digesting their cell walls.

fig.cap: Lysozymes are enzymes found in tears (and also in saliva and mucus). They break down (digest) the cell walls of bacteria. Without a strong wall, water enters the bacterium by osmosis, it swells and bursts (lysis), so it is killed before it can infect the eye.

core.p: The stomach lining makes **hydrochloric acid**, giving the stomach contents a very **low pH (about 2)**. This strongly acidic environment **kills most pathogens** that are swallowed in food, drink or mucus before they can reach the intestines and cause infection.
bullets: A **chemical defence**.
The acid **denatures enzymes and proteins** in the pathogens, so they cannot function and die.
Protects against pathogens carried in **food and water**, e.g. many food-poisoning bacteria.
Also kills pathogens in **swallowed mucus** from the airways.
The acid also gives the right pH for the stomach enzyme **protease (pepsin)** to digest protein.
Some pathogens survive (e.g. if eaten in large numbers), which is why food poisoning still happens.

callouts.p: Write 'hydrochloric acid', not just 'stomach acid', when the question asks you to name the chemical defence.

core.p: The barriers form a linked system. For a pathogen breathed in: mucus traps it, cilia sweep it to the throat, it is swallowed, and hydrochloric acid in the stomach kills it. A pathogen on the skin is blocked by the skin itself; if it gets in through a cut, a scab seals the wound, and white blood cells deal with any that got through.
bullets: Physical barriers reduce the **number** of pathogens getting in.
Chemical defences **kill** pathogens at the main openings (eyes, stomach).
Anything that gets past these meets **white blood cells** (phagocytes and lymphocytes).
Fewer pathogens entering means less chance of infection and a smaller job for the immune system.

fig.cap: Summary of the non-specific defences named in the Edexcel spec. Physical barriers stop pathogens getting in; chemical defences kill or destroy them. The arrow shows how the two systems link: mucus swept up by cilia is swallowed, so the trapped pathogens are killed by hydrochloric acid in the stomach.
