core.p: Explaining why someone gets more infections is a common application question. The answer is usually that a barrier has been **damaged or bypassed**, so more pathogens enter the body.
bullets: **Smoking**: tar and chemicals damage cilia and cause extra mucus, so pathogens stay in the airways - more bronchitis and pneumonia.
**Burns or large wounds**: the skin barrier is lost over a big area - high risk of infection.
**Dry eyes** (fewer tears): less lysozyme, more eye infections.
**Medicines that reduce stomach acid** (antacids): fewer swallowed bacteria are killed.
**Needles, insect bites, surgery**: pathogens are placed straight through the skin barrier (e.g. malaria parasites injected by mosquitoes).

callouts.p: Smoking damages cilia, so mucus is not moved out of the airways, so pathogens trapped in mucus stay in the lungs and cause infection.

core.p: This point connects to how pathogens spread (5.6) and to the immune response (5.13). Reducing spread, such as washing hands or covering coughs, stops pathogens reaching the barriers; the immune system deals with pathogens that pass them.
bullets: Airborne diseases (e.g. influenza, TB) must get past **mucus and cilia**.
Waterborne / foodborne diseases (e.g. cholera) must survive **hydrochloric acid**.
HIV and other STIs enter through **body fluids** and contact with mucous membranes, bypassing intact skin.
Plant defences (5.9B, triple) are similar in idea: physical (waxy cuticle, cell walls) and chemical (antibacterial chemicals).

analogy.p: The body is a castle. The **skin** is the thick stone wall that keeps invaders out. A **scab** is the emergency planks nailed over a hole in the wall. In the gateway (the airways), **mucus** is a sticky net that catches invaders, and **cilia** are guards on a conveyor belt carrying the net out to a pit of **acid** (the stomach). At the windows (the eyes), **lysozyme** is a sentry who dissolves the armour of attackers (bacterial cell walls). Where it breaks down: castle guards choose who to attack, but these defences are automatic and do not 'decide' or recognise anything; and lysozyme only works on bacteria with cell walls, not on every invader.

terms.d: A microorganism that causes disease (bacterium, virus, fungus or protist).
A structure that stops pathogens getting into the body, e.g. skin, mucus, cilia.
A substance made by the body that kills or destroys pathogens, e.g. lysozymes, hydrochloric acid.
A defence that acts in the same way against all pathogens, without recognising a particular antigen.
The outer covering of the body; its tough layer of dead cells is a physical barrier pathogens cannot pass through when unbroken.
A dried blood clot over a cut that seals the wound and stops pathogens entering.
A mesh of fibrin and platelets that traps blood cells and plugs a damaged blood vessel or wound.
A sticky substance secreted in the airways (and other tracts) that traps pathogens and dust.
A cell in the lining of the airways that secretes mucus.
Tiny hair-like structures on the surface of ciliated cells that beat to move mucus up towards the throat.
A cell lining the trachea and bronchi that has cilia on its surface.
An enzyme in tears (also saliva and mucus) that kills bacteria by digesting their cell walls.
The bursting or breaking open of a cell, e.g. a bacterium after its cell wall is digested.
Acid made by the stomach lining that gives a pH of about 2 and kills most swallowed pathogens.
The windpipe; the tube carrying air to the lungs, lined with mucus and cilia.
When the shape of a protein (such as an enzyme) is changed permanently so it no longer works, e.g. by strong acid.

mistakes.w: Cilia trap pathogens.
mistakes.r: Mucus traps pathogens; cilia waft / sweep the mucus (and trapped pathogens) away from the lungs to the throat.

mistakes.w: Cilia move mucus down into the lungs / stomach.
mistakes.r: Cilia move mucus up the airways towards the throat, where it is swallowed.

mistakes.w: Lysozymes are found in the stomach.
mistakes.r: Lysozymes are found in tears (also saliva and mucus); the stomach defence is hydrochloric acid.

mistakes.w: Lysozymes kill viruses by breaking their cell walls.
mistakes.r: Lysozymes digest the cell walls of bacteria; viruses do not have cell walls.

mistakes.w: Stomach acid digests the pathogens.
mistakes.r: Hydrochloric acid kills pathogens (by denaturing their proteins / enzymes) because of the low pH.

mistakes.w: Skin produces antibodies to kill pathogens.
mistakes.r: Skin is a physical barrier that prevents pathogens entering; antibodies are made by lymphocytes (white blood cells).

mistakes.w: Mucus kills pathogens.
mistakes.r: Mucus traps pathogens; the kill happens later (e.g. in the stomach by hydrochloric acid).

mistakes.w: Smoking kills the mucus so pathogens get in.
mistakes.r: Smoking damages / paralyses cilia, so mucus and trapped pathogens are not removed and build up in the airways.

mistakes.w: Physical barriers are part of the specific immune response.
mistakes.r: Barriers are non-specific first-line defences; the specific response involves lymphocytes and antibodies.

exam.q: Name one chemical defence of the human body.
model: Lysozyme (in tears) OR hydrochloric acid (in the stomach).
exam.tip: Skin, mucus and cilia are physical, so they would not score here.

exam.q: State where lysozymes are found in the body.
model: In tears (also accept saliva / mucus).
exam.tip: Tears is the answer Edexcel expects first.

exam.q: Describe how the skin protects the body from pathogens.
model: Skin acts as a physical barrier.
Prevents pathogens entering the body / tissues / blood.
exam.tip: Two ideas: what it is (barrier) and what it does (stops entry).

exam.q: Explain how lysozymes protect the body against bacteria.
model: Lysozymes are enzymes that break down / digest bacterial cell walls.
So the bacteria burst / are killed (lysis).
exam.tip: Always say 'cell walls' and 'bacteria' together.

exam.q: Explain how hydrochloric acid in the stomach protects the body from disease.
model: Hydrochloric acid gives a low pH / acidic conditions in the stomach.
This kills pathogens / bacteria swallowed in food or drink (by denaturing their enzymes).
exam.tip: Mention where the pathogens come from: food, drink or swallowed mucus.

exam.q: Explain how mucus and cilia work together to protect the lungs from pathogens.
model: Mucus is produced by (goblet) cells lining the airways / trachea.
Mucus is sticky and traps pathogens / dust.
Cilia beat / waft to move the mucus up to the throat / away from the lungs.
Mucus is swallowed and pathogens are killed by stomach (hydrochloric) acid.
exam.tip: Keep the roles separate: mucus traps, cilia move, acid kills.

exam.q: Smokers have more chest infections than non-smokers. Explain why.
model: Chemicals in smoke damage / destroy / paralyse cilia.
So mucus (and trapped pathogens) is not moved out of the airways / builds up.
Pathogens remain in the lungs and can cause infection.
exam.tip: A chain of 'so' statements earns each mark.

exam.q: A person has a condition where they produce very few tears. Suggest why they get more eye infections.
model: Less lysozyme on the surface of the eye.
So fewer bacteria are killed / bacterial cell walls are not broken down, so more bacteria survive to cause infection.
exam.tip: Link the cause (fewer tears) to the chemical (lysozyme) to the effect.

exam.q: Explain why a person with severe burns over a large area of skin is at high risk of infection.
model: The skin (physical barrier) is damaged / broken.
So pathogens can enter the body / tissues / blood more easily.
exam.tip: Say what barrier is lost and what that allows.

exam.q: Describe how the human body uses physical barriers and chemical defences to protect against pathogens.
model: Skin acts as a physical barrier that prevents pathogens entering.
If skin is cut, blood clots / a scab forms to seal the wound.
Mucus in the airways / nose traps pathogens.
Cilia waft mucus up to the throat, away from the lungs, where it is swallowed.
Lysozymes in tears break down bacterial cell walls / kill bacteria.
Hydrochloric acid in the stomach kills pathogens in food / drink / swallowed mucus.
Chemical defences kill pathogens whereas physical barriers stop them entering.
exam.tip: For 6 marks, cover both types and give the mechanism for each, with links between them, e.g. swallowed mucus meeting stomach acid.

exam.q: Explain why skin, mucus and stomach acid are described as non-specific defences.
model: They act against all (types of) pathogens in the same way.
They do not recognise / target a specific antigen (unlike antibodies).
exam.tip: Contrast with the specific immune response for the second mark.

worked.q: A student wrote: 'The cilia in the trachea trap bacteria and kill them.' Explain what is wrong and write a correct version (3 marks).
steps: Identify error 1: cilia do not trap - the sticky mucus traps bacteria.
Identify error 2: cilia do not kill - they waft mucus up towards the throat.
Add where killing happens: the mucus is swallowed and hydrochloric acid in the stomach kills the bacteria.
worked.ans: Mucus made in the trachea traps bacteria; cilia beat to sweep the mucus up to the throat, where it is swallowed and the bacteria are killed by hydrochloric acid in the stomach.

worked.q: Cholera bacteria are spread in contaminated water. Suggest which body defence protects against cholera and explain why a person who drinks a large volume of contaminated water may still get ill.
steps: Route of entry: the bacteria are swallowed, so they enter the digestive system.
Defence: hydrochloric acid in the stomach gives a low pH that kills most of the bacteria.
Explain failure: if a very large number of bacteria are swallowed, not all are killed; a large volume of water can also dilute the acid and pass through quickly.
Survivors reach the small intestine and reproduce, causing disease.
worked.ans: Hydrochloric acid in the stomach kills most swallowed cholera bacteria, but with a very large dose some survive, reach the intestine and cause infection.

worked.q: Classify each defence as physical or chemical and give its job: skin, lysozyme, cilia, hydrochloric acid, mucus.
steps: Skin - physical - barrier that prevents pathogens entering.
Lysozyme - chemical - enzyme in tears that digests bacterial cell walls.
Cilia - physical - waft mucus away from the lungs to the throat.
Hydrochloric acid - chemical - kills pathogens in the stomach.
Mucus - physical - sticky, traps pathogens in the airways.
worked.ans: Physical: skin, cilia, mucus. Chemical: lysozyme, hydrochloric acid.

bio_edx.4.8.summary: The **specific immune response** is carried out by **lymphocytes**, a type of white blood cell. When a pathogen enters the body its **antigens** trigger the one type of lymphocyte with a complementary receptor to divide and produce **antibodies** that bind only to that antigen, and also to produce **memory lymphocytes**. If the same antigen enters again, memory lymphocytes cause a **secondary response** that is faster and much larger, so the pathogen is destroyed before it causes symptoms and the person is **immune**.

core.p: Edexcel 1BI0 point 5.13 asks you to **explain the role of the specific immune system of the human body in defence against disease**, including: exposure to a pathogen; antigens triggering an immune response which causes the **production of antibodies**; antigens also triggering the **production of memory lymphocytes**; and the **role of memory lymphocytes in the secondary response** to the antigen.
bullets: Know the sequence: **exposure - antigen recognised - lymphocytes divide - antibodies made - memory lymphocytes made**.
Be able to compare the **primary** and **secondary** responses, often from a graph.
Use the words **antigen**, **antibody**, **lymphocyte**, **complementary**, **specific** and **memory lymphocyte** precisely.
This point leads straight into immunisation (5.14), which uses exactly the same process.

callouts.p: Antigens trigger lymphocytes to make antibodies and memory lymphocytes; memory lymphocytes make the secondary response faster and stronger.

core.p: Specific immunity starts when a pathogen gets past the body's barriers (skin, mucus, stomach acid) and enters the tissues or blood. This first contact with a new pathogen is called **exposure**. The body has not met these antigens before, so it has no matching antibodies ready.
bullets: Pathogens that reach the blood start to **reproduce** quickly.
Bacteria may release **toxins**; viruses enter cells and damage them as they replicate.
The **symptoms** of disease appear when pathogens and toxins build up faster than the immune system can respond.
The immune response is triggered by the pathogen's **antigens**.

core.p: **Antigens** are molecules, usually proteins, on the surface of a pathogen (or other cell). Every type of pathogen has its own **unique antigens** with a particular shape. White blood cells recognise antigens as **foreign** (not from the body), which triggers the immune response.
bullets: Your own cells also have antigens, but lymphocytes do not normally respond to these 'self' antigens.
Different strains of a pathogen can have **different antigens** - e.g. new strains of influenza virus.
Toxins made by bacteria can also act as antigens.
The shape of the antigen is what lymphocytes and antibodies recognise.

callouts.p: A molecule (usually a protein) on the surface of a cell or pathogen that triggers an immune response.

core.p: **Lymphocytes** are white blood cells that carry out the specific immune response. The body has millions of different lymphocytes, and each one has **receptors** on its surface that are complementary to **one particular antigen**. So for almost any antigen, a few lymphocytes already exist that can recognise it.
bullets: Lymphocytes are made in the bone marrow and circulate in the blood and lymph.
The type of lymphocyte that makes antibodies is called a **B lymphocyte**.
Lymphocytes are different from **phagocytes**, which engulf and digest pathogens (non-specific).
Each lymphocyte responds to only one antigen, which is why the response is called **specific**.

callouts.p: Lymphocytes make antibodies. Phagocytes engulf pathogens. Do not say phagocytes make antibodies.

core.p: When a lymphocyte with a **complementary receptor** binds to the antigen, it is **activated**. It then **divides rapidly by mitosis** to make a **clone** of many identical lymphocytes, all specific to that antigen. Many of these cells **secrete large amounts of antibodies** into the blood.
bullets: Only the lymphocytes that **match** the antigen are selected and multiply.
Mitosis makes **genetically identical** cells, so every cell in the clone makes the **same antibody**.
The cells that secrete antibodies are sometimes called **plasma cells**.
This takes several **days** the first time, so the person usually becomes ill before the infection is controlled.

fig.cap: Each lymphocyte has receptors for one antigen shape. Only the lymphocyte whose receptor is complementary to the pathogen's antigen (red triangle) is activated. It divides rapidly by mitosis to make a clone of identical lymphocytes. Some of these secrete large amounts of the matching antibody; others become memory lymphocytes that stay in the blood for years.

core.p: **Antibodies** are **Y-shaped proteins** made by lymphocytes. Each has **binding sites** with a shape that is **complementary** to one specific antigen. The antibody binds to that antigen and to no other, in the same way an enzyme's active site fits only its substrate.
bullets: Antibodies are **specific**: an antibody against measles will not bind to the chickenpox antigen.
They are carried in the **blood plasma** to the site of infection.
Antibodies are proteins, made from amino acids, with a shape set by their sequence.
Each antibody has **two binding sites**, so it can join two pathogens together.

callouts.p: A protein produced by lymphocytes that binds to a specific antigen.
Write 'the antibody is complementary to the antigen'. 'The same shape as' the antigen is wrong and loses the mark.

fig.cap: Antigens are molecules (often proteins) on the surface of a pathogen. Each antibody is a Y-shaped protein with binding sites whose shape is complementary to one specific antigen, so it can only bind to that antigen, like a key fitting one lock.

core.p: Antibodies binding to antigens do not usually kill pathogens on their own. They **label** and **disable** pathogens so that they can be destroyed.
bullets: **Clumping**: antibodies stick pathogens together, so they cannot spread and are easier to engulf.
**Marking**: antibodies attached to antigens make pathogens easy for **phagocytes** to recognise, engulf and digest.
**Neutralising**: antibodies binding to toxins or to the parts a virus uses to enter cells can stop them working.
So the specific response (lymphocytes) and the non-specific response (phagocytes) work together.

fig.cap: Antibodies have two binding sites, so they can attach to antigens on two pathogens at once, sticking pathogens together in clumps. Antibodies also act as markers. This makes it easier for phagocytes (another type of white blood cell) to engulf and digest the pathogens.

core.p: As well as cells that make antibodies, the clone produces **memory lymphocytes**. These do not make antibodies straight away. Instead they **stay in the blood for a long time (often years)**, ready to recognise the same antigen if it appears again.
bullets: Memory lymphocytes are **specific** to the antigen that triggered them.
There are **many more** of them than the original handful of matching lymphocytes.
They are why you usually only catch diseases such as chickenpox once.
This is called **immunological memory**; having it means you are **immune** to that pathogen.

callouts.p: A lymphocyte that remains in the blood after an infection and quickly produces antibodies if the same antigen enters the body again.

core.p: The **primary response** happens the first time an antigen is met. The **secondary response** happens on any later exposure to the same antigen, and is driven by memory lymphocytes. Because memory lymphocytes recognise the antigen at once and divide quickly, antibodies are made **faster, in greater amounts and for longer**.
bullets: Primary: **delay of several days**, low peak of antibodies, person often **gets ill**.
Secondary: **very short delay**, antibody level rises **rapidly** to a much **higher** peak.
Secondary: antibody level stays **high for longer**.
Secondary: the pathogen is destroyed **before it can reproduce enough to cause symptoms**, so the person does not feel ill.
The secondary response only works for the **same antigen**; a new strain with different antigens gives another primary response.

fig.cap: Antibody level after a first and second exposure to the same antigen. The primary response has a delay of several days and produces fewer antibodies, so the person may become ill. In the secondary response, memory lymphocytes divide quickly, so antibodies are made faster, in much larger amounts and for longer, rising above the level needed for immunity before symptoms can develop.

core.p: Exam graphs usually show antibody concentration against time, with two exposures marked. You may be asked to describe the difference, explain it, or calculate how much higher or quicker the secondary response is.
bullets: **Describe**: quote values - when the rise starts, the peak value, how long it stays high.
**Explain**: the secondary response is faster and bigger **because memory lymphocytes** are already present and divide rapidly.
**Calculate**: ratio of peaks = secondary peak / primary peak; difference in time to peak.
Look for a dashed line showing the level needed for **immunity** or above which the person is protected.

callouts.p: If asked to 'explain the difference', first state the difference with data, then give the reason (memory lymphocytes).

core.h: Why people still get some diseases again
core.p: Immunity is specific to antigens. If a pathogen **changes its antigens**, memory lymphocytes no longer recognise it, so the body has to make a new primary response.
bullets: **Influenza** viruses mutate often, producing new strains with different antigens - so you can catch flu many times and the flu vaccine is updated every year.
The **common cold** is caused by many different viruses, each with different antigens.
**HIV** attacks lymphocytes themselves, so the specific immune response is weakened.
Memory for some diseases fades over time, so **booster** vaccinations may be needed.

core.p: A full answer on the specific immune response follows a clear chain. Practise writing it out in order, using each key word once.
bullets: 1. Pathogen enters body; its **antigens** are foreign.
2. A lymphocyte with a **complementary** receptor binds the antigen.
3. Lymphocyte **divides by mitosis** to form a **clone**.
4. Clone cells produce **antibodies** specific to the antigen.
5. Antibodies bind to antigens; pathogens are **clumped / marked** and destroyed by phagocytes.
6. **Memory lymphocytes** are also made and stay in the blood.
7. On re-infection, memory lymphocytes give a **rapid, large secondary response**, so the person is **immune**.

analogy.t: Wanted posters and a filing cabinet
analogy.p: Think of a police force with millions of officers, each trained to recognise just one face (one antigen). When a criminal appears, only the officer who recognises that face reacts, then recruits thousands of identical officers (the clone). They hand out sticky tags (antibodies) that attach only to that criminal, so the security guards (phagocytes) can grab them. Some officers keep the criminal's file in a cabinet (memory lymphocytes), so next time the criminal is caught almost at once (secondary response). Where it breaks down: real lymphocytes do not 'learn' a new face - the matching one already exists and is selected; and if the criminal changes their face (antigen mutation), the old file is no help.

terms.d: A microorganism that causes disease.
A molecule (usually a protein) on the surface of a cell or pathogen that triggers an immune response.
A Y-shaped protein produced by lymphocytes that binds to a specific, complementary antigen.
A type of white blood cell that produces antibodies as part of the specific immune response.
The type of lymphocyte that produces antibodies and memory cells.
A long-lived lymphocyte that remains in the blood after infection and rapidly produces antibodies on re-exposure to the same antigen.
A white blood cell that engulfs and digests pathogens (non-specific).
The response of lymphocytes to one particular antigen, producing antibodies and memory lymphocytes.
Having a matching shape that fits together, like an antibody binding site and its antigen.
A group of genetically identical cells produced by mitosis from one cell.
Cell division that produces two genetically identical daughter cells; used by activated lymphocytes to multiply.
The slow, small immune response the first time an antigen is met.
The faster, larger and longer-lasting response to a second exposure to the same antigen, caused by memory lymphocytes.
Being protected against a disease because memory lymphocytes can produce antibodies quickly enough to destroy the pathogen before symptoms develop.
A poisonous substance produced by some bacteria that damages cells.
A genetic variant of a pathogen, which may have different antigens.

mistakes.w: Antibodies are the same shape as the antigen.
mistakes.r: Antibodies have a shape complementary to the antigen.

mistakes.w: Phagocytes produce antibodies.
mistakes.r: Lymphocytes produce antibodies; phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens.

mistakes.w: Antibodies stay in the blood forever, giving immunity.
mistakes.r: Antibody levels fall after infection; memory lymphocytes remain and produce antibodies quickly on re-exposure.

mistakes.w: Memory cells remember the disease.
mistakes.r: Memory lymphocytes recognise the specific antigen and rapidly divide / produce antibodies.

mistakes.w: Antibodies kill all types of pathogen.
mistakes.r: Each antibody is specific to one antigen, so it only binds to the pathogen with that antigen.

mistakes.w: The secondary response is just faster.
mistakes.r: The secondary response is faster AND produces more antibodies AND lasts longer, so pathogens are destroyed before symptoms.

mistakes.w: White blood cells learn to make the right antibody.
mistakes.r: A lymphocyte with a complementary receptor already exists; the antigen selects it and it divides by mitosis to form a clone.

mistakes.w: Antigens are produced by white blood cells.
mistakes.r: Antigens are on the surface of pathogens (and cells); antibodies are produced by lymphocytes.

mistakes.w: You get flu again because your immune system forgets.
mistakes.r: The flu virus mutates so its antigens change; memory lymphocytes do not recognise the new antigens.

exam.q: Name the type of white blood cell that produces antibodies.
model: Lymphocyte (accept B lymphocyte).
exam.tip: Not 'white blood cell' alone and not phagocyte.

exam.q: What is an antigen?
model: A molecule / protein on the surface of a pathogen / cell that triggers an immune response.
exam.tip: Mention 'surface' and 'triggers immune response'.

exam.q: Explain why an antibody against the measles virus does not protect against the mumps virus.
model: Antibodies are specific / have a complementary shape to one antigen.
The mumps virus has different antigens, so the measles antibody cannot bind to it.
exam.tip: Use 'specific' or 'complementary' plus 'different antigens'.

exam.q: Describe how lymphocytes respond when a pathogen enters the body for the first time.
model: A lymphocyte with a complementary receptor / antibody binds to / recognises the antigen.
The lymphocyte divides (by mitosis) to form a clone.
The clone produces (large amounts of) antibodies specific to the antigen.
Memory lymphocytes are also produced.
exam.tip: Any three: recognise, divide, make antibodies, make memory cells.

exam.q: Describe the role of memory lymphocytes.
model: Memory lymphocytes remain in the blood after an infection.
If the same antigen enters again, they divide rapidly / produce antibodies quickly (secondary response).
exam.tip: Two parts: they stay, then act fast on re-exposure.

exam.q: Explain how antibodies help to destroy pathogens.
model: Antibodies bind to antigens on the pathogen.
This clumps pathogens together / marks them so phagocytes can engulf and digest them.
exam.tip: Antibodies mostly label pathogens; phagocytes do the destroying.

exam.q: A graph shows antibody concentration after two exposures to the same antigen. Describe two differences between the primary and secondary response.
model: Secondary response is faster / starts sooner / shorter delay.
Secondary response produces more antibodies / higher peak / lasts longer.
exam.tip: Use comparative words: faster, higher, longer.

exam.q: Explain why a person does not usually show symptoms when exposed to a pathogen for the second time.
model: Memory lymphocytes (specific to the antigen) are present in the blood.
They recognise the antigen and divide rapidly to produce large numbers of antibodies quickly.
The pathogen is destroyed before it can reproduce enough to cause symptoms.
exam.tip: End with the link to symptoms - that is the third mark.

exam.q: People can catch influenza several times in their life. Suggest why.
model: The influenza virus mutates / new strains appear with different antigens.
Memory lymphocytes / antibodies from earlier infections are not complementary to the new antigens, so a primary response occurs.
exam.tip: Changing antigens is the key idea.

exam.q: Explain the role of the specific immune system in defence against disease.
model: Pathogen enters the body; its antigens are recognised as foreign.
A lymphocyte with a complementary receptor binds to the antigen.
The lymphocyte divides by mitosis to produce a clone.
The clone produces antibodies specific / complementary to the antigen.
Antibodies bind to antigens, clumping / marking pathogens so phagocytes destroy them.
Memory lymphocytes are also produced and remain in the blood.
On a second exposure memory lymphocytes give a faster, larger secondary response.
So the pathogen is destroyed before symptoms develop / the person is immune.
exam.tip: Organise in time order: first exposure, then second exposure. Use every key word.

exam.q: In one person, the peak antibody concentration was 15 arbitrary units in the primary response and 180 arbitrary units in the secondary response. Calculate how many times greater the secondary peak is.
model: = 12 times greater.
exam.tip: Divide the bigger value by the smaller; show your working.

worked.q: A patient's antibody level against a virus reached its peak 14 days after first infection, at 20 arbitrary units (au). After a second infection with the same virus, it peaked after 4 days at 300 au. Compare the two responses with calculations and explain the difference.
steps: Time difference: 14 - 4 = 10 days sooner for the secondary response.
Ratio of peaks: 300 / 20 = 15, so the secondary peak is 15 times higher.
Explain: after the first infection, memory lymphocytes specific to the viral antigen stayed in the blood.
On the second infection they recognised the antigen immediately and divided rapidly, so many more antibodies were made, much faster.
worked.ans: The secondary response peaked 10 days sooner and was 15 times higher because memory lymphocytes were already present and produced antibodies rapidly.

worked.q: Write a model answer (4 marks): Explain why antibodies made against one pathogen only bind to that pathogen.
steps: Antibodies are proteins with binding sites of a particular shape.
Each pathogen has antigens with a unique shape on its surface.
The binding site of the antibody is complementary to the shape of one antigen only.
So it can only bind to antigens of that pathogen and not to the different antigens of other pathogens.
worked.ans: Antibodies are specific: their binding sites are complementary to one antigen, so they cannot bind to the differently shaped antigens of other pathogens.

worked.q: Applied example: Chickenpox is usually caught only once, but colds are caught many times. Explain using memory lymphocytes.
steps: Chickenpox virus antigens stay the same, so memory lymphocytes from the first infection recognise it.
Secondary response destroys the virus before symptoms - the person is immune.
Colds are caused by many different viruses (and strains) with different antigens.
Memory lymphocytes from one cold do not recognise the antigens of a different virus, so each new one causes a primary response and illness.
worked.ans: Immunity to chickenpox lasts because its antigens do not change; colds keep coming back because each is caused by a virus with different antigens that existing memory lymphocytes cannot recognise.

bio_edx.4.9.summary: **Immunisation** (vaccination) gives a person an **inactive form of a pathogen**, such as a dead or weakened pathogen or just its antigens. The **antigens** trigger the specific immune response, so lymphocytes produce **antibodies** and **memory lymphocytes**, but the person does not become ill because the inactive pathogen cannot reproduce or cause disease. If the **live pathogen** with the same antigens enters later, the memory lymphocytes give a rapid **secondary response**, destroying it before symptoms develop, so the person is **immune**.

core.p: Edexcel 1BI0 point 5.14 asks you to **explain the body's response to immunisation using an inactive form of a pathogen**. It builds directly on 5.13: you must use the ideas of antigens, lymphocytes, antibodies, memory lymphocytes and the secondary response, but apply them to a vaccine.
bullets: Know what a vaccine **contains**: an inactive (dead / weakened) pathogen, or its antigens.
Explain why the vaccine **does not cause the disease**.
Explain why the vaccine leads to **immunity** - memory lymphocytes and a secondary response.
Compare a vaccinated and an unvaccinated person meeting the live pathogen, often using a graph.
The advantages, disadvantages and herd immunity are point 5.15B (triple) - not covered here.

callouts.p: A vaccine causes a primary response without illness, so that the real infection later causes a secondary response.

core.p: **Immunisation** means making a person immune to a disease, usually by giving them a **vaccine**. A vaccine is usually **injected**, but some are given by mouth (oral) or as a nasal spray.
bullets: Immunisation is a way of **preventing** disease rather than treating it.
It works with the body's own specific immune response - the vaccine itself does not kill pathogens.
One vaccine protects against **one** disease (or the specific pathogens it contains); MMR is three vaccines in one injection.
Examples in the UK: **MMR** (measles, mumps, rubella), **flu vaccine**, **HPV vaccine**, **polio**, **BCG** (tuberculosis).

callouts.p: Giving a person a vaccine containing an inactive form of a pathogen (or its antigens) so that they become immune to the disease.

core.h: What an inactive form of a pathogen is
core.p: The vaccine contains a version of the pathogen that **cannot cause the disease** but still has the **same antigens** on its surface as the live pathogen. Because lymphocytes respond to antigens, the body reacts as if the real pathogen had entered.
bullets: **Dead (killed) pathogen** - cannot reproduce at all.
**Weakened (attenuated) pathogen** - alive but cannot multiply enough to cause disease.
**Fragments or antigens only** - e.g. surface proteins from the pathogen.
Some vaccines contain an inactivated **toxin** from a bacterium.
The key point for every type: **same antigens, no disease**.

head: Vaccine contents
Can it reproduce?
Has the antigens?
rows: Only very slowly / not enough to cause disease

callouts.p: Do not write that the vaccine 'gives you a mild version of the disease'. Write that it contains an inactive pathogen with the same antigens that cannot cause disease.

fig.cap: An inactive form of a pathogen can be a dead (killed) pathogen, a weakened (attenuated) pathogen, or just the pathogen's antigens. None of these can cause the disease, but they all carry the same antigens (red triangles) as the live pathogen, so they trigger the same specific immune response.

core.p: After the vaccine is given, the **antigens** on the inactive pathogen are recognised as **foreign**. The few lymphocytes with receptors that are **complementary** to those antigens bind to them and are **activated**.
bullets: This is exactly the same recognition step as in a natural infection.
Only lymphocytes specific to the vaccine's antigens respond.
Phagocytes also engulf and digest the inactive pathogens.

core.p: The activated lymphocytes **divide rapidly by mitosis** to form a **clone**. The clone produces **antibodies** that are **specific** (complementary) to the antigens in the vaccine. The antibodies bind to the inactive pathogens, which are then destroyed by phagocytes.
bullets: This is a **primary response**: slow and relatively small.
The person **does not become ill**, because the inactive pathogen cannot reproduce and damage cells.
Some people feel slightly unwell or have a sore arm for a day or two - this is the immune response, not the disease.
Antibody levels then **fall** over the following weeks.

core.p: The most important product of a vaccine is **memory lymphocytes**. These are specific to the vaccine's antigens and **remain in the blood for a long time**, often years, after the antibodies from the primary response have gone.
bullets: Memory lymphocytes are what make the person **immune**.
They can recognise the antigen at once if it enters again.
There are many more of them than the original matching lymphocytes, so the next response is much bigger.
Immunity from a vaccine is called **artificial** immunity because the antigens were deliberately given.

callouts.p: Long-term protection comes from memory lymphocytes, not from antibodies staying in the blood. Examiners reward 'memory lymphocytes remain in the blood'.

core.p: Later, the person may be exposed to the **live pathogen**, which has the **same antigens** as the vaccine. The **memory lymphocytes** recognise the antigens and **divide rapidly**, producing **large amounts of antibodies very quickly**. This is a **secondary response**.
bullets: Antibodies are made **faster**, in **greater amounts** and for **longer** than in a primary response.
The pathogens are destroyed **before they can reproduce enough to cause symptoms**.
So the person does not get ill - they are **immune**.
Without the vaccine, the first contact with the live pathogen would only cause a slow primary response, and the person would likely become ill.

fig.cap: The body's response to immunisation. Steps 1 to 4 are a primary response to the vaccine's antigens, but the person does not become ill because the pathogen is inactive. Steps 5 to 7 happen months or years later: memory lymphocytes give a rapid secondary response when the live pathogen with the same antigens enters.

core.p: Exam questions often compare two people exposed to the same pathogen, one vaccinated and one not. The difference is entirely due to whether **memory lymphocytes** already exist.
bullets: Unvaccinated: primary response - delay of days, low antibody level, pathogen multiplies, **symptoms**.
Vaccinated: secondary response - rapid, high antibody level, pathogen destroyed, **no symptoms**.
Both people produce the **same type** of antibody, because the antigens are the same.
The vaccinated person's antibody level rises above the **protective level** quickly.

fig.cap: Two people meet the same live pathogen. Without vaccination the pathogen multiplies during the slow primary response and causes illness. With vaccination, memory lymphocytes already exist, so the secondary response destroys the pathogen before it can cause symptoms.

core.p: Graphs plot antibody concentration against time, with the vaccine and later infection marked. You may see a dashed line showing the level of antibody needed for protection.
bullets: The first small peak after the vaccine is the **primary response**.
The larger, faster peak after infection is the **secondary response**.
A **booster** dose given later produces a secondary response too, raising antibody and memory cell levels again.
Use data: time for the rise to start, peak height, how long it stays above the protective level.

callouts.p: When describing a graph, give values with units (e.g. 'peak of 120 au after 5 days') and compare.

fig.cap: Antibody levels after vaccination and then infection with the live pathogen. The vaccine causes a small primary response and leaves memory lymphocytes. When the live pathogen arrives, the vaccinated person (green) makes antibodies quickly and well above the protective level. An unvaccinated person (red dashed) only makes a slow primary response, so the pathogen multiplies and causes illness.

core.p: Some vaccines need **more than one dose**. A **booster** is a later dose of the same vaccine that triggers a secondary response, increasing the number of memory lymphocytes and so giving longer-lasting protection.
bullets: Some memory lymphocytes are lost over time, so protection can **fade**.
A booster raises the antibody level higher and faster than the first dose did.
The **flu vaccine** is given every year because the influenza virus **mutates**, so new strains have **different antigens** that the old memory lymphocytes do not recognise.
A vaccine only protects against pathogens with the **same antigens** as those in the vaccine.

callouts.p: Flu antigens change, so memory lymphocytes from last year's vaccine are not complementary to this year's strain.

core.p: Students often confuse vaccines with antibiotics. A vaccine **prevents** infection by preparing the immune system in advance; antibiotics (5.16) **treat** bacterial infections by killing bacteria already in the body.
bullets: Vaccines work against **viruses and bacteria** (and some other pathogens).
Vaccines are given **before** infection; antibiotics are given **after** infection.
Vaccines produce **memory lymphocytes**; antibiotics do not give any immunity.
Vaccines contain antigens; they do **not** contain antibodies.

callouts.p: A vaccine contains antigens. The body makes the antibodies itself.

core.p: Learn this sequence for 4 and 6 mark questions. Each line is roughly one mark.
bullets: 1. Vaccine contains a **dead / weakened (inactive)** pathogen or its **antigens**.
2. The inactive pathogen **cannot reproduce / cause disease**.
3. Its **antigens** trigger lymphocytes with **complementary** receptors.
4. Lymphocytes divide and produce **specific antibodies** (primary response).
5. **Memory lymphocytes** are produced and remain in the blood.
6. On infection with the **live** pathogen (same antigens), memory lymphocytes **rapidly** produce **large numbers** of antibodies (secondary response).
7. Pathogen destroyed **before symptoms** - person is **immune**.

analogy.p: A vaccine is like a fire drill. The alarm sounds and smoke machines are used (the antigens), but there is no real fire (the inactive pathogen cannot cause disease). Everyone practises the escape route, and a written plan is kept on the wall (memory lymphocytes). When a real fire starts (the live pathogen), people react at once because they already know what to do (rapid secondary response), so nobody is harmed. Where it breaks down: in a fire drill people learn something new, but lymphocytes do not learn - the right ones are selected and multiplied; and a fire drill works for any fire, while a vaccine only works for pathogens with the same antigens.

terms.d: Giving a vaccine containing an inactive form of a pathogen (or its antigens) so that a person becomes immune to a disease.
A preparation containing dead or weakened pathogens, or their antigens, given to trigger an immune response.
The act of giving a vaccine, usually by injection.
A pathogen that has been killed or weakened so it cannot cause disease but still has its antigens.
Weakened, so that the pathogen cannot reproduce enough to cause disease.
A molecule (usually a protein) on the surface of a pathogen that triggers an immune response.
A protein made by lymphocytes that binds to a specific, complementary antigen.
A white blood cell that produces antibodies in the specific immune response.
A lymphocyte that stays in the blood after the primary response and rapidly produces antibodies if the same antigen enters again.
The slow, small immune response to the first exposure to an antigen (e.g. the vaccine).
The rapid, large immune response to a later exposure to the same antigen, due to memory lymphocytes.
Protected from a disease because memory lymphocytes can destroy the pathogen before symptoms develop.
A later dose of a vaccine that triggers a secondary response and increases the number of memory lymphocytes.
A variety of a pathogen; a new strain may have different antigens.
Immunity produced by deliberately giving antigens in a vaccine, rather than by catching the disease.

mistakes.w: Vaccines contain antibodies.
mistakes.r: Vaccines contain an inactive pathogen / antigens; the body's lymphocytes make the antibodies.

mistakes.w: A vaccine gives you a mild form of the disease.
mistakes.r: The vaccine contains a dead or weakened pathogen that cannot cause disease but has the same antigens.

mistakes.w: Antibodies stay in your blood for life after vaccination.
mistakes.r: Antibody levels fall; memory lymphocytes remain and produce antibodies rapidly on infection.

mistakes.w: The vaccine kills the pathogen when you are infected.
mistakes.r: The vaccine has gone by then; memory lymphocytes produced in response to it give a rapid secondary response.

mistakes.w: White blood cells remember the disease.
mistakes.r: Memory lymphocytes recognise the specific antigen.

mistakes.w: Vaccinated people make antibodies faster (only).
mistakes.r: Antibodies are made faster AND in larger amounts, so the pathogen is destroyed before symptoms appear.

mistakes.w: The flu vaccine wears off each year.
mistakes.r: The flu virus mutates, producing new strains with different antigens, so a new vaccine is needed.

mistakes.w: Vaccines cure diseases.
mistakes.r: Vaccines prevent disease by causing immunity before infection; they do not treat an existing infection.

mistakes.w: Any vaccine protects against all diseases.
mistakes.r: A vaccine is specific: it only protects against pathogens with the same antigens as those in the vaccine.

exam.q: State what is contained in a vaccine.
model: Dead / inactive / weakened pathogen, or antigens (from the pathogen).
exam.tip: Not 'antibodies' and not 'the disease'.

exam.q: Explain why a vaccine does not make a person ill.
model: The pathogen in the vaccine is dead / inactive / weakened.
So it cannot reproduce / cause disease (but still has antigens).
exam.tip: Two parts: what state it is in, and what it therefore cannot do.

exam.q: Name the type of cell that remains in the blood after vaccination and gives long-term protection.
model: Memory lymphocytes.
exam.tip: 'Memory cells' is usually accepted, but 'memory lymphocytes' is the spec term.

exam.q: Describe how the body responds to a vaccine.
model: Antigens (on the inactive pathogen) are recognised by lymphocytes.
Lymphocytes produce (specific) antibodies.
Memory lymphocytes are produced (and remain in the blood).
exam.tip: Antigens - antibodies - memory lymphocytes.

exam.q: Explain how vaccination prevents a person from becoming ill when they are later infected with the live pathogen.
model: Memory lymphocytes (from vaccination) are present in the blood.
The live pathogen has the same antigens as the vaccine, so memory lymphocytes recognise them.
Memory lymphocytes divide rapidly / produce large numbers of antibodies quickly (secondary response).
The pathogen is destroyed before it can reproduce / cause symptoms.
exam.tip: The phrase 'same antigens' links the vaccine to the live pathogen - include it.

exam.q: Suggest why a new influenza vaccine is produced every year.
model: The influenza virus mutates / new strains appear.
New strains have different antigens, so existing memory lymphocytes / antibodies are not complementary to them.
exam.tip: Mention 'different antigens' explicitly.

exam.q: Give one difference between a vaccine and an antibiotic.
model: A vaccine prevents disease / is given before infection / gives immunity, whereas an antibiotic treats bacterial infection / kills bacteria / is given after infection.
exam.tip: Write a comparative sentence using 'whereas'.

exam.q: A graph shows antibody levels in a vaccinated and an unvaccinated person after both were infected with the same pathogen. Explain the difference in the curves.
model: Vaccinated person's antibody level rises faster / higher.
Because memory lymphocytes are already present from the vaccine.
Unvaccinated person only has a primary response, which is slow / small, so the pathogen multiplies and causes symptoms.
exam.tip: Describe first, then explain both curves.

exam.q: Explain why some vaccines are given as a booster several years after the first dose.
model: Number of memory lymphocytes / protection may decrease over time.
A booster causes a secondary response, increasing antibody levels and memory lymphocytes again.
exam.tip: Link the booster to a secondary response.

exam.q: Explain the body's response to immunisation using an inactive form of a pathogen.
model: Vaccine contains dead / weakened pathogen or its antigens.
Inactive pathogen cannot reproduce / does not cause disease.
Antigens are recognised by / trigger lymphocytes (with complementary receptors).
Lymphocytes divide / clone and produce specific antibodies.
Memory lymphocytes are produced and remain in the blood.
If the live pathogen (same antigens) enters later, memory lymphocytes recognise it.
Antibodies are produced rapidly and in large amounts (secondary response).
Pathogen destroyed before symptoms develop, so the person is immune.
exam.tip: Two halves: what happens after the vaccine, then what happens on real infection. Use 'inactive', 'antigen', 'memory lymphocyte' and 'secondary response'.

worked.q: After a vaccine, a child's antibody level peaked at 25 au after 12 days. A year later, after infection with the live pathogen, it peaked at 400 au after 3 days. The protective level is 100 au. Analyse the data and explain.
steps: Ratio of peaks: 400 / 25 = 16, so the secondary peak is 16 times higher.
Time to peak: 12 - 3 = 9 days quicker.
After the vaccine the peak (25 au) was below the protective level, but the child was not ill because the pathogen was inactive.
After infection, memory lymphocytes from the vaccine recognised the same antigens and rapidly produced antibodies above the 100 au protective level.
So the live pathogen was destroyed before it could cause symptoms.
worked.ans: The secondary response was 16 times larger and 9 days faster, well above the protective level, because memory lymphocytes made by the vaccine responded rapidly to the same antigens.

worked.q: Model answer (4 marks): Explain why a person vaccinated against measles does not develop measles when they are exposed to the measles virus.
steps: The vaccine contained inactive measles virus with the same antigens as the live virus.
This caused lymphocytes to produce antibodies and memory lymphocytes specific to measles antigens.
On exposure, memory lymphocytes recognise the measles antigens and quickly divide, producing large amounts of antibodies.
The virus is destroyed before it can reproduce enough to cause symptoms.
worked.ans: Memory lymphocytes produced in response to the vaccine give a rapid secondary response, destroying the measles virus before symptoms develop.

worked.q: Applied example: A person had the flu vaccine last winter but still caught flu this winter. Suggest two reasons.
steps: The influenza virus may have mutated, so this winter's strain has different antigens from those in last year's vaccine.
Memory lymphocytes are not complementary to the new antigens, so only a slow primary response occurs.
Or: the number of memory lymphocytes may have fallen over time, so the response was not rapid enough.
worked.ans: Either the virus has changed its antigens (new strain), or protection from memory lymphocytes has decreased, so the response was too slow to prevent illness.

bio_edx.4.16.summary: Monoclonal antibodies are many copies of one identical antibody, all made by clones of a single hybridoma cell. A hybridoma is made by fusing a lymphocyte (which makes one specific antibody but cannot divide) with a myeloma tumour cell (which divides rapidly but makes no useful antibody), so it does both. Because each antibody binds only to one specific antigen, monoclonal antibodies are used in pregnancy tests, to diagnose disease (finding blood clots and cancer cells, measuring hormones and detecting pathogens) and to treat cancer by carrying drugs or radioactive substances to cancer cells.

core.p: An antibody is a protein made by a **lymphocyte** that has a shape **complementary** to one specific **antigen**. Monoclonal means 'from one clone': every antibody in the sample is identical and binds the same antigen.
bullets: Each lymphocyte makes **one type** of antibody, specific to **one antigen**.
**Monoclonal antibodies** = identical antibodies produced by **clones of one hybridoma cell**.
They all have the **same binding site**, so they all bind to the **same antigen** and nothing else.
Because of this specificity they can be used to **find and stick to one chemical or cell** in the body or in a sample.
A normal immune response is **polyclonal**: many different lymphocytes make many different antibodies against different parts of a pathogen.

callouts.p: Identical antibodies produced from clones of a single hybridoma cell, all specific to one antigen.

core.h: The problem: lymphocytes do not divide in culture
core.p: Scientists want a huge supply of one antibody. Lymphocytes make the antibody but they **do not divide** (well) outside the body, so you cannot grow lots of them. Tumour cells do the opposite.
bullets: **Lymphocytes**: make the specific antibody but **cannot divide** to make a large population in culture.
**Myeloma cells**: a type of **tumour (cancer) cell** that **divides rapidly and repeatedly** but does **not** make the antibody we want.
Solution: **fuse** the two to get a cell that has **both** properties.
This combined cell is called a **hybridoma** ('hybrid' + '-oma', meaning tumour).

callouts.p: The lymphocyte gives the ability to make one specific antibody; the myeloma cell gives the ability to divide rapidly. The hybridoma has both.

core.h: Step by step: producing monoclonal antibodies
core.p: Learn the stages in order; 4 and 6 mark questions often ask for this sequence.
bullets: 1. A mouse (or other animal) is **injected with the antigen** you want an antibody against.
2. The mouse's immune system responds and its **lymphocytes** start making antibodies against that antigen.
3. **Lymphocytes are removed** from the mouse (usually from the spleen).
4. The lymphocytes are **fused with myeloma (tumour) cells** to make **hybridoma cells**.
5. The hybridoma cell that makes the **required antibody** is selected (identified and separated).
6. The selected hybridoma **divides by mitosis** to make **many genetically identical clones**.
7. All the clones make the **same antibody**; it is **collected and purified**.
Result: large amounts of **monoclonal antibody**, all specific to one antigen.

callouts.p: Name both cells (lymphocyte and myeloma/tumour cell), say they are fused to form a hybridoma, then say the hybridoma divides to make clones that all produce the same antibody.

fig.cap: A lymphocyte (makes one antibody) fuses with a myeloma tumour cell (divides rapidly) to form a hybridoma. The hybridoma divides by mitosis into identical clones that all secrete the same monoclonal antibody.

core.h: Why the antibodies are all identical
core.p: The hybridoma is cloned by **mitosis**, so every daughter cell has the **same genes** as the original. The gene for the antibody came from **one lymphocyte**, so every clone makes exactly the same antibody.
bullets: Mitosis produces **genetically identical** cells.
All clones carry the same antibody gene inherited from the single original lymphocyte.
So the antibodies all have the **same shape of binding site**.
This is why they are 'mono' (one) 'clonal' (from a clone).

core.h: Why monoclonal antibodies are so useful: specificity
core.p: Every use depends on one idea: an antibody binds **only** to the antigen that is **complementary** to its binding site. By making antibodies against a chosen chemical or cell, we can detect it or deliver something to it.
bullets: They bind to **specific antigens** such as a hormone (hCG), a protein on a **cancer cell**, a **pathogen**, or a protein in a **blood clot**.
Other molecules and cells without that antigen are **not** bound.
Antibodies can have other things **attached** to them: a **coloured dye**, a **fluorescent marker**, a **radioactive substance**, or a **drug**.
The antibody acts like a **guided carrier**: it finds the target, and the attached substance shows where it is or acts there.

callouts.p: Monoclonal antibodies are specific: they bind only to one antigen, because the antigen is complementary in shape to the antibody's binding site.

core.p: A pregnant woman produces the hormone **hCG (human chorionic gonadotrophin)**, made by the developing embryo/placenta, and some of it passes into her **urine**. A pregnancy test strip contains monoclonal antibodies specific to hCG.
bullets: Urine is put on the **end of the strip** and soaks along it.
**Mobile antibodies** near the start are specific to hCG and are **attached to a coloured bead/dye**. If hCG is present it **binds** to them.
The urine carries the **hCG-antibody-dye complexes** along the strip.

At the **test line (T)**, antibodies specific to hCG are **fixed (immobilised)** to the strip. They bind the hCG that is already attached to the mobile antibodies, so the **dye collects** and a **coloured line** appears.
At the **control line (C)**, fixed antibodies bind to the **mobile antibodies themselves** (not to hCG). So the dye collects here **whether or not** hCG is present.
**Two lines (T and C)** = pregnant. **Only the control line** = not pregnant.
**No control line** = test has **not worked** (e.g. urine did not travel up the strip), so the result is invalid.

head: Line
Antibodies there are
Bind to
Colour appears when
rows: Fixed, specific to the mobile antibody

callouts.p: The control line does NOT detect hCG. Its antibodies bind the mobile antibodies, showing the urine reached the end and the test worked.

fig.cap: Urine flows along the strip. Dye-linked mobile antibodies pick up any hCG. Fixed antibodies at the test line trap hCG complexes; fixed antibodies at the control line trap the mobile antibodies themselves, so a working test always shows a control line.

core.p: Monoclonal antibodies can **measure the levels of hormones and other chemicals in blood**, and **detect pathogens**, because they bind only their target.
bullets: **Measuring hormones/chemicals in blood**: antibodies attached to a dye or marker bind the chemical; the amount of colour/signal shows **how much** is present.
**Detecting pathogens**: antibodies specific to an antigen on a virus or bacterium show whether that pathogen is present in a sample (e.g. blood, saliva, plant sap).
Used in hospitals and research labs to **identify which pathogen** a patient has, so the right treatment can be chosen.
Also used to **identify specific molecules** in cells or tissue by binding a **fluorescent dye** to the antibody (it glows under UV light where the molecule is).

core.h: Use 3: locating blood clots and cancer cells in the body
core.p: Antibodies can be used to show **where** something is inside the body, by attaching a marker that can be detected from outside.
bullets: Make monoclonal antibodies against a protein found in **blood clots** (e.g. fibrin) or an **antigen on cancer cells**.
Attach a **radioactive** substance (or another marker) to the antibodies.
**Inject** them into the patient; they travel in the blood and **bind only to the clot or cancer cells**.
A **camera that detects radiation** (gamma camera / scanner) shows where the radioactivity has built up, which reveals the **position** of the clot or tumour.
Doctors can then decide on treatment, and early detection improves the chance of success.

callouts.p: Marks go for: the antibodies are specific to an antigen on the clot or cancer cell, so they bind there and the radioactive marker builds up in that place only.

core.p: Cancer cells have **antigens on their surface** that normal body cells do not have (or have far fewer of). Monoclonal antibodies against these antigens can target the cancer cells.
bullets: Antibodies can be **bound to a drug** (e.g. a toxic drug or chemotherapy drug) or a **radioactive substance**.
They are injected and **bind only to cancer cells** with the matching antigen.
The drug or radiation is **delivered directly to the cancer cells**, killing them.

**Normal body cells are not affected** (or much less affected) because they lack the antigen, so there are **fewer side effects** than conventional chemotherapy, which harms all rapidly dividing cells.
Some monoclonal antibodies work on their own: they **mark cancer cells** so the immune system attacks them, or **block receptors** that stop the cancer cells growing and dividing.

callouts.p: The antibody delivers the drug or radioactive substance only to cells carrying the specific antigen, so healthy cells are spared.

fig.cap: A monoclonal antibody carrying a drug or radioactive substance binds only to the antigens on the cancer cell surface. A normal cell has no matching antigen so it is not bound or harmed.

core.p: When asked to evaluate, give benefits that come from specificity and from being able to make lots.
bullets: **Specific**: bind only one target, so tests are accurate and treatments target only diseased cells.
Targeted treatment means **less damage to healthy cells** and **fewer side effects** than ordinary chemotherapy.
Can be made in **large quantities** because hybridomas divide quickly.
Can be made against **almost any antigen**, so very many uses (tests, diagnosis, treatment, research).
Tests such as pregnancy kits are **quick, cheap and can be done at home**.

core.p: Monoclonal antibodies are not perfect. Exam questions may ask you to evaluate their use.
bullets: They can cause **more side effects than first expected** (e.g. fever, vomiting, low blood pressure, allergic-type reactions).
Antibodies made in mice can trigger the **patient's immune system** to attack them (they are foreign proteins), although modern ones are 'humanised'.
They are **expensive** to develop and produce.
Producing them involves **using animals** (mice), which raises **ethical** concerns.
They only work if the target cell or molecule has a **known, specific antigen**.

callouts.p: Give both sides and finish with a judgement, for example: targeted treatment reduces side effects compared with chemotherapy, but cost and unexpected side effects limit their use.

core.p: This point builds on how lymphocytes and antibodies work (spec 5.13). Use the same language.
bullets: Antigens are molecules (usually proteins) on the surface of cells or pathogens.
Each lymphocyte has receptors / makes antibodies for **one** antigen.
In the mouse, the lymphocyte that matches the injected antigen is **activated**, so lymphocytes taken from the mouse include ones making the right antibody.
Monoclonal antibody technology simply turns one of those lymphocytes into a 'factory' that never stops dividing.

analogy.t: A photocopier for one perfect key
analogy.p: A lymphocyte is a locksmith who can cut one key that fits one lock (the antigen), but works slowly and alone. A myeloma cell is a photocopier that never stops copying but has nothing useful to copy. Fusing them (the hybridoma) gives a machine that endlessly copies that one key, so you get millions of identical keys. You can tie a torch (dye or radioactive marker) or a bomb (drug) to each key, and it only opens, and so only lights up or destroys, the matching lock. Where it breaks down: real keys are cut by a person, while antibodies are proteins that bind by complementary shape; and hybridomas are living cells that copy themselves by mitosis rather than copying something else.

terms.d: A protein made by lymphocytes that binds to a specific antigen because its binding site is complementary in shape.
A molecule (usually a protein) on the surface of a cell or pathogen that is recognised by, and binds to, a specific antibody.
A type of white blood cell that produces antibodies; each one makes antibodies specific to one antigen.
A type of tumour (cancer) cell that divides rapidly and repeatedly but does not make the required antibody.
A cell formed by fusing a lymphocyte with a myeloma cell; it makes one specific antibody and divides rapidly.
Identical antibodies produced from clones of a single hybridoma cell, all specific to the same antigen.
A genetically identical cell produced by mitosis from one parent cell.
Joining two cells together to form one cell containing genetic material from both.
Having a matching shape so two molecules fit together, like the antibody binding site and its antigen.
Human chorionic gonadotrophin, a hormone made only during pregnancy that is found in the urine and detected by pregnancy tests.
Antibodies in a test strip that are free to move with the urine and are attached to a coloured bead or dye.
Antibodies attached firmly to the test strip at the test or control line so they cannot move.
Line on a test strip with fixed antibodies that bind the mobile antibodies, showing the test has worked.
A radioactive substance attached to antibodies so their position in the body can be detected with a camera or scanner.
Treatment where a drug is delivered only to specific cells, such as using monoclonal antibodies to deliver a drug to cancer cells.

mistakes.w: The hybridoma is made by fusing a lymphocyte with a normal body cell.
mistakes.r: A lymphocyte is fused with a myeloma (tumour/cancer) cell.

mistakes.w: Myeloma cells are used because they make antibodies.
mistakes.r: Myeloma cells are used because they divide rapidly; the lymphocyte supplies the ability to make the specific antibody.

mistakes.w: The hybridoma divides by meiosis.
mistakes.r: The hybridoma divides by mitosis, producing genetically identical clones that all make the same antibody.

mistakes.w: The control line shows that hCG is present.
mistakes.r: The control line antibodies bind the mobile antibodies, not hCG; it shows the test has worked.

mistakes.w: The antibodies kill the cancer cells by eating them.
mistakes.r: Antibodies bind to antigens on cancer cells and deliver an attached drug or radioactive substance which kills the cell (or mark it for the immune system).

mistakes.w: Monoclonal antibodies are antibodies made from lots of different lymphocytes.
mistakes.r: They come from clones of a single hybridoma cell, so they are all identical and specific to one antigen.

mistakes.w: Antibodies fit the antigen because they are the same shape.
mistakes.r: The antibody binding site is complementary in shape to the antigen.

mistakes.w: Targeted treatment has no side effects.
mistakes.r: It has fewer side effects than conventional chemotherapy because healthy cells are not targeted, but monoclonal antibodies can still cause side effects.

mistakes.w: The radioactive antibody shows a blood clot because the radiation destroys it.
mistakes.r: The antibodies bind specifically to the clot, so the radioactive marker builds up there and its position is detected with a camera.

exam.q: Name the two types of cell that are fused to make a hybridoma cell.
model: lymphocyte (white blood cell / B cell)
myeloma cell / tumour cell / cancer cell
exam.tip: Write 'myeloma' or 'tumour'; 'cancer cell' is accepted. Do not write just 'white blood cell and blood cell'.

exam.q: State what is meant by a monoclonal antibody.
model: (many) identical antibodies produced by clones of a single hybridoma cell / all specific to one antigen
exam.tip: Key idea: identical, from one clone.

exam.q: Explain why a myeloma cell is used when making monoclonal antibodies.
model: myeloma cells divide rapidly / repeatedly
so the hybridoma can divide to produce many (identical) cells / large amounts of antibody (lymphocytes do not divide in culture)
exam.tip: Link the property (divides quickly) to the outcome (lots of antibody).

exam.q: Describe how monoclonal antibodies are produced.
model: mouse injected with (specific) antigen
lymphocytes (that make the antibody) removed from the mouse
lymphocytes fused with myeloma / tumour cells to form hybridoma cells
hybridoma (making the required antibody) selected and divides / cloned by mitosis
clones all produce the same antibody, which is collected / purified
exam.tip: Any four. Keep the order and use the word hybridoma.

exam.q: Explain why all the antibodies produced by a hybridoma clone are identical.
model: the hybridoma divides by mitosis so all cells are genetically identical
all came from one lymphocyte so they have the same gene / make antibody with the same binding site / specific to the same antigen
exam.tip: Mention mitosis and genetically identical.

exam.q: A pregnancy test has a test line and a control line. Explain why a line appears at the control line even if the woman is not pregnant.
model: antibodies at the control line are fixed and bind to the mobile antibodies (attached to dye)
the mobile antibodies reach the control line whether or not hCG is present, so the dye builds up / the line shows the test has worked
exam.tip: Say what the control antibodies bind to: the mobile antibodies, not hCG.

exam.q: Explain how a pregnancy test uses monoclonal antibodies to show that a woman is pregnant.
model: pregnant women produce the hormone hCG, which is present in urine
urine applied to the end of the strip and moves along it
mobile antibodies specific to hCG are attached to a coloured bead / dye
hCG binds to the mobile antibodies (because shapes are complementary)
the hCG-antibody complex moves to the test line where fixed antibodies specific to hCG bind it
dye collects at the test line, so a coloured line appears
fixed antibodies at the control line bind mobile antibodies so a control line appears
two lines = pregnant; only control line = not pregnant
exam.tip: Six-mark answers need a clear sequence from urine to result. Include both lines.

exam.q: Describe how monoclonal antibodies can be used to find the position of a blood clot.
model: antibodies made that are specific to (a protein / antigen in) the blood clot
radioactive marker attached to the antibodies and they are injected (into the blood)
antibodies bind to the clot, radiation detected by a camera / scanner shows where the clot is
exam.tip: The same structure works for locating cancer cells.

exam.q: Explain how monoclonal antibodies can be used to treat cancer with fewer side effects than conventional chemotherapy.
model: monoclonal antibodies made that are specific to an antigen on cancer cells
a drug / radioactive substance / toxin is attached to the antibody
antibodies bind only to cancer cells so the drug is delivered directly to them / kills them
normal cells do not have the antigen so are not damaged (chemotherapy damages all rapidly dividing cells)
exam.tip: Contrast with chemotherapy, which harms healthy dividing cells too.

exam.q: Give one use of monoclonal antibodies in the diagnosis of disease, other than locating blood clots and cancer cells.
model: measuring levels of hormones / chemicals in the blood OR detecting pathogens (in a sample)
exam.tip: Edexcel lists these two diagnostic uses.

exam.q: Evaluate the use of monoclonal antibodies to treat cancer.
model: advantage: specific to antigen on cancer cells so target only cancer cells
advantage: fewer side effects / less harm to healthy cells than chemotherapy
advantage: can carry drugs or radioactive substances directly to tumour
disadvantage: can still cause side effects (more than first expected)
disadvantage: expensive to produce / develop
disadvantage: involves use of animals (mice) / ethical issues; may trigger an immune response
judgement / conclusion given with reason
exam.tip: Balance benefits and drawbacks, then end with a justified conclusion.

worked.q: A student writes: 'Lymphocytes are fused with myeloma cells because lymphocytes divide quickly.' Correct this and explain the role of each cell.
steps: Identify the error: it is the myeloma cell, not the lymphocyte, that divides quickly.
Role of lymphocyte: produces the specific antibody (complementary to one antigen) but does not divide in culture.
Role of myeloma cell: a tumour cell that divides rapidly and repeatedly.
Fusion makes a hybridoma that both makes the antibody and divides, so it can be cloned to make large amounts.
worked.ans: Myeloma cells divide quickly; lymphocytes make the specific antibody. Fusing them gives a hybridoma cell with both properties, which is cloned to produce lots of identical antibody.

worked.q: A woman takes a pregnancy test. No line appears in either the test window or the control window. What does this mean and what should she do?
steps: The control line should appear in every working test because its fixed antibodies bind the mobile antibodies.
No control line means the mobile antibodies did not reach it: the test has failed (e.g. too little urine or a faulty strip).
So the absence of a test line tells us nothing about hCG.
worked.ans: The result is invalid because the test did not work; she should repeat it with a new test.

worked.q: A drug that kills dividing cells causes hair loss and sickness when given alone. Doctors attach it to a monoclonal antibody against a protein found only on breast cancer cells. Predict and explain the effect on side effects.
steps: The antibody is specific to the protein on breast cancer cells (complementary binding site).
After injection, antibodies bind only to cells with this antigen, so the drug is concentrated at the cancer cells.
Healthy dividing cells (hair follicles, gut lining) do not have the antigen, so receive little drug.
Some side effects may remain, because some drug may be released or antibodies may cause reactions.
worked.ans: Side effects should be reduced because the drug is delivered mainly to cancer cells and healthy dividing cells are spared, although some side effects may still occur.

bio_edx.4.17.summary: Non-communicable diseases cannot be passed from person to person, and most are caused by several risk factors acting together rather than by one cause. These include cardiovascular disease, many cancers, some lung and liver diseases and diseases linked to nutrition such as type 2 diabetes. Lifestyle factors (diet, exercise, alcohol and smoking) strongly affect the risk: poor diet and lack of exercise lead to obesity and malnutrition, alcohol damages the liver and smoking causes cardiovascular disease, with effects at local, national and global levels.

core.p: A **non-communicable disease** is one that **cannot be transmitted** from one person to another. Most are linked to **risk factors**: things that **increase the chance** of getting the disease, but do not guarantee it.
bullets: Examples: **cardiovascular disease** (heart disease, stroke), **many cancers**, **lung diseases** linked to smoking, **liver diseases** (cirrhosis), **type 2 diabetes** and other diseases influenced by nutrition.
**Risk factor** = a factor linked with an **increased likelihood** of developing a disease.
Lifestyle risk factors can be **changed**: diet, exercise, alcohol, smoking.
Some risk factors **cannot** be changed: **genes (inheritance)**, **age**, **sex**.
Having a risk factor does **not** mean you will get the disease, and people with no obvious risk factors can still get it.

callouts.p: A disease that is not transmitted from one person to another.
A factor that increases the likelihood of developing a disease.

core.p: Edexcel wants you to recall that **many non-communicable diseases are caused by the interaction of a number of factors**. No single factor explains who gets the disease; factors **add together** and **affect each other**.
bullets: **Cardiovascular disease**: smoking, high-fat diet, high salt, lack of exercise, obesity, high blood pressure, alcohol, genes, age.
**Many forms of cancer**: smoking, alcohol, obesity, UV light, some viruses, genes.
**Lung diseases** (e.g. lung cancer, COPD/bronchitis/emphysema): mainly **smoking**, plus air pollution and genes.
**Liver diseases** (e.g. cirrhosis): mainly **alcohol**, plus obesity.
**Nutrition-related diseases** including **type 2 diabetes**: poor diet, obesity, lack of exercise, genes, age.
Factors interact: e.g. poor diet **and** lack of exercise together cause obesity, and obesity is itself a risk factor for CVD and type 2 diabetes.
So the **combined risk** of several factors is greater than one alone.

callouts.p: Many non-communicable diseases are caused by the interaction of a number of factors.

fig.cap: Cardiovascular disease has many risk factors. Lifestyle factors (smoking, diet, exercise, alcohol) and non-lifestyle factors (genes, age) act together; poor diet and lack of exercise also cause obesity, which raises the risk further.

core.h: Correlation is not the same as cause
core.p: Most evidence for risk factors comes from studies of large numbers of people that show a **correlation**. A correlation alone does not prove one thing causes another.
bullets: A **correlation** means as one factor changes, the other also changes (e.g. more cigarettes smoked, higher rate of lung cancer).
To show **cause**, scientists also need a **mechanism** that explains how the factor causes the disease (e.g. carcinogens in tar cause mutations in lung cells).
Large **sample sizes** make conclusions more reliable.
Other factors (e.g. smokers may also drink more) can **confound** a study, so good studies control or match for these.

callouts.p: If a graph shows a correlation, say 'there is a correlation / link', not 'this proves X causes Y', unless a mechanism is given.

core.p: If you take in **more energy** from food than you **use**, the extra is **stored as fat**. Over time this leads to **obesity**.
bullets: Energy in (food, especially fatty and sugary foods) > energy out (metabolism + activity) = weight gain.
**Lack of exercise** means less energy is used, so more is stored as fat.
**Exercise** uses energy, helps control body mass, lowers blood pressure and strengthens the heart.
Obesity increases the risk of **type 2 diabetes**, **cardiovascular disease**, some **cancers** and joint problems.
Obesity is assessed using **BMI** and **waist:hip ratio** (BMI = mass in kg / (height in m)^2; a BMI of 30 or more is classed as obese).

callouts.p: Obesity results when energy intake is greater than energy used over a long time, so the extra is stored as fat.

core.p: **Malnutrition** means the diet does not have the **right balance** of nutrients. It includes eating **too little** food (undernutrition), **too little of a particular nutrient**, or **too much** (overnutrition, which leads to obesity).
bullets: Too little energy: weight loss, tiredness, poor growth in children, weakened immune system so more infections.
Too little of a specific nutrient causes **deficiency diseases**: e.g. lack of **vitamin C** causes **scurvy**, lack of **vitamin D** causes **rickets**, lack of **iron** causes **anaemia**.
Too much **saturated fat** raises blood **cholesterol**, increasing **fatty deposits** in arteries (cardiovascular disease).
Too much **salt** increases **blood pressure**, a risk factor for heart disease and stroke.
Undernutrition is more common in **poorer countries**; obesity is increasing in richer countries and in many developing countries too.

head: Problem
Lifestyle cause
Disease risk
rows: Too much energy, too little exercise

callouts.p: An obese person can be malnourished: malnutrition means an unbalanced diet, including too much.

core.p: The **liver** breaks down alcohol (ethanol), but some of the products are **toxic**. Drinking **too much over a long time** damages liver cells.
bullets: Liver cells are damaged and may die, and fat builds up in the liver (**fatty liver**).
Repeated damage leads to **scar tissue** replacing normal liver tissue: this is **cirrhosis**.
A cirrhotic liver **cannot carry out its functions** (e.g. removing toxins, making proteins), which can lead to **liver failure** and death.
Alcohol also increases the risk of **liver cancer** and other cancers (mouth, throat).
Alcohol also affects the **brain** (brain damage with long-term heavy use) and raises **blood pressure**.
Drinking during pregnancy can damage the developing fetus.

callouts.p: Edexcel pairs alcohol with liver disease. Say: liver breaks down alcohol, toxic products damage liver cells, leading to cirrhosis.

fig.cap: The liver breaks down alcohol into toxic products. With long-term heavy drinking these damage liver cells, scar tissue forms (cirrhosis) and the liver may stop working; the risk of liver cancer also rises.
