core.p: Tobacco smoke contains **nicotine**, **carbon monoxide**, **tar** and many other harmful chemicals. Edexcel pairs smoking with **cardiovascular disease**.
bullets: Chemicals in smoke **damage the lining of arteries**, so **fatty deposits (plaques)** build up there and the artery **narrows**.
Narrowed coronary arteries reduce blood (and oxygen) to the heart muscle: **coronary heart disease**, angina, **heart attack**.
Damaged arteries make **blood clots** more likely, which can block an artery and cause a heart attack or **stroke**.
**Nicotine** increases **heart rate** and narrows blood vessels, raising **blood pressure**.
**Carbon monoxide** binds to **haemoglobin** in red blood cells, so blood carries **less oxygen**; the heart must work harder.
Smoking also causes **lung cancer** (carcinogens in tar) and lung diseases such as **COPD**.

head: Chemical in smoke

rows: Addictive; raises heart rate and blood pressure

core.p: The spec asks you to describe effects at **local, national and global** levels. Locally means the individual, their family and the local community.
bullets: **Individual**: poorer quality of life, pain, disability, shorter life expectancy, may be unable to work.
**Family**: may need to care for the person, loss of income, emotional stress.
**Local community/health services**: more demand on GP surgeries and local hospitals; time off work affects local businesses.
Local areas with **higher poverty** often have higher rates of smoking, obesity and related disease.

core.p: Across a whole country, lifestyle diseases have large **economic and social** costs.
bullets: The **NHS** spends **billions of pounds** every year treating obesity, smoking-related disease, alcohol-related disease and type 2 diabetes.
Fewer people able to work reduces the **workforce** and **income tax**, and increases benefit payments.

Governments spend money on **public health campaigns** (e.g. anti-smoking adverts, healthy-eating advice), **taxes** on cigarettes, alcohol and sugary drinks, and laws such as banning smoking in public places.
Comparing data between **regions** shows where to target money and campaigns.

core.p: Globally, **non-communicable diseases cause most deaths** (around 7 in 10 deaths worldwide, according to the WHO).
bullets: Cardiovascular disease is the **leading cause of death** worldwide.
**Obesity and type 2 diabetes** are rising in many countries as diets include more processed, high-energy food and people do less physical activity.
Some countries face a **double burden**: undernutrition in some people and obesity in others.
Smoking rates are falling in many high-income countries but remain high in some others.
Poorer countries may have **fewer resources** to treat NCDs, so outcomes are worse.
Global organisations such as the **WHO** monitor rates and set targets to reduce risk factors.

callouts.p: In an answer about effects, name the level (individual/local, national, global) and give a specific effect at each: e.g. local = carers and local hospitals; national = NHS cost; global = most deaths worldwide.

core.p: Because lifestyle factors can be changed, the risk of these diseases can be **reduced**.
bullets: **Stop smoking** (risk of heart disease falls quickly after stopping).
Eat a **balanced diet**: less saturated fat, salt and sugar; more fruit, vegetables and fibre.
Take **regular exercise**.
Keep **alcohol** within recommended limits.
Maintain a **healthy body mass** (BMI).
Individuals make choices, but **education**, **taxes** and **laws** help change behaviour across a population.

analogy.t: Risk factors are like weights on a shelf
analogy.p: Imagine a shelf (your health) with weights placed on it. Smoking, poor diet, lack of exercise, alcohol, genes and age are each a weight. One weight alone rarely snaps the shelf, but several together, especially heavy ones, make it far more likely to break (disease develops). Some weights you can take off (lifestyle factors) and some you cannot (genes, age). Where it breaks down: real risk factors also interact with each other (poor diet and no exercise cause obesity, which adds another weight), and a shelf breaking is certain at a fixed load, while disease is a matter of probability, so some people with many risk factors never become ill.

terms.d: A disease that cannot be transmitted from one person to another.
A factor that increases the likelihood of developing a disease.
A risk factor a person can choose to change, such as diet, exercise, alcohol intake or smoking.
Disease of the heart or blood vessels, such as coronary heart disease or stroke.
Having a large amount of stored body fat, usually defined as a BMI of 30 or more.
A condition caused by a diet that does not contain the right balance of nutrients; too little, or too much.
A disease caused by lack of a specific nutrient, such as scurvy from lack of vitamin C.
Liver disease in which damaged liver tissue is replaced by scar tissue, so the liver cannot function properly; often caused by long-term heavy drinking.
Build-up of fat and cholesterol in the wall of an artery that narrows the lumen.
Gas in cigarette smoke that binds to haemoglobin and reduces the amount of oxygen the blood carries.
Addictive chemical in tobacco that increases heart rate and blood pressure.
A substance that causes cancer, such as chemicals in tar.
A non-communicable disease where body cells no longer respond properly to insulin; obesity is a major risk factor.
A link between two variables where one changes as the other changes; it does not by itself prove cause.
Body mass index: mass in kg divided by height in m squared, used to judge whether body mass is healthy.

mistakes.w: Smoking causes heart disease.
mistakes.r: Smoking is a risk factor that increases the likelihood of cardiovascular disease; it interacts with other factors.

mistakes.w: Non-communicable diseases are caused by one factor.
mistakes.r: Many non-communicable diseases are caused by the interaction of a number of factors.

mistakes.w: Malnutrition just means not eating enough.
mistakes.r: Malnutrition is an unbalanced diet, which can be too little, lack of a specific nutrient, or too much (leading to obesity).

mistakes.w: Alcohol damages the liver because the liver stores it.
mistakes.r: The liver breaks down alcohol, producing toxic products that damage liver cells, leading to cirrhosis.

mistakes.w: Carbon monoxide blocks the arteries.
mistakes.r: Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin so blood carries less oxygen; chemicals damaging the artery lining cause fatty deposits.

mistakes.w: Tar causes heart disease.
mistakes.r: Tar contains carcinogens and mainly causes lung cancer and lung damage; heart disease is linked to nicotine, carbon monoxide and artery-damaging chemicals.

mistakes.w: The graph proves that eating fat causes heart disease.
mistakes.r: The graph shows a correlation; to prove cause you need a mechanism and must control other variables.

mistakes.w: Exercise stops you getting heart disease.
mistakes.r: Regular exercise reduces the risk of heart disease (it lowers blood pressure and helps prevent obesity), but does not guarantee you will not get it.

mistakes.w: National effect: people feel ill.
mistakes.r: National effects are about the whole country, e.g. cost to the NHS, fewer people working, money spent on campaigns.

exam.q: State what is meant by a non-communicable disease.
model: a disease that cannot be passed / transmitted from one person to another
exam.tip: Use the word 'transmitted'.

exam.q: Give two non-communicable diseases that are caused by an interaction of factors.
model: any two from: cardiovascular disease / heart disease / stroke; (many forms of) cancer; lung disease (from smoking); liver disease / cirrhosis; type 2 diabetes
exam.tip: Pick from the spec list.

exam.q: Explain what is meant by a risk factor.
model: something that increases the chance / likelihood of developing a disease
but does not mean the person will definitely get the disease
exam.tip: Probability language: 'increases the chance'.

exam.q: Explain how a lack of exercise and a high energy diet can lead to obesity.
model: more energy taken in than is used
lack of exercise means less energy used
excess energy stored as fat (over a long time) leading to obesity
exam.tip: Talk about energy in versus energy out.

exam.q: Describe how drinking large amounts of alcohol over many years can cause liver disease.
model: liver breaks down alcohol / alcohol is toxic
liver cells are damaged / die
scar tissue forms / cirrhosis so the liver cannot function (properly)
exam.tip: Name cirrhosis.

exam.q: Explain how smoking increases the risk of cardiovascular disease.
model: chemicals in smoke damage the lining of arteries
fatty deposits build up / artery narrows
nicotine increases heart rate / blood pressure
carbon monoxide reduces oxygen carried by blood / binds haemoglobin
less blood/oxygen to heart muscle / blood clots form, causing heart attack / stroke
exam.tip: Any four. Separate effects of nicotine and carbon monoxide.

exam.q: A study found that people who smoked more cigarettes per day had a higher rate of heart disease. Explain why this does not prove that smoking causes heart disease.
model: it shows a correlation / link only
other factors (e.g. diet, exercise, alcohol, genes) may be involved / need a mechanism to show cause
exam.tip: Mention correlation and other variables.

exam.q: Explain why malnutrition can include people who are obese.
model: malnutrition is a diet without the right balance of nutrients
obesity results from taking in too much energy / too much fat or sugar
exam.tip: Define malnutrition first.

exam.q: Describe the effects of obesity at local, national and global levels.
model: local/individual: increased risk of type 2 diabetes / CVD / reduced quality of life / shorter life
local: family may need to care for them / lost income
local: more pressure on GPs / local hospitals
national: high cost to the NHS of treatment
national: fewer people working / lost productivity / government spends on campaigns or taxes
global: rates of obesity rising in many countries / NCDs cause most deaths worldwide
global: some countries have both obesity and undernutrition / fewer resources for treatment
exam.tip: Give at least two points for each level and label each level clearly.

exam.q: Give two ways a person can reduce their risk of cardiovascular disease by changing their lifestyle.
model: any two from: stop smoking; eat less saturated fat / salt; exercise regularly; drink less alcohol; lose weight / keep a healthy BMI
exam.tip: Lifestyle changes only: not 'change your genes'.

exam.q: Explain why the risk of type 2 diabetes is higher in a person who is obese, eats a poor diet and does little exercise than in a person with only one of these factors.
model: non-communicable diseases are caused by an interaction of factors
the factors add together / reinforce each other (e.g. poor diet and little exercise both increase obesity), so combined risk is greater
exam.tip: Use the word 'interaction'.

worked.q: Calculate the BMI of a person with mass 102 kg and height 1.80 m, and state whether they are obese (obese = BMI of 30 or more).
steps: BMI = mass (kg) / height (m)^2
31.5 is 30 or more, so the person is classed as obese.
worked.ans: BMI = 31.5; the person is obese, which increases their risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

worked.q: In a country, the percentage of adults who smoke fell from 27% to 14%, while deaths from heart disease fell by 40%. A student says this proves stopping smoking caused the fall. Evaluate this claim.
steps: There is a correlation: as smoking fell, heart disease deaths fell.
There is a known mechanism (chemicals in smoke damage arteries, nicotine raises blood pressure), which supports a causal link.
But other factors changed over the same period: better treatments (statins, stents), changes in diet, more awareness of blood pressure.
So smoking is likely to be one of several interacting factors.
worked.ans: The data support the idea that reduced smoking contributed, but they do not prove it was the only cause because other factors also changed; the fall is likely due to several factors together.

worked.q: A 55-year-old man smokes, drinks heavily, is overweight and has a father who had a heart attack. Identify which of his risk factors for cardiovascular disease he can change and explain why his risk is high.
steps: Lifestyle (changeable): smoking, heavy drinking, being overweight (through diet and exercise).
Not changeable: age (55), genes (family history).
He has many risk factors, and non-communicable diseases are caused by the interaction of several factors, so his combined risk is very high.
Stopping smoking, reducing alcohol, eating a healthier diet and exercising would reduce his risk.
worked.ans: He can change smoking, alcohol and his weight; he cannot change age or genes. With several interacting factors his risk is high, but lifestyle changes would lower it.

bio_edx.4.18.summary: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) can be treated by lifestyle changes, life-long medication or surgical procedures, and each has benefits and drawbacks that you must be able to weigh up. Lifestyle changes are cheap with no side effects but act slowly; medicines such as statins, anticoagulants and antihypertensives reduce risk but must be taken for life and have side effects; surgery such as stents, bypass operations and transplants act quickly on serious blockages but carry the risks of surgery. Evaluate by comparing effectiveness, speed, risk, side effects and cost, then reach a justified conclusion.

core.p: **Cardiovascular disease** affects the heart and blood vessels. In coronary heart disease, **fatty deposits (plaques)** build up in the **coronary arteries**, narrowing them and reducing blood and **oxygen** supply to the heart muscle. Blood clots can form on plaques and block arteries, causing a **heart attack** or **stroke**.
bullets: Main problems treatments target: **narrowed arteries**, **high blood cholesterol**, **high blood pressure**, **blood clots**, and a **failing heart**.
Treatments either **lower the risk** of further damage (lifestyle, medication) or **fix the damage directly** (surgery).
The spec groups treatments as **life-long medication**, **surgical procedures** and **lifestyle changes**.
'Evaluate' means give **advantages and disadvantages** and reach a **justified conclusion**.

callouts.p: A non-communicable disease of the heart or blood vessels, such as coronary heart disease or stroke.

core.p: Often the **first treatment** recommended, and used alongside other treatments. They tackle the **causes**: high cholesterol, high blood pressure and obesity.
bullets: **Stop smoking**: removes chemicals that damage artery linings; lowers heart rate and blood pressure; carbon monoxide no longer reduces oxygen carried.
**Eat a balanced diet** low in **saturated fat** (lowers cholesterol) and **salt** (lowers blood pressure).
**Exercise regularly**: lowers blood pressure, strengthens the heart, helps lose weight.
**Lose weight** if obese and **cut down alcohol**.

core.p: Lifestyle changes are cheap and safe, but they rely on the patient and work slowly.
bullets: **Advantages**: **no side effects**, **cheap** or free, no surgery risk, also reduce the risk of **other diseases** (type 2 diabetes, some cancers).
**Disadvantages**: **slow** to have an effect; need **willpower** so people may not stick to them; may **not be enough** if arteries are already badly narrowed.
Best for: people at **risk** or with **mild** disease, and alongside medicines or surgery for everyone.

callouts.p: Lifestyle changes are usually tried first because they have no side effects and low cost.

core.p: **Statins** reduce the amount of **cholesterol** in the blood (they reduce the liver's production of cholesterol).
bullets: Lower blood cholesterol means **fatty deposits build up more slowly** in arteries.
This **reduces the risk** of coronary heart disease, heart attack and stroke.
Advantages: effective at lowering cholesterol; **cheap**; no surgery; can be prescribed to people at risk before disease is severe.

Disadvantages: must be taken **every day for life**; **side effects** in some people (e.g. muscle pain, headaches, rarely liver damage); take time to have an effect; do not remove deposits already there.

core.p: **Anticoagulants** (e.g. **warfarin**, **heparin**) make the blood **less likely to clot**.
bullets: Fewer clots means less chance of a clot **blocking a coronary artery** (heart attack) or an artery in the brain (**stroke**).
Often given after a stent is fitted or after a heart attack.
Advantages: reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke; no surgery.
Disadvantages: risk of **excessive bleeding**, e.g. from small cuts or internal bleeding; dose must be monitored with regular blood tests; taken for life.
**Aspirin** is also used to reduce blood clotting.

callouts.p: Anticoagulants reduce blood clotting; statins reduce cholesterol; antihypertensives reduce blood pressure.

core.p: **Antihypertensives** **lower blood pressure** (hypertension = high blood pressure).
bullets: High blood pressure **damages artery walls**, making fatty deposits more likely, and makes the heart work harder.
Lowering blood pressure reduces the risk of **damage to arteries**, heart attack, stroke and kidney damage.
Advantages: effective, no surgery, cheap.
Disadvantages: taken **for life**; side effects such as **headaches**, **dizziness** (blood pressure too low) and tiredness.

head: Medicine
What it does
Main drawback
rows: Lower blood cholesterol, slow fatty deposits
Life-long; side effects e.g. muscle pain

callouts.p: All three must be taken for life, have possible side effects, and reduce risk rather than repair existing damage. But they avoid the risks of surgery.

core.p: A **stent** is a small **mesh tube** placed inside a narrowed coronary artery to **hold it open**.
bullets: A **catheter** with a deflated **balloon** and the stent is fed through an artery (from the groin or arm) to the narrowed section.
The **balloon is inflated**, squashing the fatty deposit against the wall and opening the stent.
The balloon is removed; the stent **stays in place** keeping the artery **open**.
Blood (and oxygen) can now flow to the heart muscle.
Advantages: **immediate** improvement; **minor** operation, often under **local anaesthetic**; **quick recovery** (often home in a day or two); lower risk than bypass.

Disadvantages: risk of **blood clots** forming on the stent (patient given anticoagulants); artery can **narrow again**; small risk of infection or damage to the artery; does not stop the disease elsewhere.

fig.cap: A catheter carries a balloon and mesh stent to the narrowed coronary artery. Inflating the balloon squashes the plaque and opens the stent, which stays in place to hold the artery open so blood flows freely.

core.p: In a **coronary bypass** operation, a healthy **blood vessel** (often a **vein from the leg** or an **artery from the chest**) is **grafted** onto the coronary artery so blood flows **around the blockage**.
bullets: Blood now reaches the heart muscle beyond the blocked section.
Can bypass **several** blocked arteries in one operation.
Advantages: **long-lasting**; works when arteries are too badly blocked for stents.
Disadvantages: **major surgery** (chest opened) under **general anaesthetic**; **long recovery** time; risks of **infection**, **bleeding**, blood clots and even **death**; expensive.
The grafted vessel can also become blocked over time if lifestyle does not change.

fig.cap: In a bypass a vein or artery taken from elsewhere is grafted above and below the blocked section of coronary artery, so blood flows around the blockage and the heart muscle gets oxygen again.

core.p: If the heart is **failing** badly, the whole heart (sometimes heart and lungs) may be **replaced** with one from a **donor** who has died.
bullets: Advantages: can save the life of someone whose heart cannot be treated any other way.
Disadvantages: **shortage of donors**, so long waiting lists; **major surgery** with high risks.
The immune system may **reject** the new heart (it has foreign antigens), so the patient must take **immunosuppressant drugs for life**.
Immunosuppressants increase the risk of **infections**.
**Faulty valves** can also be replaced (with mechanical or biological valves) to keep blood flowing in the right direction.

core.p: Use a table to organise an evaluation answer.
bullets: Lifestyle and medication **reduce risk**; surgery **repairs** existing blockage.
Surgery works **fastest** but has the **greatest risk** and **cost**.
Medication has **side effects** and must be taken **for life**.
Lifestyle changes have **no side effects** but depend on the **patient** and are **slow**.
In practice doctors **combine** them: e.g. stent + anticoagulants + statins + lifestyle changes.

core.h: How to write a top-grade evaluation
core.p: Evaluate questions (often 6 marks) are marked by levels. Top-level answers **compare** treatments, link each point to the **patient's situation**, and finish with a **justified conclusion**.
bullets: Give **advantages and disadvantages** of **each** treatment named in the question.
Explain **why** (e.g. 'stent: quick recovery **because** it is fitted through a catheter, not open-heart surgery').
Use any **data** given (e.g. % reduction in risk, cost, recovery time, side effect rates) and quote numbers.
Consider the **patient**: age, how severe the blockage is, other health problems, willingness to change lifestyle.
End with a **conclusion**: which treatment is best for this patient, and why.

callouts.p: A list of facts without comparison and conclusion stays in the middle band. Use words like 'however', 'whereas', 'therefore'.

analogy.t: Fixing a clogging pipe in a house
analogy.p: Coronary heart disease is like a water pipe slowly clogging with grease. Lifestyle changes are like no longer pouring fat down the sink: cheap and safe but slow, and the existing clog stays. Medication is like adding a cleaner every day for ever: it stops more grease sticking (statins), keeps the water thin so lumps do not block it (anticoagulants) and lowers the water pressure (antihypertensives). A stent is like pushing a sleeve into the pipe to hold it open; a bypass is plumbing in a new section of pipe around the clog; a transplant is replacing the whole pump. Where it breaks down: arteries are living tissue that can react, clot and reject new parts, and patients get side effects, which pipes do not.

terms.d: A disease of the heart or blood vessels, such as coronary heart disease, heart attack or stroke.
Arteries that supply the heart muscle with oxygenated blood.
Build-up of fat and cholesterol in the wall of an artery, narrowing the lumen.
Drugs that reduce blood cholesterol levels, slowing the build-up of fatty deposits in arteries.
A drug (e.g. warfarin, heparin) that reduces blood clotting, lowering the risk of heart attack and stroke.
A drug that lowers blood pressure.
High blood pressure.
A mesh tube inserted into a narrowed artery to hold it open so blood can flow.
A thin tube fed through a blood vessel to carry a stent and balloon to the narrowed artery.
Surgery in which a blood vessel from elsewhere in the body is grafted to carry blood around a blocked coronary artery.
Surgery to replace a failing heart with a healthy heart from a donor.
When the immune system attacks a transplanted organ because it has foreign antigens.
A drug that reduces the activity of the immune system to prevent rejection of a transplant.
An unwanted effect of a medicine or treatment.
Medicine that must be taken every day for the rest of the patient's life to keep its benefit.

mistakes.w: Statins thin the blood.
mistakes.r: Statins lower blood cholesterol; anticoagulants reduce blood clotting.

mistakes.w: A stent removes the fatty deposit.
mistakes.r: A stent holds the artery open; the balloon squashes the deposit against the artery wall, it is not removed.

mistakes.w: Bypass surgery unblocks the artery.
mistakes.r: A bypass grafts a new blood vessel so blood flows around the blockage; the blockage stays.

mistakes.w: Medication cures CVD.
mistakes.r: Medication reduces the risk of further damage and must be taken for life; it does not repair existing damage.

mistakes.w: Lifestyle changes have no disadvantages.
mistakes.r: They have no side effects but are slow, depend on willpower and may not be enough for severe disease.

mistakes.w: Stents are major open-heart surgery.
mistakes.r: Stents are inserted through a catheter, usually under local anaesthetic, with quick recovery; bypass is major surgery.

mistakes.w: Anticoagulants are safe with no risks.
mistakes.r: Anticoagulants can cause excessive bleeding.

mistakes.w: Evaluation answer lists facts with no conclusion.
mistakes.r: Compare advantages and disadvantages and give a justified conclusion about the best treatment for the patient.

exam.q: State what statins do.
model: reduce (blood) cholesterol (levels)
exam.tip: Cholesterol, not 'fat in arteries'.

exam.q: Give one disadvantage of taking anticoagulants.
model: risk of excessive bleeding / blood does not clot (e.g. after a cut)
exam.tip: Link to the effect of the drug.

exam.q: Name the type of drug used to reduce high blood pressure.
model: antihypertensive(s)
exam.tip: Hypertension = high blood pressure.

exam.q: Explain how statins reduce the risk of a heart attack.
model: statins reduce cholesterol in the blood
so fewer fatty deposits / plaques form in (coronary) arteries
arteries less narrowed so blood / oxygen supply to heart muscle maintained (less risk of clot / blockage)
exam.tip: Follow the chain: cholesterol, deposits, blood flow.

exam.q: Describe how a stent is used to treat coronary heart disease.
model: (mesh) stent inserted via catheter into the narrowed (coronary) artery
balloon inflated to widen artery / push fatty deposit against wall
stent left to hold artery open so blood flows to heart muscle
exam.tip: Say what keeps the artery open after the balloon is removed.

exam.q: Explain why a patient who has had a stent fitted is often given anticoagulants.
model: blood clots can form on / around the stent
anticoagulants reduce clotting so the artery does not become blocked again
exam.tip: Two linked points.

exam.q: Give two advantages of fitting a stent compared with coronary bypass surgery.
model: any two from: less invasive / minor surgery / local anaesthetic; quicker recovery / shorter hospital stay; lower risk of infection / death; cheaper
exam.tip: Comparative answers: use 'quicker', 'lower risk'.

exam.q: Explain why a heart transplant patient must take drugs for the rest of their life.
model: the immune system recognises the donor heart as foreign / has different antigens and may reject it
immunosuppressant drugs are needed to prevent rejection
exam.tip: Name rejection and immunosuppressants.

exam.q: Suggest why doctors often recommend lifestyle changes before prescribing medication.
model: lifestyle changes have no side effects / cheap
may reduce risk enough (lower cholesterol / blood pressure) so medication not needed / also reduce risk of other diseases
exam.tip: Give a reason and a benefit.

exam.q: A 70-year-old man has two badly narrowed coronary arteries. He has high cholesterol and smokes. Evaluate the treatments available to him.
model: lifestyle: stopping smoking / healthier diet reduces further damage, no side effects, but slow and arteries already badly narrowed so not enough alone
statins lower cholesterol so slow further deposits, but life-long and side effects
anticoagulants reduce clot risk but risk of bleeding
stents: quick improvement, minor procedure, quick recovery (suitable for older patient), but artery may narrow again / clots
bypass: long-lasting and can treat two blockages, but major surgery / general anaesthetic / higher risk at age 70 / long recovery
conclusion: e.g. stents plus statins, anticoagulants and stopping smoking, because quick with low surgical risk
exam.tip: Apply to this patient (age, two arteries, smoker) and give a justified conclusion.

exam.q: Compare the use of life-long medication and surgery to treat cardiovascular disease.
model: medication avoids risks of surgery / no anaesthetic or infection risk
but medication must be taken for life / side effects
surgery (stent or bypass) gives an immediate / direct improvement in blood flow
but surgery has risks (infection, bleeding, death) / recovery time / more expensive
exam.tip: Compare means each point should mention both treatments.

worked.q: A patient has to choose between bypass surgery and a stent. Data: bypass hospital stay 7 days, risk of death 2%, artery re-narrows within 5 years in 10% of patients; stent hospital stay 1 day, risk of death 0.5%, re-narrowing in 25% of patients. Use the data to evaluate the two treatments.
steps: Recovery: stent stay is 1 day vs 7 days, so 6 days shorter (7 times shorter).
Immediate risk: stent risk of death 0.5% vs 2% for bypass, so bypass is 4 times riskier.
Long-term: re-narrowing 25% for stent vs 10% for bypass, so stent is 2.5 times more likely to need further treatment.
Weigh up: stent is safer and quicker in the short term; bypass is more long-lasting.
worked.ans: A stent is the better choice for most patients because it has a 4 times lower risk of death and a much shorter hospital stay, but a bypass may be better for a younger, fit patient because it is 2.5 times less likely to re-narrow.

worked.q: A woman has high blood pressure and high cholesterol but her arteries are only slightly narrowed. Suggest and justify a treatment plan.
steps: Arteries only slightly narrowed, so surgery is not needed and its risks are not justified.
Start with lifestyle changes: less salt (lowers blood pressure), less saturated fat (lowers cholesterol), more exercise, lose weight.
If levels remain high, prescribe antihypertensives and statins.
Explain trade-off: medication works well but must be taken for life with possible side effects.
worked.ans: Lifestyle changes first because they are cheap with no side effects and her disease is mild; add antihypertensives and statins if needed; avoid surgery as the risks outweigh the benefits.

worked.q: A drug trial gave 4000 people a statin and 4000 a placebo. Over 5 years 120 statin users and 200 placebo users had a heart attack. Calculate the percentage reduction in heart attacks and comment.
steps: Rate with placebo = 200 / 4000 x 100 = 5%.
Rate with statin = 120 / 4000 x 100 = 3%.
Percentage reduction = (200 - 120) / 200 x 100 = 40%.
Comment: large sample and placebo control make the result reliable; but statins still did not prevent all heart attacks and side effects must be considered.
worked.ans: Heart attacks were reduced by 40% (from 5% to 3%), showing statins are effective, though not every heart attack is prevented and they must be taken long-term.
